This article is about the Soviet dog. For the Greek genre of music, see [Laïko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La%C3%AFko "Laïko"). For other uses, see [Laika (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika_(disambiguation) "Laika (disambiguation)").

Laika[![Image 1: A photo of Laika taken in 1957](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Laika_in_1957.jpg/330px-Laika_in_1957.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Laika_in_1957.jpg)

[Species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species "Species")_[Canis familiaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canis\_familiaris "Canis familiaris")_
[Breed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breed "Breed")[Mongrel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongrel "Mongrel"), possibly part-[husky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husky "Husky") (or part-[Samoyed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samoyed_(dog) "Samoyed (dog)")) and part-[terrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrier "Terrier")

**Laika** ( [_LY-kə_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); Russian: Лáйка, IPA:[[ˈlajkə]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Russian "Help:IPA/Russian"); c. 1954 – 3 November 1957) was a [Soviet space dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_space_dog "Soviet space dog") who was one of the first [animals in space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animals_in_space "Animals in space") and the first to [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit "Orbit") the Earth. A [stray mongrel from the streets of Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_dogs_in_Moscow "Street dogs in Moscow"), she flew aboard the [Sputnik 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_2 "Sputnik 2") spacecraft, launched into [low orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit") on 3 November 1957. As the technology to [re-enter the atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_entry "Atmospheric entry") had not yet been developed, Laika's survival was never expected. She died by [overheating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperthermia "Hyperthermia") hours into the flight, on the craft's fourth orbit.

Little was known about the effects of [spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceflight "Spaceflight") on living creatures at the time of Laika's mission, and animal flights were viewed by engineers as a necessary precursor to [human missions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_spaceflight "Human spaceflight").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-RussiaOpensMonument-1) The experiment, which monitored Laika's vital signs, aimed to prove that a living organism could survive being launched into orbit and continue to function under conditions of [weakened gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") and increased radiation, providing scientists with some of the first data on the [biological effects of spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_effects_of_spaceflight "Biological effects of spaceflight").

Laika's death was possibly caused by a failure of the central [R‑7 sustainer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R-7_Semyorka "R-7 Semyorka") to separate from the payload: this affected the thermal control mechanisms, which then caused the cabin to overheat. The true cause and time of her death were not made public until 2002; instead, it was widely reported that she died when her oxygen ran out on day six or, as the Soviet government initially claimed, she was [euthanised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euthanised "Euthanised") prior to [oxygen depletion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_depletion "Oxygen depletion"). In 2008, a small monument to Laika depicting her standing atop a rocket was unveiled near the military research facility in Moscow that prepared her flight. She also appears on the _[Monument to the Conquerors of Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument\_to\_the\_Conquerors\_of\_Space "Monument to the Conquerors of Space")_ in Moscow. [Korabl-Sputnik 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korabl-Sputnik_2 "Korabl-Sputnik 2") returned the first animals from orbit safely in 1960, dogs [Belka and Strelka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belka_and_Strelka "Belka and Strelka"), testing the crewed [Vostok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_(spacecraft) "Vostok (spacecraft)") craft.

## Sputnik 2

After the success of [Sputnik 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_1 "Sputnik 1") in October 1957, [Nikita Khrushchev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev "Nikita Khrushchev"), leader of the Soviet Union, wanted a spacecraft launched on 7 November 1957 to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the [October Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution "October Revolution").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChertok2006387-2) Khrushchev specifically wanted to deliver a "space spectacular", a mission that would repeat the triumph of Sputnik 1, stunning the world with Soviet prowess.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AJL-3)

While construction had already started on [Sputnik 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_3 "Sputnik 3"), a more sophisticated satellite, it would not be ready until December. To meet the November deadline, a new simple satellite would need to be built.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NASA3-4)[Sergei Korolev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Korolev "Sergei Korolev") proposed that a dog be placed in the satellite, an idea which was quickly adopted by planners.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChertok2006388-5) Soviet rocket engineers had long intended a canine orbit before attempting human spaceflight; since 1951, they had lofted 12 dogs into sub-orbital space on ballistic flights, working gradually toward an orbital mission set for some time in 1958. To satisfy Khrushchev's demands, they expedited the orbital canine flight for the November launch.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AJL-3)

According to Russian sources, the official decision to launch Sputnik 2 was made on 10 or 12 October, leaving less than four weeks to design and build the spacecraft.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AZ-6) Sputnik 2, therefore, was something of a rushed job, with most elements of the spacecraft being constructed from rough sketches. Aside from the primary mission of sending a living passenger into space, Sputnik 2 also contained instrumentation for measuring [solar irradiance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_irradiance "Solar irradiance") and [cosmic rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray "Cosmic ray").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NASA3-4)

The craft was equipped with a life-support system consisting of an [oxygen generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_generator "Oxygen generator") and devices to avoid [oxygen poisoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_poisoning "Oxygen poisoning") and to absorb [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide"). A fan, designed to activate whenever the cabin temperature exceeded 15°C (59°F), was added to keep the dog cool. Enough food (in a gelatinous form) was provided for a seven-day flight, and the dog was fitted with a bag to collect waste. A [harness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_harness "Dog harness") was designed to be fitted to the dog, and there were chains to restrict her movements to standing, sitting, or lying down; there was no room to turn around in the cabin. An [electrocardiogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrocardiogram "Electrocardiogram") monitored heart rate and further instrumentation tracked respiration rate, maximum arterial pressure, and the dog's movements.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-DM-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-SPUT1-8)

## Training

Laika was found as a [stray dog wandering the streets of Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_dogs_in_Moscow "Street dogs in Moscow").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AJL-3) Soviet scientists chose to use Moscow strays since they assumed that such animals had already learned to endure conditions of extreme cold and hunger.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AJL-3) She was a 5 kg (11 lb)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-laika-9)[mongrel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongrel "Mongrel") female, approximately three years old. Another account reported that she weighed about 6 kg (13 lb).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AJL-3) Soviet personnel gave her several names and nicknames, among them **Kudryavka** (Russian for _Little Curly_), **Zhuchka** (_Little Bug_), and **Limonchik** (_Little Lemon_).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-10) Laika, the Russian name for several [breeds of dogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika_(dog_breed) "Laika (dog breed)") similar to the [husky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husky "Husky"), was the name popularised around the world. Its literal translation would be "Barker", from the Russian verb "layat" (_лаять_), "to bark".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11) According to some accounts, the technicians actually renamed her from Kudryavka to Laika owing to her loud barking.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-12) The American press dubbed her Muttnik (_[mutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongrel "Mongrel")_ + suffix _[-nik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/-nik "-nik")_) as a pun on [Sputnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_program "Sputnik program"),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NASA-13) or referred to her as _Curly_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-BL-14) Her true pedigree is unknown, although it is generally accepted that she was part husky or other Nordic breed, and possibly part [terrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrier "Terrier").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AJL-3) NASA refers to Laika as a "part-[Samoyed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samoyed_(dog) "Samoyed (dog)") terrier".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-Sputnik2-15) A Russian magazine described her temperament as [phlegmatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phlegmatic "Phlegmatic"), saying that she did not quarrel with other dogs.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-laika-9)

The Soviet Union and United States had previously sent animals only on [sub-orbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-orbital_spaceflight "Sub-orbital spaceflight") flights.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-STO-16) Three dogs were trained for the Sputnik 2 flight: [Albina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_space_dogs#Albina_and_Tsyganka "Soviet space dogs"), [Mushka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mushka "Mushka"), and Laika.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-BBC-17) Soviet space-life scientists [Vladimir Yazdovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Yazdovsky "Vladimir Yazdovsky") and [Oleg Gazenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleg_Gazenko "Oleg Gazenko") trained the dogs.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NLM-18)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11)

To adapt the dogs to the confines of the tiny cabin of Sputnik 2, they were kept in progressively smaller cages for periods of up to twenty days. The extensive close confinement caused them to stop urinating or defecating, made them restless, and caused their general condition to deteriorate. [Laxatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laxatives "Laxatives") did not improve their condition, and the researchers found that only long periods of training proved effective. The dogs were placed in [centrifuges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrifuge "Centrifuge") that simulated the acceleration of a rocket launch and were placed in machines that simulated the noises of the spacecraft. This caused their pulses to double and their [blood pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_pressure "Blood pressure") to increase by 30–65 [torrs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torr "Torr") (4.0–8.7[kPa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)")). The dogs were trained to eat a special high-nutrition gel that would be their food in space. It was made up of 40% [bread crumbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadcrumbs "Breadcrumbs"), 40% [powdered meat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meat "Meat") and 20% [beef fat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beef_fat "Beef fat") mixed with [agar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agar "Agar") and water. Presumably the formula was 200 mL (7.0 imp fl oz) of water, agar, and 100 g (3.5 oz) of food.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-SPUT1-8)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11)

Ten days before the launch, Vladimir Yazdovsky chose Laika to be the primary flight dog.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChertok2006396-19) Before the launch, Yazdovsky took Laika home to play with his children. In a book chronicling the story of Soviet space medicine, he wrote, "Laika was quiet and charming... I wanted to do something nice for her: She had so little time left to live."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-APSTAT-20)

## Preflight preparations

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/%D0%9B%D0%B0%D0%B9%D0%BA%D0%B0_%28%D1%81%D0%BE%D0%B1%D0%B0%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%BA%D0%BE%D1%81%D0%BC%D0%BE%D0%BD%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%82%291.jpg/250px-%D0%9B%D0%B0%D0%B9%D0%BA%D0%B0_%28%D1%81%D0%BE%D0%B1%D0%B0%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%BA%D0%BE%D1%81%D0%BC%D0%BE%D0%BD%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%82%291.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%D0%9B%D0%B0%D0%B9%D0%BA%D0%B0_(%D1%81%D0%BE%D0%B1%D0%B0%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%BA%D0%BE%D1%81%D0%BC%D0%BE%D0%BD%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%82)1.jpg)

Laika in a mock cockpit

Yazdovsky made the final selection of dogs and their designated roles. Laika was to be the "flight dog"– a sacrifice to science on a one-way mission to space.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-russianspaceweb1-21) Albina, who had already flown twice on a high-altitude test [rocket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocket "Rocket"), was to act as Laika's backup. She was not sent as the primary due to Albina recently giving birth to three pups, and thus Yazdovsky thought it cruel to send Albina as the primary and separate a mother from her children.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11) The third dog, Mushka, was a "[control dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_control "Scientific control")"– she was to stay on the ground and be used to test instrumentation and [life support](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_support "Life support").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-SPUT1-8)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-STO-16)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11)

Before leaving for the [Baikonur Cosmodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikonur_Cosmodrome "Baikonur Cosmodrome"), Yazdovsky and Gazenko conducted surgery on the dogs, routing the cables from the transmitters to the sensors that would measure breathing, pulse, and blood pressure.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiddiqi2000173-22)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11)

Because the existing airstrip at [Turatam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turatam "Turatam") near the cosmodrome was small, the dogs and crew had to be first flown aboard a [Tu‑104](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tu-104 "Tu-104") plane to [Tashkent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tashkent "Tashkent"). From there, a smaller and lighter [Il‑14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilyushin_Il-14 "Ilyushin Il-14") plane took them to Turatam. Training of dogs continued upon arrival; one after another they were placed in the capsules to get familiar with the feeding system.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-russianspaceweb1-21)

According to a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") document, Laika was placed in the capsule of the satellite on 31 October 1957– three days before the start of the mission.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-SPUT1-8) At that time of year, the temperatures at the launch site were extremely low, and a hose connected to a heater was used to keep her container warm. Two assistants were assigned to keep a constant watch on Laika before launch. Just prior to liftoff on 3 November 1957, from Baikonur Cosmodrome, Laika's fur was sponged in a weak [ethanol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethanol "Ethanol") solution and carefully groomed, while [iodine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iodine "Iodine") was painted onto the areas where sensors would be placed to monitor her bodily functions.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-LM-23)

One of the technicians preparing the capsule before final lift-off stated: "After placing Laika in the container and before closing the hatch, we kissed her nose and wished her bon voyage, knowing that she would not survive the flight."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-russianspaceweb1-21)

## Voyage

Accounts of the time of launch vary from source to source, given as 05:30:42 or 07:22 [Moscow Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_Time "Moscow Time").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-russianspaceweb1-21)

At peak acceleration, Laika's respiration increased to between three and four times the pre-launch rate.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-SPUT1-8) The sensors showed her heart rate was 103 beats/min before launch and increased to 240 beats/min during the early acceleration. After reaching orbit, Sputnik 2's [nose cone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nose_cone "Nose cone") was jettisoned successfully; however, the "Block A" core did not separate as planned, preventing the thermal control system from operating correctly. Some of the [thermal insulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_insulation "Thermal insulation") tore loose, raising the cabin temperature to 40°C (104°F).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-Sputnik2-15) After three hours of [weightlessness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlessness "Weightlessness"), Laika's pulse rate had settled back to 102 beats/min,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-JAP-24) three times longer than it had taken during earlier ground tests, an indication of the stress she was under. The early [telemetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telemetry "Telemetry") indicated that Laika was agitated but eating her food.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-Sputnik2-15) After approximately five to seven hours into the flight, no further signs of life were received from the spacecraft.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-SPUT1-8)

The Soviet scientists had planned to euthanise Laika with a serving of poisoned food. For many years, the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") gave conflicting statements that she had died either from [asphyxia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asphyxia "Asphyxia"),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-Beischer1962-25) when the batteries failed, or that she had been euthanised. Many rumours circulated about the exact manner of her death. In 1999, several Russian sources reported that Laika had died when the cabin overheated on the fourth day.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AZ-6) In October 2002, Dimitri Malashenkov, one of the scientists behind the Sputnik 2 mission, revealed that Laika had died by the fourth circuit[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-26) of flight from overheating. According to a paper he presented to the [World Space Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Space_Congress "World Space Congress") in [Houston, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston"), "It turned out that it was practically impossible to create a reliable temperature control system in such limited time constraints."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-DM-7)

Over five months later, after 2,570 orbits, Sputnik 2 disintegrated during re-entry on 14 April 1958.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-MA-27)

## Ethics of animal testing

Due to the overshadowing issue of the Soviet–U.S. [Space Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Race "Space Race"), the ethical issues raised by this experiment, which were a matter of concern in the west,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11) went largely unaddressed for some time. As newspaper clippings from 1957 show, the press was initially focused on reporting the political perspective, while Laika's health and retrieval– or lack thereof– only became an issue later.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-45YRSLATER-28)

Sputnik 2 was not designed to be retrievable, and it had always been accepted that Laika would die.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AZ-6)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11) The mission sparked a debate across the globe on the [mistreatment of animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistreatment_of_animals "Mistreatment of animals") and [animal testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_testing "Animal testing") in general to advance science.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NLM-18) In the United Kingdom, the [National Canine Defence League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dogs_Trust "Dogs Trust") called on all dog owners to observe a minute's silence on each day Laika remained in space, while the [Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society_for_the_Prevention_of_Cruelty_to_Animals "Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals") (RSPCA) received protests even before [Radio Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Moscow "Radio Moscow") had finished announcing the launch. [Animal rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_rights "Animal rights") groups at the time called on members of the public to protest at Soviet embassies.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-BBCold-29) In the U.S., people demonstrated outside the United Nations in New York,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NLM-18) and laboratory researchers offered some support for the Soviets, at least before the news of Laika's death.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NLM-18)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NSMR-30)

In [Warsaw Pact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact "Warsaw Pact") countries, open criticism of the Soviet space program was difficult because of political censorship, but there were notable cases of criticism in Polish scientific circles. A Polish scientific periodical, _Kto, Kiedy, Dlaczego_ ("Who, When, Why"), published in 1958, discussed the mission of Sputnik 2. In the periodical's section dedicated to astronautics, [Krzysztof Boruń](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krzysztof_Boru%C5%84 "Krzysztof Boruń") described the Sputnik 2 mission as "regrettable" and criticised not bringing Laika back to Earth alive as "undoubtedly a great loss for science".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-KKD-31)

In the Soviet Union, there was less controversy. Neither the media, books in the following years, nor the public openly questioned the decision to send a dog into space. In 1998, after the collapse of the Soviet regime, [Oleg Gazenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleg_Gazenko "Oleg Gazenko"), one of the scientists responsible for sending Laika into space, expressed regret for allowing her to die:

> Work with animals is a source of suffering to all of us. We treat them like babies who cannot speak. The more time passes, the more I'm sorry about it. We shouldn't have done it[...] We did not learn enough from this mission to justify the death of the dog.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-MA-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-45YRSLATER-28)

Future space missions carrying dogs would be designed to be recovered; the first successful recovery followed the flight of [Korabl-Sputnik 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korabl-Sputnik_2 "Korabl-Sputnik 2"), wherein the dogs [Belka and Strelka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belka_and_Strelka "Belka and Strelka"), alongside dozens of other organisms, safely returned to Earth.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-32) Nonetheless, four other dogs later died in Soviet space missions: [Bars and Lisichka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_space_dogs#Bars_and_Lisichka "Soviet space dogs") were killed when their R‑7 rocket exploded shortly after launch on 28 July 1960,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiddiqi2000252-33) while [Pchyolka and Mushka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_space_dogs#Pchyolka_and_Mushka "Soviet space dogs") died when [Korabl-Sputnik 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korabl-Sputnik_3 "Korabl-Sputnik 3") suffered an emergency and had to be detonated.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiddiqi2000259-34)

## Tributes

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Posta_Romana_-_1959_-_Laika_120_B.jpg/250px-Posta_Romana_-_1959_-_Laika_120_B.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Posta_Romana_-_1959_-_Laika_120_B.jpg)

"Laika, first traveller into cosmos" stamp issued by [Poșta Română](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Po%C8%99ta_Rom%C3%A2n%C4%83 "Poșta Română") in 1957

Laika is memorialised in the form of a statue and plaque at [Star City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_City,_Russia "Star City, Russia"), the Russian Cosmonaut training facility.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-redOrbit-35) Created in 1997, Laika is positioned behind the cosmonauts with her ears erect.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-redOrbit-35) The [Monument to the Conquerors of Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Conquerors_of_Space "Monument to the Conquerors of Space") in Moscow, constructed in 1964, also includes Laika.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-Telstar-36) On 11 April 2008[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-37) at the military research facility where staff had been responsible for readying Laika for the flight, officials unveiled a monument of her poised on top of a space rocket.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-RussiaOpensMonument-1) Stamps and envelopes picturing Laika were produced, as well as branded cigarettes and matches.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-38)

In 1988 the Spanish band [Mecano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecano "Mecano") released the song ["Laika"](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laika_(Mecano)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Laika (Mecano) (page does not exist)")[[es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika_(canci%C3%B3n_de_Mecano) "es:Laika (canción de Mecano)")] paying tribute to the flight of the dog. The end of the song alludes to Laika's death: "There is one less dog on the Earth / And one more star in the sky".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-39)

[Karl Schroeder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Schroeder "Karl Schroeder") wrote a pessimistic [near future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_future_(fiction) "Near future (fiction)") science fiction novellette _[Laika's Ghost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika%27s\_Ghost "Laika's Ghost")_ with the idea that in the pragmatic world, "only people ready to take up the dream of flight to other worlds are aged remnants of the former Soviet Union".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-40)

The 2007 graphic novel _[Laika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika\_(comics) "Laika (comics)")_ by [Nick Abadzis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Abadzis "Nick Abadzis") won several awards, landing itself on the [YALSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Adult_Library_Services_Association "Young Adult Library Services Association") "Top Ten Great Graphic Novels for Teens"[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-41) and earning multiple [Eisner Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisner_Awards "Eisner Awards"). The book gives a fictionalized account of Laika's life. The story is told from multiple points of view and features politicians, scientists, and engineers.

_[Lajka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lajka "Lajka")_ is a 2017 Czech science fiction comedy animated film inspired by the dog.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-CSFD-42)

Norwegian singer [Emmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_(Norwegian_singer) "Emmy (Norwegian singer)") released a song in 2025 titled "[Laika Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika_Party "Laika Party")" to compete in the [Irish _Eurosong_ selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland_in_the_Eurovision_Song_Contest_2025#Eurosong_2025 "Ireland in the Eurovision Song Contest 2025") for the [2025 Eurovision Song Contest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurovision_Song_Contest_2025 "Eurovision Song Contest 2025"). The song tells a story about the singer wishing that Laika had never died and was living happily in space. Emmy won the selection to represent Ireland at the contest.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-43)

This article is about the Soviet dog. For the Greek genre of music, see [Laïko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La%C3%AFko "Laïko"). For other uses, see [Laika (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika_(disambiguation) "Laika (disambiguation)").

Laika[![Image 1: A photo of Laika taken in 1957](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/Laika_in_1957.jpg/330px-Laika_in_1957.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Laika_in_1957.jpg)
Laika in 1957
Other names Kudryavka (Кудрявка, "Curly")
[Species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species "Species")_[Canis familiaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canis\_familiaris "Canis familiaris")_
[Breed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breed "Breed")[Mongrel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongrel "Mongrel"), possibly part-[husky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husky "Husky") (or part-[Samoyed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samoyed_(dog) "Samoyed (dog)")) and part-[terrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrier "Terrier")
Sex Female
Born Laika (Лайка)

c. 1954

Moscow, [Russian SFSR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_SFSR "Russian SFSR"), Soviet Union
Died 3 November 1957 (aged 2–3)

[Sputnik 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_2 "Sputnik 2"), in [low Earth orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit")
Cause of death[Hyperthermia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperthermia "Hyperthermia") (overheating)
Known for First animal to orbit the Earth
Owner[Soviet space program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_space_program "Soviet space program")
Weight 5 kg (11 lb)

**Laika** ( [_LY-kə_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); Russian: Лáйка, IPA:[[ˈlajkə]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Russian "Help:IPA/Russian"); c. 1954 – 3 November 1957) was a [Soviet space dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_space_dog "Soviet space dog") who was one of the first [animals in space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animals_in_space "Animals in space") and the first to [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit "Orbit") the Earth. A [stray mongrel from the streets of Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_dogs_in_Moscow "Street dogs in Moscow"), she flew aboard the [Sputnik 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_2 "Sputnik 2") spacecraft, launched into [low orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit "Low Earth orbit") on 3 November 1957. As the technology to [re-enter the atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_entry "Atmospheric entry") had not yet been developed, Laika's survival was never expected. She died by [overheating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperthermia "Hyperthermia") hours into the flight, on the craft's fourth orbit.

Little was known about the effects of [spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceflight "Spaceflight") on living creatures at the time of Laika's mission, and animal flights were viewed by engineers as a necessary precursor to [human missions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_spaceflight "Human spaceflight").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-RussiaOpensMonument-1) The experiment, which monitored Laika's vital signs, aimed to prove that a living organism could survive being launched into orbit and continue to function under conditions of [weakened gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") and increased radiation, providing scientists with some of the first data on the [biological effects of spaceflight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_effects_of_spaceflight "Biological effects of spaceflight").

Laika's death was possibly caused by a failure of the central [R‑7 sustainer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R-7_Semyorka "R-7 Semyorka") to separate from the payload: this affected the thermal control mechanisms, which then caused the cabin to overheat. The true cause and time of her death were not made public until 2002; instead, it was widely reported that she died when her oxygen ran out on day six or, as the Soviet government initially claimed, she was [euthanised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euthanised "Euthanised") prior to [oxygen depletion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_depletion "Oxygen depletion"). In 2008, a small monument to Laika depicting her standing atop a rocket was unveiled near the military research facility in Moscow that prepared her flight. She also appears on the _[Monument to the Conquerors of Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument\_to\_the\_Conquerors\_of\_Space "Monument to the Conquerors of Space")_ in Moscow. [Korabl-Sputnik 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korabl-Sputnik_2 "Korabl-Sputnik 2") returned the first animals from orbit safely in 1960, dogs [Belka and Strelka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belka_and_Strelka "Belka and Strelka"), testing the crewed [Vostok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_(spacecraft) "Vostok (spacecraft)") craft.

## Sputnik 2

After the success of [Sputnik 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_1 "Sputnik 1") in October 1957, [Nikita Khrushchev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev "Nikita Khrushchev"), leader of the Soviet Union, wanted a spacecraft launched on 7 November 1957 to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the [October Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution "October Revolution").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChertok2006387-2) Khrushchev specifically wanted to deliver a "space spectacular", a mission that would repeat the triumph of Sputnik 1, stunning the world with Soviet prowess.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AJL-3)

While construction had already started on [Sputnik 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_3 "Sputnik 3"), a more sophisticated satellite, it would not be ready until December. To meet the November deadline, a new simple satellite would need to be built.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NASA3-4)[Sergei Korolev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Korolev "Sergei Korolev") proposed that a dog be placed in the satellite, an idea which was quickly adopted by planners.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChertok2006388-5) Soviet rocket engineers had long intended a canine orbit before attempting human spaceflight; since 1951, they had lofted 12 dogs into sub-orbital space on ballistic flights, working gradually toward an orbital mission set for some time in 1958. To satisfy Khrushchev's demands, they expedited the orbital canine flight for the November launch.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AJL-3)

According to Russian sources, the official decision to launch Sputnik 2 was made on 10 or 12 October, leaving less than four weeks to design and build the spacecraft.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AZ-6) Sputnik 2, therefore, was something of a rushed job, with most elements of the spacecraft being constructed from rough sketches. Aside from the primary mission of sending a living passenger into space, Sputnik 2 also contained instrumentation for measuring [solar irradiance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_irradiance "Solar irradiance") and [cosmic rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray "Cosmic ray").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NASA3-4)

The craft was equipped with a life-support system consisting of an [oxygen generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_generator "Oxygen generator") and devices to avoid [oxygen poisoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_poisoning "Oxygen poisoning") and to absorb [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide"). A fan, designed to activate whenever the cabin temperature exceeded 15°C (59°F), was added to keep the dog cool. Enough food (in a gelatinous form) was provided for a seven-day flight, and the dog was fitted with a bag to collect waste. A [harness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_harness "Dog harness") was designed to be fitted to the dog, and there were chains to restrict her movements to standing, sitting, or lying down; there was no room to turn around in the cabin. An [electrocardiogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrocardiogram "Electrocardiogram") monitored heart rate and further instrumentation tracked respiration rate, maximum arterial pressure, and the dog's movements.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-DM-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-SPUT1-8)

## Training

Laika was found as a [stray dog wandering the streets of Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_dogs_in_Moscow "Street dogs in Moscow").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AJL-3) Soviet scientists chose to use Moscow strays since they assumed that such animals had already learned to endure conditions of extreme cold and hunger.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AJL-3) She was a 5 kg (11 lb)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-laika-9)[mongrel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongrel "Mongrel") female, approximately three years old. Another account reported that she weighed about 6 kg (13 lb).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AJL-3) Soviet personnel gave her several names and nicknames, among them **Kudryavka** (Russian for _Little Curly_), **Zhuchka** (_Little Bug_), and **Limonchik** (_Little Lemon_).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-10) Laika, the Russian name for several [breeds of dogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika_(dog_breed) "Laika (dog breed)") similar to the [husky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husky "Husky"), was the name popularised around the world. Its literal translation would be "Barker", from the Russian verb "layat" (_лаять_), "to bark".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11) According to some accounts, the technicians actually renamed her from Kudryavka to Laika owing to her loud barking.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-12) The American press dubbed her Muttnik (_[mutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongrel "Mongrel")_ + suffix _[-nik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/-nik "-nik")_) as a pun on [Sputnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_program "Sputnik program"),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NASA-13) or referred to her as _Curly_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-BL-14) Her true pedigree is unknown, although it is generally accepted that she was part husky or other Nordic breed, and possibly part [terrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrier "Terrier").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AJL-3) NASA refers to Laika as a "part-[Samoyed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samoyed_(dog) "Samoyed (dog)") terrier".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-Sputnik2-15) A Russian magazine described her temperament as [phlegmatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phlegmatic "Phlegmatic"), saying that she did not quarrel with other dogs.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-laika-9)

The Soviet Union and United States had previously sent animals only on [sub-orbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-orbital_spaceflight "Sub-orbital spaceflight") flights.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-STO-16) Three dogs were trained for the Sputnik 2 flight: [Albina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_space_dogs#Albina_and_Tsyganka "Soviet space dogs"), [Mushka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mushka "Mushka"), and Laika.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-BBC-17) Soviet space-life scientists [Vladimir Yazdovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Yazdovsky "Vladimir Yazdovsky") and [Oleg Gazenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleg_Gazenko "Oleg Gazenko") trained the dogs.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NLM-18)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11)

To adapt the dogs to the confines of the tiny cabin of Sputnik 2, they were kept in progressively smaller cages for periods of up to twenty days. The extensive close confinement caused them to stop urinating or defecating, made them restless, and caused their general condition to deteriorate. [Laxatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laxatives "Laxatives") did not improve their condition, and the researchers found that only long periods of training proved effective. The dogs were placed in [centrifuges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrifuge "Centrifuge") that simulated the acceleration of a rocket launch and were placed in machines that simulated the noises of the spacecraft. This caused their pulses to double and their [blood pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_pressure "Blood pressure") to increase by 30–65 [torrs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torr "Torr") (4.0–8.7[kPa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_(unit) "Pascal (unit)")). The dogs were trained to eat a special high-nutrition gel that would be their food in space. It was made up of 40% [bread crumbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadcrumbs "Breadcrumbs"), 40% [powdered meat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meat "Meat") and 20% [beef fat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beef_fat "Beef fat") mixed with [agar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agar "Agar") and water. Presumably the formula was 200 mL (7.0 imp fl oz) of water, agar, and 100 g (3.5 oz) of food.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-SPUT1-8)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11)

Ten days before the launch, Vladimir Yazdovsky chose Laika to be the primary flight dog.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChertok2006396-19) Before the launch, Yazdovsky took Laika home to play with his children. In a book chronicling the story of Soviet space medicine, he wrote, "Laika was quiet and charming... I wanted to do something nice for her: She had so little time left to live."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-APSTAT-20)

## Preflight preparations

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/%D0%9B%D0%B0%D0%B9%D0%BA%D0%B0_%28%D1%81%D0%BE%D0%B1%D0%B0%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%BA%D0%BE%D1%81%D0%BC%D0%BE%D0%BD%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%82%291.jpg/250px-%D0%9B%D0%B0%D0%B9%D0%BA%D0%B0_%28%D1%81%D0%BE%D0%B1%D0%B0%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%BA%D0%BE%D1%81%D0%BC%D0%BE%D0%BD%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%82%291.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%D0%9B%D0%B0%D0%B9%D0%BA%D0%B0_(%D1%81%D0%BE%D0%B1%D0%B0%D0%BA%D0%B0-%D0%BA%D0%BE%D1%81%D0%BC%D0%BE%D0%BD%D0%B0%D0%B2%D1%82)1.jpg)

Laika in a mock cockpit

Yazdovsky made the final selection of dogs and their designated roles. Laika was to be the "flight dog"– a sacrifice to science on a one-way mission to space.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-russianspaceweb1-21) Albina, who had already flown twice on a high-altitude test [rocket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocket "Rocket"), was to act as Laika's backup. She was not sent as the primary due to Albina recently giving birth to three pups, and thus Yazdovsky thought it cruel to send Albina as the primary and separate a mother from her children.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11) The third dog, Mushka, was a "[control dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_control "Scientific control")"– she was to stay on the ground and be used to test instrumentation and [life support](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_support "Life support").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-SPUT1-8)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-STO-16)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11)

Before leaving for the [Baikonur Cosmodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikonur_Cosmodrome "Baikonur Cosmodrome"), Yazdovsky and Gazenko conducted surgery on the dogs, routing the cables from the transmitters to the sensors that would measure breathing, pulse, and blood pressure.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiddiqi2000173-22)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11)

Because the existing airstrip at [Turatam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turatam "Turatam") near the cosmodrome was small, the dogs and crew had to be first flown aboard a [Tu‑104](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tu-104 "Tu-104") plane to [Tashkent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tashkent "Tashkent"). From there, a smaller and lighter [Il‑14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilyushin_Il-14 "Ilyushin Il-14") plane took them to Turatam. Training of dogs continued upon arrival; one after another they were placed in the capsules to get familiar with the feeding system.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-russianspaceweb1-21)

According to a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") document, Laika was placed in the capsule of the satellite on 31 October 1957– three days before the start of the mission.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-SPUT1-8) At that time of year, the temperatures at the launch site were extremely low, and a hose connected to a heater was used to keep her container warm. Two assistants were assigned to keep a constant watch on Laika before launch. Just prior to liftoff on 3 November 1957, from Baikonur Cosmodrome, Laika's fur was sponged in a weak [ethanol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethanol "Ethanol") solution and carefully groomed, while [iodine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iodine "Iodine") was painted onto the areas where sensors would be placed to monitor her bodily functions.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-LM-23)

One of the technicians preparing the capsule before final lift-off stated: "After placing Laika in the container and before closing the hatch, we kissed her nose and wished her bon voyage, knowing that she would not survive the flight."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-russianspaceweb1-21)

## Voyage

Accounts of the time of launch vary from source to source, given as 05:30:42 or 07:22 [Moscow Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_Time "Moscow Time").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-russianspaceweb1-21)

At peak acceleration, Laika's respiration increased to between three and four times the pre-launch rate.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-SPUT1-8) The sensors showed her heart rate was 103 beats/min before launch and increased to 240 beats/min during the early acceleration. After reaching orbit, Sputnik 2's [nose cone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nose_cone "Nose cone") was jettisoned successfully; however, the "Block A" core did not separate as planned, preventing the thermal control system from operating correctly. Some of the [thermal insulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_insulation "Thermal insulation") tore loose, raising the cabin temperature to 40°C (104°F).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-Sputnik2-15) After three hours of [weightlessness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weightlessness "Weightlessness"), Laika's pulse rate had settled back to 102 beats/min,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-JAP-24) three times longer than it had taken during earlier ground tests, an indication of the stress she was under. The early [telemetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telemetry "Telemetry") indicated that Laika was agitated but eating her food.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-Sputnik2-15) After approximately five to seven hours into the flight, no further signs of life were received from the spacecraft.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-SPUT1-8)

The Soviet scientists had planned to euthanise Laika with a serving of poisoned food. For many years, the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") gave conflicting statements that she had died either from [asphyxia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asphyxia "Asphyxia"),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-Beischer1962-25) when the batteries failed, or that she had been euthanised. Many rumours circulated about the exact manner of her death. In 1999, several Russian sources reported that Laika had died when the cabin overheated on the fourth day.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AZ-6) In October 2002, Dimitri Malashenkov, one of the scientists behind the Sputnik 2 mission, revealed that Laika had died by the fourth circuit[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-26) of flight from overheating. According to a paper he presented to the [World Space Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Space_Congress "World Space Congress") in [Houston, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston"), "It turned out that it was practically impossible to create a reliable temperature control system in such limited time constraints."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-DM-7)

Over five months later, after 2,570 orbits, Sputnik 2 disintegrated during re-entry on 14 April 1958.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-MA-27)

## Ethics of animal testing

Due to the overshadowing issue of the Soviet–U.S. [Space Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Race "Space Race"), the ethical issues raised by this experiment, which were a matter of concern in the west,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11) went largely unaddressed for some time. As newspaper clippings from 1957 show, the press was initially focused on reporting the political perspective, while Laika's health and retrieval– or lack thereof– only became an issue later.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-45YRSLATER-28)

Sputnik 2 was not designed to be retrievable, and it had always been accepted that Laika would die.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-AZ-6)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-:0-11) The mission sparked a debate across the globe on the [mistreatment of animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistreatment_of_animals "Mistreatment of animals") and [animal testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_testing "Animal testing") in general to advance science.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NLM-18) In the United Kingdom, the [National Canine Defence League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dogs_Trust "Dogs Trust") called on all dog owners to observe a minute's silence on each day Laika remained in space, while the [Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society_for_the_Prevention_of_Cruelty_to_Animals "Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals") (RSPCA) received protests even before [Radio Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Moscow "Radio Moscow") had finished announcing the launch. [Animal rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_rights "Animal rights") groups at the time called on members of the public to protest at Soviet embassies.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-BBCold-29) In the U.S., people demonstrated outside the United Nations in New York,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NLM-18) and laboratory researchers offered some support for the Soviets, at least before the news of Laika's death.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NLM-18)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-NSMR-30)

In [Warsaw Pact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact "Warsaw Pact") countries, open criticism of the Soviet space program was difficult because of political censorship, but there were notable cases of criticism in Polish scientific circles. A Polish scientific periodical, _Kto, Kiedy, Dlaczego_ ("Who, When, Why"), published in 1958, discussed the mission of Sputnik 2. In the periodical's section dedicated to astronautics, [Krzysztof Boruń](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krzysztof_Boru%C5%84 "Krzysztof Boruń") described the Sputnik 2 mission as "regrettable" and criticised not bringing Laika back to Earth alive as "undoubtedly a great loss for science".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-KKD-31)

In the Soviet Union, there was less controversy. Neither the media, books in the following years, nor the public openly questioned the decision to send a dog into space. In 1998, after the collapse of the Soviet regime, [Oleg Gazenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleg_Gazenko "Oleg Gazenko"), one of the scientists responsible for sending Laika into space, expressed regret for allowing her to die:

> Work with animals is a source of suffering to all of us. We treat them like babies who cannot speak. The more time passes, the more I'm sorry about it. We shouldn't have done it[...] We did not learn enough from this mission to justify the death of the dog.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-MA-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-45YRSLATER-28)

Future space missions carrying dogs would be designed to be recovered; the first successful recovery followed the flight of [Korabl-Sputnik 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korabl-Sputnik_2 "Korabl-Sputnik 2"), wherein the dogs [Belka and Strelka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belka_and_Strelka "Belka and Strelka"), alongside dozens of other organisms, safely returned to Earth.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-32) Nonetheless, four other dogs later died in Soviet space missions: [Bars and Lisichka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_space_dogs#Bars_and_Lisichka "Soviet space dogs") were killed when their R‑7 rocket exploded shortly after launch on 28 July 1960,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiddiqi2000252-33) while [Pchyolka and Mushka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_space_dogs#Pchyolka_and_Mushka "Soviet space dogs") died when [Korabl-Sputnik 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korabl-Sputnik_3 "Korabl-Sputnik 3") suffered an emergency and had to be detonated.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiddiqi2000259-34)

## Tributes

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Posta_Romana_-_1959_-_Laika_120_B.jpg/250px-Posta_Romana_-_1959_-_Laika_120_B.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Posta_Romana_-_1959_-_Laika_120_B.jpg)

"Laika, first traveller into cosmos" stamp issued by [Poșta Română](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Po%C8%99ta_Rom%C3%A2n%C4%83 "Poșta Română") in 1957

Laika is memorialised in the form of a statue and plaque at [Star City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_City,_Russia "Star City, Russia"), the Russian Cosmonaut training facility.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-redOrbit-35) Created in 1997, Laika is positioned behind the cosmonauts with her ears erect.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-redOrbit-35) The [Monument to the Conquerors of Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monument_to_the_Conquerors_of_Space "Monument to the Conquerors of Space") in Moscow, constructed in 1964, also includes Laika.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-Telstar-36) On 11 April 2008[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-37) at the military research facility where staff had been responsible for readying Laika for the flight, officials unveiled a monument of her poised on top of a space rocket.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-RussiaOpensMonument-1) Stamps and envelopes picturing Laika were produced, as well as branded cigarettes and matches.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-38)

In 1988 the Spanish band [Mecano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecano "Mecano") released the song ["Laika"](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Laika_(Mecano)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Laika (Mecano) (page does not exist)")[[es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika_(canci%C3%B3n_de_Mecano) "es:Laika (canción de Mecano)")] paying tribute to the flight of the dog. The end of the song alludes to Laika's death: "There is one less dog on the Earth / And one more star in the sky".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-39)

[Karl Schroeder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Schroeder "Karl Schroeder") wrote a pessimistic [near future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_future_(fiction) "Near future (fiction)") science fiction novellette _[Laika's Ghost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika%27s\_Ghost "Laika's Ghost")_ with the idea that in the pragmatic world, "only people ready to take up the dream of flight to other worlds are aged remnants of the former Soviet Union".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-40)

The 2007 graphic novel _[Laika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika\_(comics) "Laika (comics)")_ by [Nick Abadzis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Abadzis "Nick Abadzis") won several awards, landing itself on the [YALSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Adult_Library_Services_Association "Young Adult Library Services Association") "Top Ten Great Graphic Novels for Teens"[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-41) and earning multiple [Eisner Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisner_Awards "Eisner Awards"). The book gives a fictionalized account of Laika's life. The story is told from multiple points of view and features politicians, scientists, and engineers.

_[Lajka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lajka "Lajka")_ is a 2017 Czech science fiction comedy animated film inspired by the dog.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-CSFD-42)

Norwegian singer [Emmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_(Norwegian_singer) "Emmy (Norwegian singer)") released a song in 2025 titled "[Laika Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika_Party "Laika Party")" to compete in the [Irish _Eurosong_ selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland_in_the_Eurovision_Song_Contest_2025#Eurosong_2025 "Ireland in the Eurovision Song Contest 2025") for the [2025 Eurovision Song Contest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurovision_Song_Contest_2025 "Eurovision Song Contest 2025"). The song tells a story about the singer wishing that Laika had never died and was living happily in space. Emmy won the selection to represent Ireland at the contest.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika#cite_note-43)

![Image 2: Engineers and scientists around the country are working hard to develop the technologies astronauts will use to one day live and work on Mars, and safely return home from the next giant leap for humanity.](https://www.greatfallstribune.com/gcdn/-mm-/b6e599633e331be49822c7ca7608bd1b01a4e454/c=0-0-1037-586/local/-/media/2015/09/16/GreatFalls/B9318876152Z.1_20150916233109_000_G6EBUO27R.1-0.jpg?width=660&height=373&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)
July 14, 1965 — Mariner 4 provides first close-up photos of the red planet.

July 20, 1969 — Astronauts Buzz Aldrin and Neil Armstrong land on the moon.

July 20, 1976 — Viking 1 makes first successful robotic landing on Mars.

July 4, 1997 — Mars Pathfinder lands first roving robotic probe.

Nov. 20, 1998 — International Space Station launched.

[Montana to Mars: Newman guides NASA effort](https://www.greatfallstribune.com/story/news/local/2015/09/16/montana-mars-newman-guides-nasa-effort/32539225/)

Oct. 24, 2001 — Mars Odyssey orbiter begins probe for water on the red planet.

Aug. 6, 2012 — Curiosity rover lands on Mars, searches for signs of water, life.

Dec. 5, 2014 — Orion spacecraft makes first successful earth orbit.

2018 — First test launch of NASA’s Space Launch System.

2020 — Mars Rover lands in preparation for future human missions.

2025 — Orion spacecraft fully operational. Combined Earth/Moon orbits.

2028 — Asteroid Redirect Mission collects samples from near-earth asteroid.

2033 — First orbital mission to Mars.

2039 — Four-man crew makes first landing on the red planet, 70 years after moon landing.

verifications.original_text:
Title: Every mission to Mars ever

URL Source: https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/every-mars-mission

Published Time: Sun, 31 May 2026 06:13:27 GMT

Markdown Content:
Today, there are more spacecraft operating at [Mars](https://www.planetary.org/worlds/mars) than any planet besides [Earth](https://www.planetary.org/worlds/earth) — from orbiters to landers and rovers.

Mars has been historically unkind to our attempts to send spacecraft there, with roughly half of all Mars missions failing. That percentage has improved in recent years.

[![Image 1: What is on Mars and where?](blob:http://localhost/5afaa6b17d1751e45073a0aa4498c546)](https://www.planetary.org/space-images/what-is-on-mars-and-where)

What is on Mars and where? This infographic shows the location of every successful mission that has landed on Mars. It is free for media and non-commercial use with attribution._Image: The Planetary Society_

[![Image 2: The Mars Exploration Family Portrait](blob:http://localhost/96709f23efe0a38282c901c022334713)](https://www.planetary.org/space-images/the-mars-exploration-family-portrait)

The Mars Exploration Family Portrait The Mars Exploration Family Portrait shows every dedicated space mission to Mars._Image: NASA/JPL/Roscosmos/JAXA/ESA/ISRO/MBRSC/Jason Davis/The Planetary Society_

## Active Missions

### [MAVEN, studying how Mars lost its atmosphere](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/maven)

NASA's Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution spacecraft, MAVEN, studies how Mars loses its atmosphere to space. The orbiter also relays communications between surface missions and Earth.

## Future Missions

### [Tianwen-3: China’s Mars sample return mission](https://www.planetary.org/articles/tianwen-3-china-mars-sample-return-mission)

China's Tianwen-3 aims to be the first to collect samples from Mars and deliver them to Earth, potentially landing back home two years ahead of the NASA and the European Space Agency MSR project

## Past Missions

> ### [Rosetta and Philae](https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Rosetta/The_surprising_comet)
> 
> 
> The European Space Agency's Rosetta and Philae spacecraft flew by Mars on 25 February 2007 on its way to comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko.

> ### [](https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/missions/phoenix/in-depth)[](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/every-mars-mission)**[Phoenix](https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/missions/phoenix/in-depth)**
> 
> 
> NASA's Phoenix spacecraft landed near Mars' north pole to study the water ice found close to the surface there. Its arm dug trenches into the soil and delivered samples to sophisticated chemical analysis instruments. It carried [The Planetary Society's Visions of Mars DVD](https://www.planetary.org/outreach/visions-of-mars).

### [Mars Exploration Rovers](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/mars-exploration-rovers)

The twin Mars Exploration Rovers (MER), Spirit and Opportunity, were robot field geologists. They confirmed liquid water once flowed across the Martian surface. Both long outlasted their planned 90-day lifetimes. Following their landings on 3 and 24 January 2004, Spirit drove 7.73 kilometers and worked for 2210 sols (Martian days), until 22 March 2010. Opportunity drove 45.16 kilometers and worked for at least 5111 sols; the rover stopped responding on 10 June 2018, and the mission was declared over on 13 February 2019.

> ### [Nozomi](https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/missions/nozomi/in-depth)
> 
> 
> Originally scheduled to arrive at Mars in October 1999, Nozomi failed to gain enough speed during an Earth flyby on December 21, 1998. The spacecraft also used much more fuel than predicted. A looping trajectory was developed, including two more Earth flybys, to return Nozomi to Mars for orbit insertion in December 2003. But on April 21, 2002, a powerful solar flare damaged Nozomi’s computer. As a result, Nozomi’s hydrazine fuel froze during the long interplanetary trek and mission controllers were unable to place it into orbit. Nozomi flew by Mars in 2003 at a distance of 1,000 kilometers (600 miles), and is now in a two-year orbit around the Sun.

> ### [Mars Climate Orbiter](https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/missions/mars-climate-orbiter/in-depth)
> 
> 
> #### Failed Mars orbiter (NASA)
> 
> 
> **Launch:** December 11, 1998
> 
> 
> Mars Climate Orbiter was lost on September 23, 1999, when a mathematical conversion error placed the spacecraft too close to Mars at the time of orbital insertion. Mars Climate Orbiter carried a few re-flown instruments from Mars Observer, marking the second failure for those experiments.

Today, there are more spacecraft operating at [Mars](https://www.planetary.org/worlds/mars) than any planet besides [Earth](https://www.planetary.org/worlds/earth) — from orbiters to landers and rovers.

Mars has been historically unkind to our attempts to send spacecraft there, with roughly half of all Mars missions failing. That percentage has improved in recent years.

What is on Mars and where? This infographic shows the location of every successful mission that has landed on Mars. It is free for media and non-commercial use with attribution._Image: The Planetary Society_

[![Image 2: The Mars Exploration Family Portrait](blob:http://localhost/96709f23efe0a38282c901c022334713)](https://www.planetary.org/space-images/the-mars-exploration-family-portrait)

The Mars Exploration Family Portrait The Mars Exploration Family Portrait shows every dedicated space mission to Mars._Image: NASA/JPL/Roscosmos/JAXA/ESA/ISRO/MBRSC/Jason Davis/The Planetary Society_

## Active Missions

### [MAVEN, studying how Mars lost its atmosphere](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/maven)

NASA's Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution spacecraft, MAVEN, studies how Mars loses its atmosphere to space. The orbiter also relays communications between surface missions and Earth.

## Future Missions

### [Tianwen-3: China’s Mars sample return mission](https://www.planetary.org/articles/tianwen-3-china-mars-sample-return-mission)

China's Tianwen-3 aims to be the first to collect samples from Mars and deliver them to Earth, potentially landing back home two years ahead of the NASA and the European Space Agency MSR project

>

Title: Mars landing

URL Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_landing

[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Insight_landing-640x350.gif/500px-Insight_landing-640x350.gif)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Insight_landing-640x350.gif)

Animation of a Mars landing touchdown, the InSight lander in 2018

A **Mars landing** is a landing of a [spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacecraft "Spacecraft") on the surface of [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"). Of multiple attempted Mars landings by [robotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robotic_spacecraft "Robotic spacecraft"), uncrewed spacecraft, ten have had successful soft landings. There have also been studies for a possible [human mission to Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_mission_to_Mars "Human mission to Mars") including a landing, but none has been attempted.

As of 2023, the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), and [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") have conducted Mars landings successfully.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_landing#cite_note-1) Soviet [Mars 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_3 "Mars 3"), which landed in 1971, was the first successful Mars landing, though the spacecraft failed after 110 seconds on the surface. All other Soviet Mars landing attempts failed.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_landing#cite_note-2)[Viking 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_1 "Viking 1") and [Viking 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_2 "Viking 2") were first successful NASA landers, launched in 1975. NASA's [Mars Pathfinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Pathfinder "Mars Pathfinder"), launched in 1996, successfully delivered the first [Mars rover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_rover "Mars rover"), _[Sojourner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sojourner\_(rover) "Sojourner (rover)")_. In 2021, first Chinese lander and rover, [Tianwen 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tianwen_1 "Tianwen 1"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_landing#cite_note-3) successfully landed on Mars. The British [Beagle 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beagle_2 "Beagle 2") landed in 2003, but because of loss of contact and mission failure its landing would only be confirmed in 2015.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_landing#cite_note-4)

## Methods of descent and landing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mars_landing&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Methods of descent and landing")]

As of 2021, all methods of landing on Mars have used an [aeroshell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeroshell "Aeroshell") and [parachute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachute "Parachute") sequence for [Mars atmospheric entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_atmospheric_entry "Mars atmospheric entry") and descent, but after the parachute is detached, there are three options. A stationary lander can drop from the parachute back shell and ride [retrorockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrorocket "Retrorocket") all the way down, but a [rover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rover_(space_exploration) "Rover (space exploration)") cannot be burdened with rockets that serve no purpose after touchdown.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_landing#cite_note-5)

One method for lighter rovers is to enclose the rover in a [tetrahedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrahedron "Tetrahedron") structure which in turn is enclosed in [airbags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbag "Airbag"). After the aeroshell drops off, the tetrahedron is lowered clear of the parachute back shell on a tether so that the airbags can inflate. Retrorockets on the back shell can slow descent. When it nears the ground, the tetrahedron is released to drop to the ground, using the airbags as [shock absorbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shock_absorber "Shock absorber"). When it has come to rest, the tetrahedron opens to expose the rover.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_landing#cite_note-6)

If a rover is too heavy to use airbags, the retrorockets can be mounted on a [sky crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_crane_(landing_system) "Sky crane (landing system)"). The sky crane drops from the parachute back shell and, as it nears the ground, the rover is lowered on a tether. When the rover touches ground, it cuts the tether so that the sky crane (with its rockets still firing) will crash well away from the rover. Both _[Curiosity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curiosity\_(rover) "Curiosity (rover)")_ and _[Perseverance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perseverance\_(rover) "Perseverance (rover)")_ used sky crane for landing.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_landing#cite_note-7)
