Nakamura's first over-the-board event of 2025 was February's [Freestyle Chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freestyle_Chess_Grand_Slam_Tour#Weissenhaus_(1st_Leg) "Freestyle Chess Grand Slam Tour") tournament in [Weissenhaus, Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gut_Wei%C3%9Fenhaus "Gut Weißenhaus"). This ten-player [Fischer Random](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess960 "Chess960") event consisted of a [rapid-play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_chess#Rapid_(FIDE),_quick_(USCF),_or_active "Fast chess")[round-robin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round-robin_tournament "Round-robin tournament") followed by a series of playoff matches, which were played at classical time limits with rapid and [blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_chess#Blitz "Fast chess") tiebreakers if necessary. Nakamura placed fifth in the round-robin with a +3-1=5 record that included wins against [Fabiano Caruana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabiano_Caruana "Fabiano Caruana"), [Vincent Keymer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Keymer "Vincent Keymer") and [Vladimir Fedoseev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Fedoseev "Vladimir Fedoseev"). He then lost his playoff match against [Javokhir Sindarov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javokhir_Sindarov "Javokhir Sindarov") (2.5-1.5) but won matches against [Gukesh Dommaraju](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gukesh_Dommaraju "Gukesh Dommaraju") (2.5-1.5) and [Nodirbek Abdusattorov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nodirbek_Abdusattorov "Nodirbek Abdusattorov") (2-0) to finish fifth in the tournament.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-184)

Also in February Nakamura played in the online [double-elimination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-elimination_tournament "Double-elimination tournament") Chessable Masters rapid tournament on [chess.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess.com "Chess.com"). He won matches against [Alexander Grischuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Grischuk "Alexander Grischuk") (2.5-0.5), [Ian Nepomniachtchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Nepomniachtchi "Ian Nepomniachtchi") (3-0) and [Alireza Firouzja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alireza_Firouzja "Alireza Firouzja") (3-2) but lost in the winners bracket final to [Magnus Carlsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen "Magnus Carlsen") (2.5-0.5). He then faced Nepomniachtchi again in the losers bracket final. The match went to an [Armageddon game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_chess#Armageddon "Fast chess") where he drew with black and thus earned the victory (1.5-1.5) and a rematch with Carlsen in the tournament grand final.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-185) Nakamura lost the rematch (2.5-1.5) to finish second in the tournament and qualify for the [Esports World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Esports_World_Cup "2025 Esports World Cup").[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-186)

In March Nakamura played in the six-player Champions Showdown at the [Saint Louis Chess Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Louis_Chess_Club "Saint Louis Chess Club"). This event consisted of matches with games at blitz, rapid and "semi-classical" (60 minutes for the game with a 15-second increment) time limits. Cash prizes were awarded for each game. Nakamura lost his match with [Fabiano Caruana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabiano_Caruana "Fabiano Caruana") (2-1), won his match with [Ray Robson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Robson "Ray Robson") (2-1) and drew his match with [Levon Aronian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levon_Aronian "Levon Aronian") (1.5-1.5). He finished fourth on the prize money list with $37,625.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-187)

Later in March Nakamura played in the [American Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Cup_(chess) "American Cup (chess)"), an eight-player [double elimination tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-elimination_tournament "Double-elimination tournament") also held at the St. Louis Chess Club. The event featured matches with games at classical, rapid and blitz time limits. He defeated [Abhimanyu Mishra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abhimanyu_Mishra "Abhimanyu Mishra") (3.5-2.5), [Leinier Dominguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leinier_Dom%C3%ADnguez "Leinier Domínguez") (1.5-0.5) and Fabiano Caruana (2.5-1.5) to win the winners bracket. In the tournament grand final he beat Caruana again (1.5-0.5) to take first place in the event.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-188) He also won the subsequent American Cup Blitz tournament, a nine-round [Swiss event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss-system_tournament "Swiss-system tournament") at blitz time limits, which featured a large field of grandmasters and other strong players.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-189)

Nakamura continued a busy tournament schedule with April's Freestyle Chess tournament in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"). In this Fischer Random event he placed sixth in the preliminary rapid-play round robin (+4-3=4) and then won knockout matches at classical time limits against [Arjun Erigaisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arjun_Erigaisi "Arjun Erigaisi") (1.5-0.5) and [Vincent Keymer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Keymer "Vincent Keymer") (1.5-0.5) to reach the tournament grand final. He lost the final to Magnus Carlsen (1.5-0.5) to finish second in the event.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-190) In May Nakamura participated in the sixteen-player online Chess.com Classic. He won matches against [Levon Aronian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levon_Aronian "Levon Aronian") (3-2), [Ding Liren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ding_Liren "Ding Liren") (2.5-0.5) and [Ian Nepomniachtchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Nepomniachtchi "Ian Nepomniachtchi") (3-2) to reach the winners bracket final against [Magnus Carlsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen "Magnus Carlsen"). He lost the match to Carlsen (3-1) and, in an odd turn of events, resigned a winning position against Carlsen in the fourth and final game.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-191)[Maxime Vachier-Lagrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxime_Vachier-Lagrave "Maxime Vachier-Lagrave") then beat Nakamura in the losers bracket final (1.5-0.5) in a match where a power outage in Nakamura's hotel affected play. He thus finished third in the tournament.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-192)

Nakamura's next event was [Norway Chess 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway_Chess_2025 "Norway Chess 2025"), held in May and June. This was an extremely strong tournament with five of the world's top six ranked players participating. The event was a six-player double round robin with its normal format of classical games followed by Armageddon playoffs in case of a draw. Nakamura compiled a +1 record in classical (+2-1=7) with victories against [Fabiano Caruana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabiano_Caruana "Fabiano Caruana") and reigning world champion [Gukesh Dommaraju](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gukesh_Dommaraju "Gukesh Dommaraju"). But his poor record in the Armageddon playoffs (two wins and five losses) meant that he finished fourth overall. He expressed satisfaction with the result because it cemented his place as the world's number-two ranked player in classical and thus improved his chances of earning the ratings spot in the [2026 Candidates tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Chess_Championship_2026#Candidates_Tournament "World Chess Championship 2026").[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-193)

Later in June Nakamura played as part of team WR Chess in the [World Rapid and Blitz Team Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Rapid_and_Blitz_Team_Championships_2025 "World Rapid and Blitz Team Championships 2025") in London. He compiled strong records in rapid (+6-0=5) and blitz (+11-1=3), including wins against [Anish Giri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anish_Giri "Anish Giri"), [Richard Rapport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rich%C3%A1rd_Rapport "Richárd Rapport") and [Michael Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Adams_(chess_player) "Michael Adams (chess player)"). His team won the blitz title and finished fifth in rapid.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-194) In July Nakamura was one of sixteen players in the [Fischer Random](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess960 "Chess960")[Freestyle event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freestyle_Chess_Grand_Slam_Tour "Freestyle Chess Grand Slam Tour") in [Las Vegas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas "Las Vegas"). He placed first in the round robin in his group of eight with a +5-0=2 score, including wins against [Hans Niemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Niemann "Hans Niemann") and [Arjun Erigaisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arjun_Erigaisi "Arjun Erigaisi"). He then lost his first knockout match to [Levon Aronian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levon_Aronian "Levon Aronian") (3-1), won matches against Wesley So (1.5-0.5) and Fabiano Caruana (3-1), and lost his final match to Magnus Carlsen (1.5-0.5) to finish fourth in the tournament.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-195)

Also in July Nakamura played in the sixteen-player rapid tournament as part of the [Esports World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esports_World_Cup "Esports World Cup"). In the group stage he defeated [Javokhir Sindarov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javokhir_Sindarov "Javokhir Sindarov") (2-0), lost in Armageddon to [Alireza Firouzja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alireza_Firouzja "Alireza Firouzja") (1.5-1.5) and won against [Wei Yi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wei_Yi "Wei Yi") (2-1). This qualified him for the final knockout phase, where he beat [Levon Aronian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levon_Aronian "Levon Aronian") (2.5-1.5), lost to [Magnus Carlsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen "Magnus Carlsen") in Armageddon (4-3) and defeated [Arjun Erigaisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arjun_Erigaisi "Arjun Erigaisi") (3.5-2.5) to take third place in the event.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-196)

Based on FIDE Regulations, in order to qualify for the 2026 [Candidates Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candidates_Tournament "Candidates Tournament") based on rating, a player must have played at least 40 games calculated for FIDE Standard Rating Lists from February 1, 2025 till January 1, 2026.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-197) Due to this regulation, Nakamura did not meet the requirements to qualify for the Candidates Tournament as of August 1 and thus needed to play 22 additional games. From August 30 to September 1, Nakamura played in the 2025 Louisiana State Championship where he finished with a 7/7 score, improving his rating by 4.8 points.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-198) The following week, Nakamura participated in the 70th Iowa Open where he also achieved a perfect score of 5/5. His live rating increased to 2815.8, which when rounded to 2816 is equal to his peak rating which he achieved 10 years ago.[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-199)

In October Nakamura played in the Checkmate: USA vs India event, where he defeated [Gukesh Dommaraju](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gukesh_Dommaraju "Gukesh Dommaraju") (2-1) as part of the American team's overall 5-0 victory. This event was staged extravagantly with a large live crowd encouraged to cheer loudly during the games. After Nakamura defeated Gukesh in the final game, he picked up Gukesh's king from the board and tossed it into the crowd.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-200) Later in the month Nakamura played in the Comet Open, a 32-player double-elimination online blitz event. He won the tournament by defeating GMs [Emin Ohanyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emin_Ohanyan "Emin Ohanyan") (2.5-0.5), [Pranav V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pranav_V "Pranav V") (2.5-1.5), [Parham Maghsoodloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parham_Maghsoodloo "Parham Maghsoodloo") (3-2), [Nihal Sarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihal_Sarin "Nihal Sarin") (3-2), [Dmitry Andreikin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitry_Andreikin "Dmitry Andreikin") (3-1) and [Denis Lazavik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Lazavik "Denis Lazavik") (2.5-1.5).[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-201)

Nakamura is particularly skilled at [rapid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_chess#Rapid_(FIDE),_quick_(USCF)_or_active "Fast chess") and [blitz chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blitz_chess "Blitz chess"), a variety of time controls in which players have less than an hour to complete all or most of their moves. In August 2022, Nakamura was ranked No. 1 on both the FIDE blitz list[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-202) and the FIDE rapid list.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-203) He is also strong at [bullet chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullet_chess "Bullet chess"), a time control giving the players one minute each.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-204) In 2009, Nakamura authored the book _Bullet Chess: One Minute to Mate_.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-205) Nakamura said in September 2020, "At least at blitz chess, I'm probably the best or second-best player ever, in the entire history, at least online."[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-NYT_Sep20-206)

Nakamura has been nicknamed "The H Bomb" because of his explosive style of playing.[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-207) Nakamura's long-time [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_(chess) "Second (chess)") is [USCF National Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_title#Master "Chess title") Kris Littlejohn,[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-208) who works with [chess engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_engine "Chess engine") to prepare lines for Nakamura to play.[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-209)

Nakamura has set several "youngest-ever" records in U.S. chess history, including:[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-210)

*   Youngest to defeat an International Master in a USCF-rated game (10 years, 0 months); later surpassed by [Praveen Balakrishnan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praveen_Balakrishnan "Praveen Balakrishnan") at 9 years 29 days, and then by [Awonder Liang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awonder_Liang "Awonder Liang") at 8 years 118 days;
*   Youngest to defeat a Grandmaster in a USCF-rated game (10 years, 117 days); later surpassed by [Fabiano Caruana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabiano_Caruana "Fabiano Caruana") at 10 years, 61 days; then surpassed by Awonder Liang at 9 years 112 days;
*   Youngest International Master (13 years, 2 months); later surpassed by [Ray Robson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Robson "Ray Robson") at 13 years, 1 month, by [Samuel Sevian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Sevian "Samuel Sevian") at 12 years, 10 months, and by [Awonder Liang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awonder_Liang "Awonder Liang") at 12 years, 7 months and 6 days old.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-211) and then by [Abhimanyu Mishra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abhimanyu_Mishra "Abhimanyu Mishra") at 10 years, 9 months, and 20 days.[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-212)

Nakamura has played on the [Internet Chess Club (ICC)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Chess_Club "Internet Chess Club") (as "Capilanobridge"; formerly as "Smallville") and [Playchess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playchess "Playchess") (as "Star Wars"). He served as a commentator and game annotator on the ChessNinja website, operated by chess author [Mig Greengard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mig_Greengard "Mig Greengard"). Hikaru Nakamura is sponsored by [Chess.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess.com "Chess.com"), the largest chess website.[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-Verge-213)

In 2018, Nakamura began streaming on the platform [Twitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitch_(service) "Twitch (service)") under the name "GMHikaru". He plays speed chess games, variously against grandmasters, other streamers, and viewers who pay to subscribe to his channel.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-NYT_Sep20-206)[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-Economist-214)[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-FC-215) He may play [blindfolded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blindfold_chess "Blindfold chess") or with piece [handicaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handicap_(chess) "Handicap (chess)"), such as odds of a queen.[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-FC-215) He also reviews his tournament games on stream.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-NPR-216)[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-Kotaku-217) In 2020, during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), chess became significantly more popular on Twitch, with Nakamura widely identified as a significant reason for this.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-NYT_Sep20-206)[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-FC-215)[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-Verge-213)[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-Kotaku-217) His channel received a tenfold increase in audience size between February and June 2020.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-Economist-214) Around August 2020, Nakamura averaged 14,000 concurrent viewers and streamed on Twitch most days.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-218) By September 2020, he had reached 500,000 followers.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-NYT_Sep20-206) As of September 2025, the channel has reached 2 million followers.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-219) Nakamura often plays games using "joke openings" while on stream, including the [Bongcloud Attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongcloud_Attack "Bongcloud Attack"), the [Jerome Gambit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome_Gambit "Jerome Gambit") and the [Botez Gambit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botez_Gambit "Botez Gambit").[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-220) Nakamura has stated that he prioritizes his streaming career over his chess playing career.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-221)

On August 27, 2020, Nakamura signed with the esports organization [Team SoloMid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_SoloMid "Team SoloMid") (TSM) for a six-figure sum, making him one of the first chess players to join an esports team.[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-Verge-213)[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-NYT_Sep20-206) On June 14, 2022, he joined [Misfits Gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misfits_Gaming "Misfits Gaming") as a content creator and influencer.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-222) On February 17, 2025, Nakamura signed with [Team Falcons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_Falcons "Team Falcons"), who are rumored to have connections to the [Saudi Arabian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia")[royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Saud "House of Saud").[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-EsportsIllustrated-223)

Nakamura operates a [Discord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discord_(software) "Discord (software)") server named "Naka's PogUniversity" and has a [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") account.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-NYT_Sep20-206)[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-Verge-213) Nakamura also has a [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") channel, which has 3,010,000 subscribers as of September 2025,[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-224) up from 78,900 subscribers in the beginning of 2020.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-225) When asked about his popularity online, Nakamura attributed it to "the ability to play extremely high-level chess" while "seemingly ... not focused on the game" and conversing with his viewers.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-NYT_Sep20-206) Nathan Grayson of _[Kotaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kotaku "Kotaku")_ called it a "combination of teacherly wisdom, galaxy-brained skills, and uncommon expressiveness".[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-Kotaku-217)

Nakamura has also coached beginner chess players on his Twitch platform, including the streamer [xQc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XQc "XQc").[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-Kotaku-217) He gave lessons to players in [PogChamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PogChamps "PogChamps"), an amateur tournament for Twitch streamers hosted by Chess.com, and its sequel, PogChamps 2. He additionally provided commentary.[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-226) At its peak, the tournament was the most-watched channel on Twitch for a short period, with 63,000 viewers.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-NYT_Sep20-206) Nakamura told _Kotaku_ that though the competition had been met with some criticism, he believed that such tournaments with varying levels of skills among players could become popular.[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-Kotaku-217) On February 14, 2021, PogChamps 3 began. During the xQc vs. Rubius match on the second day of the event, chess hit its all-time high of 115,000 viewers in the chess category on Twitch.

On February 14, 2021, Nakamura reached a milestone of one million followers on his Twitch channel, GMHikaru.[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-227) During the [FIDE Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIDE_Grand_Prix_2022 "FIDE Grand Prix 2022") in March 2022, Twitch suspended Nakamura for three days (later reduced to two days) after he broadcast and commented on chess games being played by [Dr Disrespect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr_Disrespect "Dr Disrespect"), who is permanently suspended from the streaming platform.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-228)[_[unreliable source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable\_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")_]

Nakamura appeared as himself in season 5, episode 2 of the [Showtime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Showtime_(TV_network) "Showtime (TV network)") series _[Billions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billions\_(TV\_series) "Billions (TV series)")_, which premiered May 10, 2020.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-229) Nakamura is also an active [stock market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_market "Stock market")[investor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investor "Investor"). In April 2017 he appeared on [Bloomberg Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_Television "Bloomberg Television") to discuss the relationship between chess and stock trading.[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-230) During his chess streams Nakamura occasionally discusses stock market investing and general financial topics.[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-231)

Nakamura married [Atousa Pourkashiyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atousa_Pourkashiyan "Atousa Pourkashiyan"), an Iranian [Woman Grandmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woman_Grandmaster "Woman Grandmaster"), in 2023.[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-232) In July 2025 he announced during one of his chess streams that he and his wife were expecting their first child.[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-233) They announced the birth of their child in December 2025.

**Christopher Hikaru Nakamura**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-fn-1) ([Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): 中村光; born December 9, 1987) is an American [chess grandmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_grandmaster "Chess grandmaster"), [internet personality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_personality "Internet personality"), five-time [U.S. Chess Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Chess_Champion "U.S. Chess Champion"), and the 2022 [World Fischer Random Chess Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIDE_World_Fischer_Random_Chess_Championship_2022 "FIDE World Fischer Random Chess Championship 2022"). A [chess prodigy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_prodigy "Chess prodigy"), he earned his grandmaster title at the age of 15, the youngest American at the time to do so. With a peak [rating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elo_rating_system "Elo rating system") of 2816, Nakamura is tied as the [tenth-highest-rated player in history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_of_top_chess_players_throughout_history#Elo_system "Comparison of top chess players throughout history").

Nakamura has represented the United States at seven [Chess Olympiads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_Olympiad "Chess Olympiad") (2006, 2008, 2010, 2012, 2014, 2016, 2018), securing a team gold medal and two team bronze medals, and participated in three [Candidates Tournaments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candidates_Tournament "Candidates Tournament"), finishing second in the [2024 edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candidates_Tournament_2024 "Candidates Tournament 2024"), fourth in the [2022 edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candidates_Tournament_2022 "Candidates Tournament 2022"), and seventh in the [2016 edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candidates_Tournament_2016 "Candidates Tournament 2016"). In May 2014, when FIDE began publishing official [rapid and blitz chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_and_blitz_chess "Rapid and blitz chess") ratings, Nakamura ranked No. 1 in the world on both lists.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-chess-news.ru-2)

Since 2018, Nakamura has pursued a career as a [content creator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Content_creator "Content creator") and subsequently signed with an esports organization [TSM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSM_(esports) "TSM (esports)"), later joining [Misfits Gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misfits_Gaming "Misfits Gaming") and then [Team Falcons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_Falcons "Team Falcons"). Having popular channels on [Twitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitch_(service) "Twitch (service)"), [Kick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kick_(service) "Kick (service)") and [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube"), Nakamura is one of the most popular chess streamers in the world, and is widely credited with contributing to the growth in popularity of [online chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_chess "Online chess").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-4)

Nakamura was born in [Hirakata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirakata "Hirakata"), Osaka Prefecture, Japan, to an American mother, Carolyn Merrow Nakamura, a classically trained musician and former public school teacher, and a Japanese father, Shuichi Nakamura.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-6) Nakamura has an older brother, Asuka.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-:0-7) When he was two years old, his family moved to the United States, and, a year later in 1990, his parents divorced.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-8) He was raised in [White Plains, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Plains,_New_York "White Plains, New York"). He began playing chess at the age of seven and was coached by his [Sri Lankan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka "Sri Lanka")-American stepfather, FIDE Master and chess author [Sunil Weeramantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunil_Weeramantry "Sunil Weeramantry").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-9) Weeramantry began coaching the Nakamura brothers after Asuka Nakamura won the National Kindergarten Championship in 1992, which led him to develop a relationship with their mother.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-:0-7)

At age 10, he became the youngest American to beat an [International Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Master "International Master") when he defeated [Jay Bonin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Bonin "Jay Bonin") at the [Marshall Chess Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Chess_Club "Marshall Chess Club").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-:0-7)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-10) Also at age 10, Nakamura became the youngest player to achieve the title of [chess master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_master "Chess master") from the [United States Chess Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Chess_Federation "United States Chess Federation"), breaking the record previously set by [Vinay Bhat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinay_Bhat "Vinay Bhat"). (Nakamura's record stood until 2008 when Nicholas Nip achieved the master title at the age of 9 years and 11 months.) In 1999, Nakamura won the [Laura Aspis Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Aspis_Prize "Laura Aspis Prize"), given annually to the top USCF-rated player under age 13. In 2003, at age 15 years and 79 days, Nakamura solidified his reputation as a [chess prodigy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_prodigy "Chess prodigy"), becoming the youngest American to earn the grandmaster title at the time, breaking the record of [Bobby Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Fischer "Bobby Fischer") by three months.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-12)

In April 2004, Nakamura finished in fourth place in the "B" group at the [Corus tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corus_chess_tournament "Corus chess tournament") at [Wijk aan Zee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wijk_aan_Zee "Wijk aan Zee"), the Netherlands.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-13)

Nakamura qualified for the [FIDE World Chess Championship 2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIDE_World_Chess_Championship_2004 "FIDE World Chess Championship 2004"), played in [Tripoli, Libya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripoli,_Libya "Tripoli, Libya"), and reached the fourth round, defeating grandmasters [Sergey Volkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Volkov_(chess) "Sergey Volkov (chess)"), [Aleksej Aleksandrov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksej_Aleksandrov "Aleksej Aleksandrov"), and [Alexander Lastin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Lastin "Alexander Lastin") before falling to England's [Michael Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Adams_(chess_player) "Michael Adams (chess player)"), who eventually finished in second place.

In June 2005, Nakamura was selected as the 19th Frank Samford Chess Fellow, receiving a grant of $32,000 to further his chess education and competition.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-14)

Nakamura won the 2005 [U.S. Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Chess_Championship "U.S. Chess Championship") (held in November and December 2004), scoring an undefeated seven points out of nine rounds to tie grandmaster [Alexander Stripunsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Stripunsky "Alexander Stripunsky") for first place. Nakamura defeated Stripunsky in the rapid playoff to claim the title and become the youngest U.S. champion since Bobby Fischer.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-16)

Following that victory, Nakamura played a challenge match dubbed the "Duelo de Jóvenes Prodigios" in Mexico against [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russians "Russians") grandmaster [Sergey Karjakin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Karjakin "Sergey Karjakin") and defeated his fellow prodigy by 4½–1½.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-17)

In November and December 2005, Nakamura competed in the [2005 FIDE World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_World_Cup_2005 "Chess World Cup 2005") in [Khanty-Mansiysk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khanty-Mansiysk "Khanty-Mansiysk"), Russia, seeded 28th (of 128 players) but failed to advance beyond the first round. He lost each of his two games to Indian grandmaster [Surya Ganguly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surya_Ganguly "Surya Ganguly").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-18)

In 2006, Nakamura was offered a full scholarship to the [University of Texas at Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Dallas "University of Texas at Dallas") but instead attended [Dickinson College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickinson_College "Dickinson College"), with a partial scholarship, in order to take a break from chess. Later in the year, he announced that he would leave college and resume playing chess.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-19) The same year, he helped the U.S. team win the bronze medal in the [Chess Olympiad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_Olympiad "Chess Olympiad") at [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin"), Italy, playing on the third board behind [Gata Kamsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gata_Kamsky "Gata Kamsky") and 2006 U.S. Champion [Alexander Onischuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Onischuk "Alexander Onischuk"). In the same year, he won the 16th North American Open in Las Vegas.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-20)

In January 2007, Nakamura shared second place at the [GibTelecom Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibraltar_Chess_Festival "Gibraltar Chess Festival") in [Gibraltar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibraltar "Gibraltar").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-21) He placed joint first in the tournament the following year, finishing with five straight wins to tie with Chinese GM [Bu Xiangzhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bu_Xiangzhi "Bu Xiangzhi"), whom he then proceeded to beat in the rapidplay playoff.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-gibtel-22)

In October 2007, Nakamura won the _Magistral D'Escacs_ tournament in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona")[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-23) and the [Corsican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica "Corsica") circuit rapid chess tournament.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-24)

Nakamura won the 2008 Finet Chess960 Open in Mainz, Germany.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-25) In November 2008, he won the Cap d'Agde Rapid Tournament in [Cap d'Agde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cap_d%27Agde "Cap d'Agde"), defeating [Anatoly Karpov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoly_Karpov "Anatoly Karpov") in the semifinals and [Vassily Ivanchuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassily_Ivanchuk "Vassily Ivanchuk") in the finals.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-26) In February 2009, he came joint third at the 7th Gibtelecom Masters in Gibraltar, again finishing strongly with 4½/5 to end the event on 7½/10.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-27)

### 2009: Second U.S. Championship and other tournament successes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hikaru_Nakamura&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2009: Second U.S. Championship and other tournament successes")]

Nakamura won the 2009 U.S. Chess Championship (St Louis, Missouri, May 2009), scoring 7/9 to take clear first place.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-28)

In July 2009, Nakamura won the [Donostia-San Sebastian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donostia-San_Sebastian "Donostia-San Sebastian") Chess Festival, tying with former FIDE world champion [Ruslan Ponomariov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruslan_Ponomariov "Ruslan Ponomariov") with 6½/9 before defeating Ponomariov in a blitz playoff to win the title over a field including former undisputed world champion [Anatoly Karpov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoly_Karpov "Anatoly Karpov"), former FIDE world champions [Rustam Kasimdzhanov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustam_Kasimdzhanov "Rustam Kasimdzhanov") and Ponomariov, 2009 World Junior champion [Maxime Vachier-Lagrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxime_Vachier-Lagrave "Maxime Vachier-Lagrave"), and [Peter Svidler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Svidler "Peter Svidler") among others.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-29)

In November 2009, Nakamura participated in the BNbank blitz tournament in Oslo, Norway. He reached the final by winning all 12 of his games. In the championship, he faced the world No. 2 and reigning World Blitz Champion [Magnus Carlsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen "Magnus Carlsen"). Nakamura won the match 3–1, further cementing his reputation as one of the best blitz players in the world, despite having not been invited to the 2009 World Blitz championship.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-31)

Nakamura skipped the [2009 FIDE World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_World_Cup_2009 "Chess World Cup 2009") in favor of the [London Chess Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Chess_Classic "London Chess Classic") in December 2009. Although he drew with the black pieces against eventual winner Magnus Carlsen and with White against former world champion [Vladimir Kramnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Kramnik "Vladimir Kramnik"), Nakamura failed to win a game during the tournament and ended in seventh place.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-32)

### 2010: Gold medalist and top-ten player

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hikaru_Nakamura&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2010: Gold medalist and top-ten player")]

Nakamura began 2010 playing first board for the US at the [World Team Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Team_Chess_Championship "World Team Chess Championship") held in [Bursa, Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bursa,_Turkey "Bursa, Turkey"). His performance, including a win over world No. 6 [Boris Gelfand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Gelfand "Boris Gelfand") on the black side of a [King's Indian Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Indian_Defense "King's Indian Defense"), won him the gold medal for board one and led the U.S. to a silver medal finish behind Russia.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-34)

Nakamura participated in the [Corus Chess Tournament 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corus_Chess_Tournament_2010 "Corus Chess Tournament 2010"). He finished with a score of 7½/13, tying for fourth place with [Viswanathan Anand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viswanathan_Anand "Viswanathan Anand").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-35)

In May, Nakamura participated in the 2010 [U.S. Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Chess_Championship "U.S. Chess Championship") in [Saint Louis, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Louis "St Louis"). Seeded first, he scored 5/7 points to qualify for the round-robin stage against the former champions [Gata Kamsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gata_Kamsky "Gata Kamsky"), [Alexander Onischuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Onischuk "Alexander Onischuk"), and [Yuri Shulman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Shulman "Yuri Shulman"). In the round-robin stage, he drew with Kamsky before losing to Shulman, with the white pieces in both games.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-36) The loss to Shulman eliminated him from the competition.

From November 5–14, Nakamura competed in the 2010 [Mikhail Tal Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Tal_Memorial "Mikhail Tal Memorial") in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"); the field consisted of [Levon Aronian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levon_Aronian "Levon Aronian"), [Vladimir Kramnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Kramnik "Vladimir Kramnik"), [Alexander Grischuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Grischuk "Alexander Grischuk"), [Shakhriyar Mamedyarov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakhriyar_Mamedyarov "Shakhriyar Mamedyarov"), [Sergey Karjakin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Karjakin "Sergey Karjakin"), [Pavel Eljanov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavel_Eljanov "Pavel Eljanov"), [Boris Gelfand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Gelfand "Boris Gelfand"), [Alexei Shirov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexei_Shirov "Alexei Shirov"), and [Wang Hao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Hao_(chess_player) "Wang Hao (chess player)"). The average Elo of the field was 2757, making it the third-strongest tournament in chess history at the time. Nakamura finished with +1, defeating Eljanov and drawing every other player to finish in a tie for fourth place.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-37) Nakamura's round two win over Eljanov placed him in the world top-ten in the live ratings for the first time in his career.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-38) Nakamura's performance at this tournament, his first involving an entirely super-elite field allowed him to "force (the chess elite) to respect him", according to noted Russian commentator grandmaster [Sergey Shipov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Shipov "Sergei Shipov").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-39)

From November 16–18, Nakamura made his debut at the 2010 [World Blitz Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Blitz_Championship "World Blitz Championship") in Moscow. Despite losing four of his first five games to [Magnus Carlsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen "Magnus Carlsen"), [Vladimir Kramnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Kramnik "Vladimir Kramnik"), [Maxime Vachier-Lagrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxime_Vachier-Lagrave "Maxime Vachier-Lagrave"), and [Sergey Karjakin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Karjakin "Sergey Karjakin"), he recovered to score 5/7 in the second half of the day and finished with a score of 7½/14, 2½ points behind co-leaders Carlsen and [Levon Aronian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levon_Aronian "Levon Aronian"), whom he defeated in their individual games. On the second day, Nakamura avenged his earlier losses against both Carlsen and Kramnik and scored 8/14, for a total of 15½/28, three points behind Aronian and a point and a half behind Carlsen. Nakamura finished with 21½/38 for fifth place.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-40)

In December 2010, Nakamura finished fourth in the [London Chess Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Chess_Classic "London Chess Classic"), among a field including Anand, [Carlsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen "Magnus Carlsen"), Kramnik, [Michael Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Adams_(chess_player) "Michael Adams (chess player)"), [Nigel Short](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Short "Nigel Short"), [David Howell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Howell_(chess_player) "David Howell (chess player)"), and [Luke McShane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luke_McShane "Luke McShane").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-41) Nakamura's performance ensured that he would officially join the world top ten in January 2011.

### 2011: Tata Steel Group A victory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hikaru_Nakamura&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2011: Tata Steel Group A victory")]

Nakamura began training with former world champion [Garry Kasparov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garry_Kasparov "Garry Kasparov"). The first of several training sessions were held in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)") at the beginning of January,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-42) but the training ended in December 2011.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-43)

From January 14–30, Nakamura competed in the [Tata Steel Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tata_Steel_Chess_Tournament_2011 "Tata Steel Chess Tournament 2011") in [Wijk aan Zee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wijk_aan_Zee "Wijk aan Zee") among a field of [Magnus Carlsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen "Magnus Carlsen"), [Viswanathan Anand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viswanathan_Anand "Viswanathan Anand"), [Levon Aronian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levon_Aronian "Levon Aronian"), [Vladimir Kramnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Kramnik "Vladimir Kramnik"), [Alexander Grischuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Grischuk "Alexander Grischuk"), [Ruslan Ponomariov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruslan_Ponomariov "Ruslan Ponomariov"), [Ian Nepomniachtchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Nepomniachtchi "Ian Nepomniachtchi"), [Wang Hao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Hao_(chess_player) "Wang Hao (chess player)"), [Maxime Vachier-Lagrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxime_Vachier-Lagrave "Maxime Vachier-Lagrave"), [Alexei Shirov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexei_Shirov "Alexei Shirov"), [Anish Giri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anish_Giri "Anish Giri"), [Jan Smeets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Smeets "Jan Smeets"), and [Erwin L'Ami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erwin_L%27Ami "Erwin L'Ami"). The average rating of the field was 2740, making this thirteen-round event a category 20 tournament. After twelve rounds, Nakamura was in clear first place with 8½ points going into the final round, half a point ahead of Anand and a full point ahead of Carlsen and Aronian.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-45) In the final round, Nakamura drew against Wang with the black pieces in a [King's Indian Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Indian_Defense "King's Indian Defense"). With the draw, Nakamura finished with 9/13 (+5), a tournament [performance rating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performance_rating_(chess) "Performance rating (chess)") of 2879, and guaranteed at least a share of first place. With Anand's final round draw against Nepomniachtchi, Nakamura clinched sole possession of first place,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-46) making him the first American to win the Wijk aan Zee tournament since 1980. The win also guaranteed that Nakamura would join Carlsen (winner of the 2010 [Pearl Spring chess tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Spring_chess_tournament "Pearl Spring chess tournament")) as qualifiers for [Grand Slam Masters Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilbao_Chess_Masters_Final "Bilbao Chess Masters Final") 2011 in September 2011.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-47) Nakamura after the tournament stated that his goal was to reach a 2800 rating by the end of the year; the win raised his rating from 2751 to 2774 and from world No. 10 to world No. 7 on the unofficial live rating list.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-48)

Kasparov called Nakamura's victory the best by an American in more than 100 years:

> In an e-mail, Kasparov said, "Fischer never won a tournament ahead of the world champion. He was second in Santa Monica", referring to the Second [Piatigorsky Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piatigorsky_Cup "Piatigorsky Cup"). "Of course, there were far fewer such events back then, and Fischer had several great tournament results like Stockholm 62", the interzonal qualifier for the world championship. "Reuben Fine only equaled Keres on points at AVRO in 38." Referring to the breakout performance of Frank J. Marshall, the United States Champion from 1909 to 1936, Mr. Kasparov continued, "Then you have Marshall at Cambridge Springs in 1904 ahead of Lasker, though Tarrasch wasn't there. So unless you include Capablanca as an American player, I think you can go back to Pillsbury at Hastings 1895 for an American tournament victory on par with Nakamura's.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-Kasparov2011-49)

Following his super tournament triumph, Nakamura was given the [key to the city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_to_the_city "Key to the city") of [Memphis, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee") on February 15, 2011.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-50) The victory also opened the door for Nakamura to receive invitations from other super grandmaster tournaments for the first time, and increased his world ranking to a career-high number eight. In May, he contested a six-game match in the United States against world No. 11 Ponomariov, where he lost the first game but rallied to win the match 3½–2½, raising his rating to 2777 and ranking to world No. 6 on the unofficial live rating list, both career-highs to that date. From June 11–21, he made his debut at the Bazna Kings Tournament in Romania in a field including Carlsen, world No. 5 [Vassily Ivanchuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassily_Ivanchuk "Vassily Ivanchuk"), world No. 6 [Sergey Karjakin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Karjakin "Sergey Karjakin"), world No. 13 [Teimour Radjabov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teimour_Radjabov "Teimour Radjabov") and [Liviu-Dieter Nisipeanu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liviu-Dieter_Nisipeanu "Liviu-Dieter Nisipeanu"); the tournament was a Category XXI event with an average ELO of 2760, making it the third strongest tournament in history; Nakamura finished 4½/10; the tournament was won by Carlsen on tiebreak over Karjakin.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-51)

From July 21–31, Nakamura made his debut at [Dortmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dortmund_Sparkassen_Chess_Meeting "Dortmund Sparkassen Chess Meeting"); the field consisted of Kramnik, Ponomariov, [Lê Quang Liêm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%AA_Quang_Li%C3%AAm "Lê Quang Liêm"), Giri, and [Georg Meier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Meier_(chess_player) "Georg Meier (chess player)").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-52) Nakamura had a second consecutive disappointing performance, beginning at −3 before winning his last two games, including a last-round win over tournament winner Kramnik on the black side of the [King's Indian Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Indian_Defense "King's Indian Defense"), to finish at 4½/10.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-53)

Nakamura competed in the [Grand Slam Masters Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilbao_Chess_Masters_Final "Bilbao Chess Masters Final") 2011 in September, after which he played in the [Tal Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tal_Memorial "Tal Memorial") for the second consecutive year in a field comprising Carlsen, Anand, Aronian, Karjakin, Kramnik, Ivanchuk, Gelfand, Hao, and Nepomniachtchi. He finished the year by participating in the [London Chess Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Chess_Classic "London Chess Classic") for the third consecutive time.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-54)

### 2012: Third U.S. Championship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hikaru_Nakamura&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2012: Third U.S. Championship")]

Starting in 2012, he participated in the Reggio Emilia Tournament, tying for second with Alexander Morozevich and Fabiano Caruana. Nakamura then played in the Tata Steel Chess Tournament, finishing fifth.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-55) He won the US Championship in May with a score of 8½, one point ahead of [Gata Kamsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gata_Kamsky "Gata Kamsky").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-56)

In June 2012, Nakamura played at the [Tal Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tal_Memorial "Tal Memorial") in Moscow. In a tightly bunched field, he finished tied for eighth with [Luke McShane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luke_McShane "Luke McShane"), 1½ points behind winner [Magnus Carlsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen "Magnus Carlsen").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-57) He participated in the [Biel Chess Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biel_Chess_Festival "Biel Chess Festival"), finishing third with [Anish Giri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anish_Giri "Anish Giri"), behind Carlsen and [Wang Hao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Hao_(chess_player) "Wang Hao (chess player)").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-58) At the 2012 Chess Olympiad in August and September, he led the U.S. team to a fifth-place finish with a +4−1=4 record on the first board.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-59) Nakamura then suffered through the FIDE London Grand Prix tournament, at one point losing four games in a row. He finished tied for last with Giri.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-60) After another lackluster performance in the European Club Championship in Eilat, Israel, Nakamura finished first in the "crown group" at the Univé tournament in Hoogeveen, the Netherlands.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-61) In December he tied for third with Mickey Adams in the London Chess Classic with a +3−1=4 score.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-62) Nakamura finished the year by winning three silver medals in the three chess events (rapid, blitz and blindfold) at the [World Mind Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Mind_Sports_Games "World Mind Sports Games") in Beijing.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-63)

After what was to him a disappointing tournament at the fifth edition of the King's Tournament in [Medias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medias "Medias") (although Nakamura placed third of six among a cadre of top Grandmasters),[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-64) Nakamura tweeted that he was focusing on the [2011 World Series of Poker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_World_Series_of_Poker "2011 World Series of Poker"),[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-65) in which he played, although busted out on the second day.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-66) Kasparov, who had been training Nakamura at the time, publicly grumbled about his interest in poker.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-67)

### 2013: Top FIDE blitz rating

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hikaru_Nakamura&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2013: Top FIDE blitz rating")]

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/TataSteelChess2013CarlsenNakamura.jpg/500px-TataSteelChess2013CarlsenNakamura.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TataSteelChess2013CarlsenNakamura.jpg)

Nakamura vs Carlsen from the Tata Steel 2013

Nakamura began 2013 with a 7/13 (+3−2=8) result at the Tata Steel tournament in [Wijk aan Zee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wijk_aan_Zee "Wijk aan Zee"), finishing sixth.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-68) He scored a win against then world number five [Fabiano Caruana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabiano_Caruana "Fabiano Caruana") with the black pieces in an [Old Indian Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Indian_Defense "Old Indian Defense"). He then played at the [FIDE Grand Prix tournament in Zug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIDE_Grand_Prix_2012%E2%80%9313#Zug_2013 "FIDE Grand Prix 2012–13"), Switzerland in April, scoring 6½/11 (+3−1=7) and finishing clear second behind [Veselin Topalov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veselin_Topalov "Veselin Topalov").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-69)

Nakamura did not participate in the 2013 U.S. championship. Instead, he played in the [Norway Chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway_Chess "Norway Chess") tournament, finishing tied with [Magnus Carlsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen "Magnus Carlsen") for second behind winner [Sergey Karjakin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Karjakin "Sergey Karjakin"). His 5½/9 score (+4−2=3) featured a win over then-world champion [Viswanathan Anand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viswanathan_Anand "Viswanathan Anand") with the black pieces in a [Ruy Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruy_Lopez "Ruy Lopez").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-70) He then scored 5/11 at the [FIDE Grand Prix in Thessaloniki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIDE_Grand_Prix_2012%E2%80%9313#Thessaloniki_2013 "FIDE Grand Prix 2012–13"), Greece.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-71) Nakamura had an up-and-down Tal Memorial in June, at one point winning three straight games and then later losing three straight. He finished in sixth place with a 4½/9 score (+4−4=1).[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-72) However, he won the blitz tournament before the classical competition, raising his FIDE blitz rating to 2879, first in the world at the time. In the [World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_World_Cup_2013 "Chess World Cup 2013") in Tromsø, Norway, Nakamura scored 6/8 (+5−1=2), eventually losing in the fourth round to [Anton Korobov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Korobov "Anton Korobov").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-73) Nakamura finished second at the [Sinquefield Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinquefield_Cup "Sinquefield Cup") in his hometown of St. Louis, behind Carlsen with a 3½/6 (+2−1=3) score, including a win over then world number two [Levon Aronian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levon_Aronian "Levon Aronian").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-74)

At the [FIDE Grand Prix in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIDE_Grand_Prix_2012%E2%80%9313#Paris_2013 "FIDE Grand Prix 2012–13"), Nakamura scored 6½/11 (+3−1=7) and tied for third with [Étienne Bacrot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tienne_Bacrot "Étienne Bacrot"), behind co-winners Caruana and [Boris Gelfand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Gelfand "Boris Gelfand"). He defeated Caruana in their individual encounter but lost to Gelfand. Overall, Nakamura finished sixth in the FIDE Grand Prix 2012–13 series.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-75) He then played first board for O.R. Padova in the [European Club Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Chess_Club_Cup "European Chess Club Cup") in Rhodes, Greece and scored 4/6 (+2−0=4).[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-76) He defeated current Russian champion [Peter Svidler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Svidler "Peter Svidler") with the black pieces in an extremely sharp King's Indian Defense.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-77) At the [World Team Chess Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Team_Chess_Championship "World Team Chess Championship") in [Antalya, Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antalya,_Turkey "Antalya, Turkey"), Nakamura led the U.S. team to a fourth-place finish.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-78) His personal record of 4½/7 (+3−1=3) earned him an individual silver medal on board one.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-79) Nakamura closed out his tournament schedule for the year with a win at the [London Chess Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Chess_Classic "London Chess Classic"), which was converted to a [rapid chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_chess "Rapid chess") event in 2013. He won his pool in the first stage of the tournament, then defeated [Nigel Short](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Short "Nigel Short"), [Vladimir Kramnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Kramnik "Vladimir Kramnik"), and [Boris Gelfand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Gelfand "Boris Gelfand") in the knockout stage. His overall record was +5−0=7.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-80)

### 2014: No. 3 ranking and Zurich Chess Challenge

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hikaru_Nakamura&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2014: No. 3 ranking and Zurich Chess Challenge")]

Entering 2014, Nakamura had achieved a No. 3 position in the FIDE ratings, below Carlsen and Aronian. He began his 2014 schedule with a ninth-place finish in the [Tata Steel Chess Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tata_Steel_Chess_Tournament "Tata Steel Chess Tournament") at Wijk Aan Zee, with a 5/11 score (+2−3=6).[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-81) He then played the [Zurich Chess Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zurich_Chess_Challenge "Zurich Chess Challenge"), drawing with Caruana in the first round and winning against Anand in the second. In the third round, Nakamura achieved a winning position against Carlsen but later made several mistakes and eventually lost the game.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-82) Nakamura finished fourth of the six players in the event, with a 7½/15 score.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-83)

In April, Nakamura finished third of the six players in the [Gashimov Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gashimov_Memorial "Gashimov Memorial"). In the double round-robin event, he lost both of his games to Carlsen but defeated [Shakhriyar Mamedyarov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakhriyar_Mamedyarov "Shakhriyar Mamedyarov") twice to close with a 5/10 score (+2−2=6).[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-84) He then played a four-game match against Czech grandmaster [David Navara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Navara "David Navara") in June and won easily 3½/4.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-85)

In November, Nakamura played a match against Levon Aronian consisting of four classical and sixteen blitz games. The two tied the classical games 2–2; Nakamura won the match with a 9½–6½ score in blitz games.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-86)

### 2015: 2800 rating and fourth U.S. Championship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hikaru_Nakamura&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2015: 2800 rating and fourth U.S. Championship")]

In January, Nakamura won the Gibraltar Chess Masters tournament, scoring 8½/10 (+7−0=3).[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-87) In February, Nakamura won the [Zurich Chess Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zurich_Chess_Challenge "Zurich Chess Challenge") after a playoff event to settle a tie.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-88) Nakamura had one of his best-ever months as a chess professional in February 2015, and as a result on the March FIDE classical list Nakamura moved to his then-career highest 2798 and No. 3 in the world.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-89) That April, Nakamura won his fourth U.S. Chess Championship with a score of 8/11.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-90) In the final stage of the 4-stage Grand Prix event, Nakamura finished equal first with Fabiano Caruana and Dmitry Jakovenko with 6½ out of 11 points at Khanty-Mansiysk, giving him an overall second place Grand Prix placement, which automatically qualified him for the Candidates tournament to determine the challenger for Magnus Carlsen in the next Chess World Championship.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-91) In the first stage of the June [Norway Chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway_Chess "Norway Chess") tournament for the [Grand Chess Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Chess_Tour "Grand Chess Tour"), Nakamura finished equal second with Viswanathan Anand with 6 out of 9 points and a 2900 performance. This gave Nakamura 8 points in the first leg of the Grand Chess Tour. It also propelled his rating to a career-high of 2814 and put him at number 4 in the July 2015 world rankings.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-92)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-93)

### 2016–2018: Multiple Tournament Victories and Grand Chess Tour

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hikaru_Nakamura&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2016–2018: Multiple Tournament Victories and Grand Chess Tour")]

In February 2016, Nakamura won the [Gibraltar Chess Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibraltar_Chess_Festival "Gibraltar Chess Festival") for the second year in a row, scoring 8/10 (+6−0=4) and beating [Maxime Vachier-Lagrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxime_Vachier-Lagrave "Maxime Vachier-Lagrave") on tiebreaks.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-94) That same month, he also won the Zurich Chess Challenge for the second year in a row. He tied with [Viswanathan Anand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viswanathan_Anand "Viswanathan Anand") on the number of points; however, Nakamura was declared the overall winner due to his higher [Sonneborn–Berger score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonneborn%E2%80%93Berger_score "Sonneborn–Berger score").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-95) In March 2016, Nakamura came seventh out of eight in the [Candidates Tournament 2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candidates_Tournament_2016 "Candidates Tournament 2016"), which decided the challenger—[Sergey Karjakin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Karjakin "Sergey Karjakin")—to face Magnus Carlsen for the [World Chess Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Chess_Championship "World Chess Championship"). He scored 7/14, as did the three players directly above him.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-96) In September 2016, Nakamura was part of the U.S. team that won the 42nd Chess Olympiad that took place in [Baku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baku "Baku"), [Azerbaijan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azerbaijan "Azerbaijan").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-97)

In January–February 2017, Nakamura won the [Gibraltar Chess Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibraltar_Chess_Festival "Gibraltar Chess Festival") with a score of 8/10 points (+6−0=4) and beating [David Antón Guijarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Ant%C3%B3n_Guijarro "David Antón Guijarro") in the tie-break final by 1½–½.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-98)

In January 2018, Nakamura took second place in the [Chess.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess.com "Chess.com") Speed Chess Championships after winning matches in 2017 with Sergey Grigoriants, [Fabiano Caruana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabiano_Caruana "Fabiano Caruana"), and then-World Blitz Champion [Sergey Karjakin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergey_Karjakin "Sergey Karjakin"), only losing to Carlsen in the January finals.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-99) That February, Nakamura participated in the unofficial [Chess960](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess960 "Chess960") Championship, losing 10–14 to Carlsen.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-100) From May 28 to June 7, he competed in the [sixth edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway_Chess#2018 "Norway Chess") of Norway Chess, placing third with 4½/8 (+1–0=7).[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-101) The Paris Grand Chess Tour Rapid and Blitz tournament took place 20 to 24 June 2018. Nakamura won the event with 23 points, ahead of [Sergei Karjakin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Karjakin "Sergei Karjakin") with 21½ points and [Wesley So](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesley_So "Wesley So") who had 21 points. Nakamura won the St. Louis Rapid & Blitz tournament that ran from 11 to 15 August 2018.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-102)

Nakamura won the Rapid portion of the inaugural Tata Steel India Chess tournament, held in November 2018 in [Kolkata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolkata "Kolkata").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-103) He also finished runner-up, losing 1½–½ in a tiebreaker to [Viswanathan Anand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viswanathan_Anand "Viswanathan Anand"), in the blitz portion of the same event.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-105) From December 11–17, Nakamura defeated [Fabiano Caruana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabiano_Caruana "Fabiano Caruana") with a score of 18–10[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-106) in the semifinal match at the [London Chess Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Chess_Classic "London Chess Classic") and, in the final match with [Maxime Vachier-Lagrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxime_Vachier-Lagrave "Maxime Vachier-Lagrave"), scored a victory in the fourth and final blitz game after the previous seven games were drawn.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-CB_2018_GCT-107) Nakamura thus won the 2018 [Grand Chess Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Chess_Tour "Grand Chess Tour").[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-CB_2018_GCT-107)

### 2019: Fifth U.S. Championship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hikaru_Nakamura&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 2019: Fifth U.S. Championship")]

In March, Nakamura won his fifth U.S. Chess Championship by a score of 8/11.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-108)

In April, Nakamura won the Bullet Chess Championship hosted by [Chess.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess.com "Chess.com").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-109) Defeating Grandmasters [Alireza Firouzja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alireza_Firouzja "Alireza Firouzja") and [Levon Aronian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levon_Aronian "Levon Aronian") in the quarterfinals and the semifinals, respectively, he then defeated Ukrainian Grandmaster [Olexandr Bortnyk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olexandr_Bortnyk "Olexandr Bortnyk") to win the tournament.

In early May, Nakamura shared second place[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-110) with French grandmaster [Maxime Vachier-Lagrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxime_Vachier-Lagrave "Maxime Vachier-Lagrave") in the first leg of the 2019 [Grand Chess Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Chess_Tour "Grand Chess Tour") which was held in [Côte d’Ivoire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B4te_d%E2%80%99Ivoire "Côte d’Ivoire"). The tournament was a combination [rapid & blitz format](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_chess "Fast chess"), with world champion [Magnus Carlsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen "Magnus Carlsen") placing first.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-111)

In late May, Hikaru participated in the Moscow [FIDE Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIDE_Grand_Prix_2019#Events_Results "FIDE Grand Prix 2019") tournament, which is part of the qualification cycle for the [2020 World Chess Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Chess_Championship_2020 "World Chess Championship 2020"). The tournament was a 16-player event. Nakamura defeated grandmasters [Teimour Radjabov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teimour_Radjabov "Teimour Radjabov") and [Daniil Dubov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniil_Dubov "Daniil Dubov") but lost to grandmaster [Alexander Grischuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Grischuk "Alexander Grischuk") in the semi-final match.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-112)

In early September, Hikaru participated in the Champions Showdown: [Chess 9LX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fischer_random_chess "Fischer random chess")[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-113) tournament, which featured seven other grandmasters playing a 4-day match in [Chess960](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess960 "Chess960"). Players faced only one opponent through the entire event. Hikaru was paired against [Levon Aronian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levon_Aronian "Levon Aronian").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-114) Despite scoring only half a point out of 8 at the start of the match, Hikaru eventually defeated Aronian by a score of 14½ to 11½.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-115)

### 2020: Magnus Carlsen Chess Tour

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hikaru_Nakamura&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 2020: Magnus Carlsen Chess Tour")]

Nakamura started 2020 as the top-ranked blitz chess player in the world. Owing to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), chess moved online, with Nakamura playing an important role in popularizing it.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-116)

Since April 2020, Nakamura participated in the [Magnus Carlsen Chess Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen_Chess_Tour "Magnus Carlsen Chess Tour") with a prize pool of $1 million.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-117) He won the group stage of [Magnus Carlsen Invitational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen_Invitational "Magnus Carlsen Invitational") and finished second behind [Magnus Carlsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnus_Carlsen "Magnus Carlsen"). He beat Carlsen in the semi-finals of [Lindores Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindores_Abbey "Lindores Abbey") Rapid Challenge but finished second, losing to eventual champion Daniil Dubov in the final. Nakamura qualified for the Magnus Carlsen Chess Tour Finals against Carlsen, where he took his opponent to seven matches before drawing an [armageddon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_chess#Armageddon "Fast chess") tiebreaker game as white, thus losing the match. The world champion praised Nakamura after the match, saying, "he played a great match, he made it extremely difficult for me".[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-118)

In September, Nakamura tied for first with Carlsen in Champions Showdown: Chess 9LX[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-119) and finished third in St. Louis Rapid & Blitz.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-120)

After many victories in shorter tournaments on [Chess.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess.com "Chess.com"), including Titled Tuesday[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-121) and Super Swiss,[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-122) Nakamura failed in his defense of his [U.S. Chess Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Chess_Championship "U.S. Chess Championship") title, finishing seventh. The tournament, which took place online in a rapid format, was won by [Wesley So](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesley_So "Wesley So").[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-123)

In October, Nakamura held a 77-board charity simultaneous exhibition online, raising around $9,500 for [Doctors Without Borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctors_Without_Borders "Doctors Without Borders").[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-124) Before the [2020 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"), he challenged President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") to a game of chess to raise funds for the presidential nominee [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden")’s victory fund and [ActBlue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ActBlue "ActBlue").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-125)

Nakamura won the Chess.com Speed Chess Championship in December. It was his third victory in the format. The site promoted the knockout tournament by emphasizing a possible rematch of Nakamura and world champion Magnus Carlsen in the final. However, French grandmaster [Maxime Vachier-Lagrave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxime_Vachier-Lagrave "Maxime Vachier-Lagrave") defeated Carlsen in their semi-final match, earning a spot in the final against Nakamura. In the Speed Chess Championship final, Nakamura defeated Vachier-Lagrave by a score of 18½ to 12½. Nakamura's skill at bullet chess proved to be the deciding factor, as he beat Vachier-Lagrave 8–3 in the bullet section of the match. Previous to the final, Nakamura had defeated grandmasters [Haik Martirosyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haik_M._Martirosyan "Haik M. Martirosyan") 21–5, [Vladimir Fedoseev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Fedoseev "Vladimir Fedoseev") 21½–5½, and [Wesley So](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesley_So "Wesley So") 13½–12½.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikaru_Nakamura#cite_note-126)

From November, Nakamura participated in the [Champions Chess Tour 2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champions_Chess_Tour_2021 "Champions Chess Tour 2021"), qualifying for the knockout stage of [Skilling Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skilling_Open "Skilling Open") and [Airthings Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champions_Chess_Tour_2021#Airthings_Masters "Champions Chess Tour 2021").
