The resulting merger is an [excited state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excited_state "Excited state")[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-23)—termed a [compound nucleus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reaction#Compound_nuclear_reactions "Nuclear reaction")—and thus it is very unstable.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_n+1-18) To reach a more stable state, the temporary merger may [fission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fission "Nuclear fission") without formation of a more stable nucleus.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_CzechNuclear-24) Alternatively, the compound nucleus may eject a few [neutrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron "Neutron"), which would carry away the excitation energy; if the latter is not sufficient for a neutron expulsion, the merger would produce a [gamma ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_ray "Gamma ray"). This happens in about 10−16 seconds after the initial nuclear collision and results in creation of a more stable nucleus.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_CzechNuclear-24) The definition by the [IUPAC/IUPAP Joint Working Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUPAC/IUPAP_Joint_Working_Party "IUPAC/IUPAP Joint Working Party") (JWP) states that a [chemical element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element") can only be recognized as discovered if a nucleus of it has not [decayed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_decay "Radioactive decay") within 10−14 seconds. This value was chosen as an estimate of how long it takes a nucleus to acquire [electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron") and thus display its chemical properties.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-25)[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-27)

### Decay and detection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Module:Excerpt&action=edit&section=T-2 "Edit section: Decay and detection")]

The beam passes through the target and reaches the next chamber, the separator; if a new nucleus is produced, it is carried with this beam.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_SHEhowvideo-28) In the separator, the newly produced nucleus is separated from other nuclides (that of the original beam and any other reaction products)[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-31) and transferred to a [surface-barrier detector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_detector "Semiconductor detector"), which stops the nucleus. The exact location of the upcoming impact on the detector is marked; also marked are its energy and the time of the arrival.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_SHEhowvideo-28) The transfer takes about 10−6 seconds; in order to be detected, the nucleus must survive this long.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZagrebaevKarpovGreiner20133-32) The nucleus is recorded again once its decay is registered, and the location, the [energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decay_energy "Decay energy"), and the time of the decay are measured.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_SHEhowvideo-28)

Stability of a nucleus is provided by the strong interaction. However, its range is very short; as nuclei become larger, its influence on the outermost [nucleons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleon "Nucleon") ([protons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton "Proton") and neutrons) weakens. At the same time, the nucleus is torn apart by electrostatic repulsion between protons, and its range is not limited.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeiser2003432-33) Total [binding energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_binding_energy "Nuclear binding energy") provided by the strong interaction increases linearly with the number of nucleons, whereas electrostatic repulsion increases with the square of the atomic number, i.e. the latter grows faster and becomes increasingly important for heavy and superheavy nuclei.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsAlpha-34)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsSF-35) Superheavy nuclei are thus theoretically predicted[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-36) and have so far been observed[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAudi_et_al.2017030001-129%E2%80%93030001-138-37) to predominantly decay via decay modes that are caused by such repulsion: [alpha decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_decay "Alpha decay") and [spontaneous fission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_fission "Spontaneous fission").[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-39) Almost all alpha emitters have over 210 nucleons,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeiser2003433-40) and the lightest nuclide primarily undergoing spontaneous fission has 238.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAudi_et_al.2017030001-125-41) In both decay modes, nuclei are inhibited from decaying by corresponding [energy barriers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectangular_potential_barrier "Rectangular potential barrier") for each mode, but they can be tunneled through.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsAlpha-34)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsSF-35)

[![Image 4: Apparatus for creation of superheavy elements](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Apparatus_for_creation_of_superheavy_elements_en.svg/500px-Apparatus_for_creation_of_superheavy_elements_en.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apparatus_for_creation_of_superheavy_elements_en.svg)

Scheme of an apparatus for creation of superheavy elements, based on the Dubna Gas-Filled Recoil Separator set up in the [Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flerov_Laboratory_of_Nuclear_Reactions "Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions") in JINR. The trajectory within the detector and the beam focusing apparatus changes because of a [dipole magnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dipole "Magnetic dipole") in the former and [quadrupole magnets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadrupole_magnet "Quadrupole magnet") in the latter.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_Aksenov-42)

Alpha particles are commonly produced in radioactive decays because the mass of an alpha particle per nucleon is small enough to leave some energy for the alpha particle to be used as kinetic energy to leave the nucleus.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeiser2003432%E2%80%93433-43) Spontaneous fission is caused by electrostatic repulsion tearing the nucleus apart and produces various nuclei in different instances of identical nuclei fissioning.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsSF-35) As the atomic number increases, spontaneous fission rapidly becomes more important: spontaneous fission partial half-lives decrease by 23 orders of magnitude from [uranium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium "Uranium") (element 92) to [nobelium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobelium "Nobelium") (element 102),[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_Oganessian12-44) and by 30 orders of magnitude from [thorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thorium "Thorium") (element 90) to [fermium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermium "Fermium") (element 100).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-45) The earlier [liquid drop model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_drop_model "Liquid drop model") thus suggested that spontaneous fission would occur nearly instantly due to disappearance of the [fission barrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fission_barrier "Fission barrier") for nuclei with about 280 nucleons.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsSF-35)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_Oganessian04-46) The later [nuclear shell model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_shell_model "Nuclear shell model") suggested that nuclei with about 300 nucleons would form an [island of stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_of_stability "Island of stability") in which nuclei will be more resistant to spontaneous fission and will primarily undergo alpha decay with longer half-lives.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsSF-35)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_Oganessian04-46) Subsequent discoveries suggested that the predicted island might be further than originally anticipated; they also showed that nuclei intermediate between the long-lived actinides and the predicted island are deformed, and gain additional stability from shell effects.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-47) Experiments on lighter superheavy nuclei,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-48) as well as those closer to the expected island,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_Oganessian12-44) have shown greater than previously anticipated stability against spontaneous fission, showing the importance of shell effects on nuclei.[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-49)

Alpha decays are registered by the emitted alpha particles, and the decay products are easy to determine before the actual decay; if such a decay or a series of consecutive decays produces a known nucleus, the original product of a reaction can be easily determined.[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-53) (That all decays within a decay chain were indeed related to each other is established by the location of these decays, which must be in the same place.)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_SHEhowvideo-28) The known nucleus can be recognized by the specific characteristics of decay it undergoes such as decay energy (or more specifically, the [kinetic energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinetic_energy "Kinetic energy") of the emitted particle).[[i]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-54) Spontaneous fission, however, produces various nuclei as products, so the original nuclide cannot be determined from its daughters.[[j]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-57)

The information available to physicists aiming to synthesize a superheavy element is thus the information collected at the detectors: location, energy, and time of arrival of a particle to the detector, and those of its decay. The physicists analyze this data and seek to conclude that it was indeed caused by a new element and could not have been caused by a different nuclide than the one claimed. Often, provided data is insufficient for a conclusion that a new element was definitely created and there is no other explanation for the observed effects; errors in interpreting data have been made.[[k]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-63)

Elements 114 to 118 ([flerovium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flerovium "Flerovium") through [oganesson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oganesson "Oganesson")) were discovered in "hot fusion" reactions bombarding the actinides [plutonium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium "Plutonium") through [californium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Californium "Californium") with [calcium-48](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium-48 "Calcium-48"), a quasi-stable neutron-rich isotope which could be used as a projectile to produce more neutron-rich isotopes of superheavy elements.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Folden-64) This cannot easily be continued to elements 119 and 120, because it would require a target of the next actinides [einsteinium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einsteinium "Einsteinium") and [fermium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermium "Fermium"). Tens of milligrams of these would be needed to create such targets, but only micrograms of einsteinium and picograms of fermium have so far been produced.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-usprogram-65) More practical production of further superheavy elements would require bombarding actinides with projectiles heavier than 48 Ca,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Folden-64) but this is expected to be more difficult.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-usprogram-65) Attempts to synthesize elements 119 and 120 push the limits of current technology, due to the decreasing [cross sections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_(physics) "Cross section (physics)") of the production reactions and their probably short [half-lives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-life "Half-life"),[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZagrebaevKarpovGreiner2013-66) expected to be on the order of microseconds.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Hofmann-67)

Following their success in obtaining [oganesson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oganesson "Oganesson") by the reaction between [249 Cf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Californium-249 "Californium-249") and 48 Ca in 2006, the team at the [Joint Institute for Nuclear Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Institute_for_Nuclear_Research "Joint Institute for Nuclear Research") (JINR) in [Dubna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubna "Dubna") started experiments in March–April 2007 to attempt to create unbinilium with a [58 Fe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron-58 "Iron-58") beam and a [244 Pu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium-244 "Plutonium-244") target.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-68)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-69) The attempt was unsuccessful,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Oganessian120-70) and the Russian team planned to upgrade their facilities before attempting the reaction again.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Oganessian120-70)

244

26 Fe → 302

120 Ubn* → no atoms
In April 2007, the team at the [GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GSI_Helmholtz_Centre_for_Heavy_Ion_Research "GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research") in [Darmstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darmstadt "Darmstadt"), Germany attempted to create unbinilium using a 238[U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium "Uranium") target and a 64[Ni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel "Nickel") beam:[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-GSI08-71)

238

No atoms were detected. The GSI repeated the experiment with higher sensitivity in three separate runs in April–May 2007, January–March 2008, and September–October 2008, all with negative results, reaching a cross section limit of 90 fb.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-GSI08-71)

In 2011, after upgrading their equipment to allow the use of more radioactive targets, scientists at the GSI attempted the rather asymmetrical fusion reaction:[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Duellmann-72)

248

96 Cm + 54

24 Cr → 302

120 Ubn* → no atoms
It was expected that the change in reaction would quintuple the probability of synthesizing unbinilium,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-73) as the yield of such reactions is strongly dependent on their asymmetry.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZagrebaevKarpovGreiner2013-66) Although this reaction is less asymmetric than the 249 Cf+50 Ti reaction, it also creates more neutron-rich unbinilium isotopes that should receive increased stability from their proximity to the shell closure at _N_ = 184.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Hofmann2016-74) Three signals were observed in May 2011; a possible assignment to 299 Ubn and its daughters was considered,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-EXON-75) but could not be confirmed,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Hoffman-76)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-77)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Hofmann2016-74) and a different analysis suggested that what was observed was simply a random sequence of events.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-78)

In August–October 2011, a different team at the GSI using the TASCA facility tried a new, even more asymmetrical reaction:[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Duellmann-72)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Yakushev-79)

249

98 Cf + 50

22 Ti → 299

120 Ubn* → no atoms
Because of its asymmetry,[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-80) the reaction between 249 Cf and 50 Ti was predicted to be the most favorable practical reaction for synthesizing unbinilium, though it produces a less neutron-rich isotope of unbinilium than any other reaction studied. No unbinilium atoms were identified.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Yakushev-79)

This reaction was investigated again in April to September 2012 at the GSI. This experiment used a 249 Bk target and a 50 Ti beam to produce [element 119](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ununennium "Ununennium"), but since 249 Bk decays to 249 Cf with a half-life of about 327 days, both elements 119 and 120 could be searched for simultaneously:

249

22 Ti → 299

119 Uue* → no atoms 249

98 Cf + 50

22 Ti → 299

120 Ubn* → no atoms
Neither element 119 nor element 120 was observed.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-search-81)

The team at the [Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Berkeley_National_Laboratory "Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory") (LBNL) in [Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley,_California "Berkeley, California"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), United States had made plans to use the 88-inch cyclotron to make new elements using 50 Ti projectiles.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-usprogram-65) (Such a plan had already been made before the [Russian invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Russian invasion of Ukraine") began in 2022, cutting off collaborations between the JINR and other institutes, in response to theoretical predictions that an attempt to produce element 120 would be feasible.)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-nelson-82) First, the 244 Pu+50 Ti reaction was tested, successfully creating two atoms of 290 Lv in 2024. Since this was successful, an attempt to make element 120 in the 249 Cf+50 Ti reaction was planned to begin in late 2025.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-83)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-84)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-85)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-86) The [Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Livermore_National_Laboratory "Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory") (LLNL), which previously collaborated with the JINR, is collaborating with the LBNL on this project.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-nelson-82) By June 2025, updates were underway at the LBNL in preparation for the search for element 120,[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-87)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-88) and by September, the search had begun.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-89)

The JINR's plans to investigate the 249 Cf+50 Ti reaction in their new facility were disrupted by the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, after which collaboration between the JINR and other institutes completely ceased due to sanctions. Thus, 249 Cf could no longer be used as a target, as it would have to be produced at the [Oak Ridge National Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Ridge_National_Laboratory "Oak Ridge National Laboratory") (ORNL) in the United States.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-90)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-91)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-ft-92) Instead, the 248 Cm+54 Cr reaction will be used.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-93) In 2023, the director of the JINR, [Grigory Trubnikov](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grigory_Trubnikov&action=edit&redlink=1 "Grigory Trubnikov (page does not exist)"), stated that he hoped that the experiments to synthesise element 120 will begin in 2025.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-94) In preparation for this, the JINR reported success in the 238 U+54 Cr reaction in late 2023, making a new isotope of livermorium, [288 Lv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livermorium-288 "Livermorium-288"). This was an unexpectedly good result; the aim had been to experimentally determine the cross-section of a reaction with 54 Cr projectiles and prepare for the synthesis of element 120. It is the first successful reaction producing a superheavy element using an actinide target and a projectile heavier than 48 Ca.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Lv288-95)

The team at the Heavy Ion Research Facility in [Lanzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanzhou "Lanzhou"), which is operated by the [Institute of Modern Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Modern_Physics "Institute of Modern Physics") (IMP) of the [Chinese Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Academy_of_Sciences "Chinese Academy of Sciences"), also plans to synthesise elements 119 and 120. The reactions used will involve actinide targets (e.g. 243 Am, 248 Cm) and first-row transition metal projectiles (e.g. 50 Ti, 51 V, 54 Cr, 55 Mn).[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-96)

[Mendeleev's nomenclature for unnamed and undiscovered elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendeleev%27s_predicted_elements "Mendeleev's predicted elements") would call unbinilium _eka-[radium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium "Radium")_.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-97) The 1979 IUPAC [recommendations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systematic_element_name "Systematic element name")[temporarily call it](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Placeholder_name "Placeholder name")_unbinilium_ (symbol _Ubn_) until it is discovered, the discovery is confirmed and a permanent name chosen.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-iupac-98) Although the IUPAC systematic names are widely used in the chemical community on all levels, from chemistry classrooms to advanced textbooks, scientists who work theoretically or experimentally on superheavy elements typically call it "element 120", with the symbol _E120_, _(120)_ or _120_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1)

## Predicted properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Unbinilium&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Predicted properties")]

### Nuclear stability and isotopes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Unbinilium&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Nuclear stability and isotopes")]

[![Image 5: A 2D graph with rectangular cells colored in black-and-white colors, spanning from the llc to the urc, with cells mostly becoming lighter closer to the latter](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Island_of_Stability_derived_from_Zagrebaev.svg/960px-Island_of_Stability_derived_from_Zagrebaev.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Island_of_Stability_derived_from_Zagrebaev.svg)

A chart of nuclide stability as used by the Dubna team in 2010. Characterized isotopes are shown with borders. Beyond element 118 (oganesson, the last known element), the line of known nuclides is expected to rapidly enter a region of instability. The elliptical region encloses the predicted location of the island of stability, centered on element 112, [copernicium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copernicium "Copernicium").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZagrebaevKarpovGreiner2013-66)

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Next_proton_shell.svg/330px-Next_proton_shell.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Next_proton_shell.svg)

Orbitals with high [azimuthal quantum number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azimuthal_quantum_number "Azimuthal quantum number") are raised in energy, eliminating what would otherwise be a gap in orbital energy corresponding to a closed proton shell at element 114, as shown in the left diagram which does not take this effect into account. This raises the next proton shell to the region around element 120, as shown in the right diagram, potentially increasing the half-lives of element 119 and 120 isotopes.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Kratz-99)

The stability of nuclei decreases greatly with the increase in atomic number after [curium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curium "Curium"), element 96, whose half-life is four orders of magnitude longer than that of any currently known higher-numbered element. All isotopes with an atomic number above [101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendelevium "Mendelevium") undergo [radioactive decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_decay "Radioactive decay") with half-lives of less than 30 hours. No elements with atomic numbers above 82 (after [lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead "Lead")) have stable isotopes.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-100) Nevertheless, because of reasons not yet well understood, there is a slight increase of nuclear stability around atomic numbers [110](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darmstadtium "Darmstadtium")–[114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flerovium "Flerovium"), which leads to the appearance of what is known in nuclear physics as the "[island of stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_of_stability "Island of stability")". This concept, proposed by [University of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley") professor [Glenn Seaborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Seaborg "Glenn Seaborg"), explains why superheavy elements last longer than predicted.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-101)

Isotopes of unbinilium are predicted to have alpha decay half-lives of the order of [microseconds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsecond "Microsecond").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-prc08ADNDT08-102)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-sciencedirect1-103) In a [quantum tunneling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_tunneling "Quantum tunneling") model with mass estimates from a macroscopic-microscopic model, the [alpha-decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_decay "Alpha decay") half-lives of several unbinilium [isotopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope "Isotope") (292–304 Ubn) have been predicted to be around 1–20 microseconds.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-prc08ADNDT08-102)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-half-lifesall-104)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-105)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-sciencedirect1-103) Some heavier isotopes may be more stable; Fricke and Waber predicted 320 Ubn to be the most stable unbinilium isotope in 1971.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Fricke1971-3) Since unbinilium is expected to decay via a cascade of alpha decays leading to [spontaneous fission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_fission "Spontaneous fission") around [copernicium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copernicium "Copernicium"), the total half-lives of unbinilium isotopes are also predicted to be measured in microseconds.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Hofmann-67) This has consequences for the synthesis of unbinilium, as isotopes with half-lives below one microsecond would decay before reaching the detector.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Hofmann-67) Nevertheless, new theoretical models show that the expected gap in energy between the [proton orbitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_shell_model "Nuclear shell model") 2f 7/2 (filled at element 114) and 2f 5/2 (filled at element 120) is smaller than expected, so that element 114 no longer appears to be a stable spherical closed nuclear shell, and this energy gap may increase the stability of elements 119 and 120. The next [doubly magic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubly_magic "Doubly magic") nucleus is now expected to be around the spherical 306 Ubb (element 122), but the expected low half-life and low production [cross section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_(physics) "Cross section (physics)") of this nuclide makes its synthesis challenging.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Kratz-99)

Given that element 120 fills the 2f 5/2 proton orbital, much attention has been given to the compound nucleus 302 Ubn* and its properties. Several experiments have been performed between 2000 and 2008 at the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions in Dubna studying the fission characteristics of the compound nucleus 302 Ubn*. Two nuclear reactions have been used, namely 244 Pu+58 Fe and 238 U+64 Ni. The results have revealed how nuclei such as this fission predominantly by expelling closed shell nuclei such as 132[Sn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin "Tin") (_[Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic\_number "Atomic number")_=50, _[N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron\_number "Neutron number")_=82). It was also found that the yield for the fusion-fission pathway was similar between 48 Ca and 58 Fe projectiles, suggesting a possible future use of 58 Fe projectiles in superheavy element formation.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-106)

In 2008, the team at [GANIL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Acc%C3%A9l%C3%A9rateur_National_d%27Ions_Lourds "Grand Accélérateur National d'Ions Lourds"), France, described the results from a new technique which attempts to measure the fission [half-life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-life "Half-life") of a compound nucleus at high excitation energy, since the yields are significantly higher than from neutron evaporation channels. It is also a useful method for probing the effects of shell closures on the survivability of compound nuclei in the super-heavy region, which can indicate the exact position of the next proton shell (_Z_=114, 120, 124, or 126). The team studied the nuclear fusion reaction between uranium ions and a target of natural nickel:[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Natowitz-107)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Morjean-108)

238

92 U + nat

28 Ni → 296,298,299,300,302

120 Ubn* → fission
The results indicated that nuclei of unbinilium were produced at high (≈70 MeV) excitation energy which underwent fission with measurable half-lives just over 10−18 s.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Natowitz-107)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Morjean-108) Although very short (indeed insufficient for the element to be considered by [IUPAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUPAC "IUPAC") to exist, because a compound nucleus has no internal structure and its nucleons have not been arranged into shells until it has survived for 10−14 s, when it forms an electronic cloud),[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-109) the ability to measure such a process indicates a strong shell effect at _Z_=120. At lower excitation energy (see neutron evaporation), the effect of the shell will be enhanced and ground-state nuclei can be expected to have relatively long half-lives. This result could partially explain the relatively long half-life of 294 Og measured in experiments at Dubna. Similar experiments have indicated a similar phenomenon at [element 124](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbiquadium "Unbiquadium") but not for [flerovium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flerovium "Flerovium"), suggesting that the next proton shell does in fact lie beyond element 120.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Natowitz-107)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Morjean-108) In September 2007, the team at RIKEN began a program utilizing 248 Cm targets and have indicated future experiments to probe the possibility of 120 being the next proton magic number (and 184 being the next neutron magic number) using the aforementioned nuclear reactions to form 302 Ubn*, as well as 248 Cm+54 Cr. They also planned to further chart the region by investigating the nearby compound nuclei 296 Og*, 298 Og*, 306 Ubb*, and 308 Ubb*.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-110)

The most likely isotopes of unbinilium to be synthesised in the near future are 295 Ubn through 299 Ubn, because they can be produced in the 3n and 4n channels of the 249–251 Cf+50 Ti, 245 Cm+54 Cr, and 248 Cm+54 Cr reactions.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-jinr2024-111)

### Atomic and physical

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Unbinilium&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Atomic and physical")]

Being the second [period 8 element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Period_8_element "Period 8 element"), unbinilium is predicted to be an alkaline earth metal, below [beryllium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beryllium "Beryllium"), [magnesium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium "Magnesium"), [calcium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium "Calcium"), [strontium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strontium "Strontium"), [barium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barium "Barium"), and [radium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium "Radium"). Each of these elements has two [valence electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valence_electron "Valence electron") in the outermost s-orbital (valence electron configuration _n_ s 2), which is easily lost in chemical reactions to form the +2 [oxidation state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation_state "Oxidation state"): thus the alkaline earth metals are rather [reactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactivity_(chemistry) "Reactivity (chemistry)") elements, with the exception of beryllium due to its small size. Unbinilium is predicted to continue the trend and have a valence electron configuration of 8s 2. It is therefore expected to behave much like its lighter [congeners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congener_(chemistry) "Congener (chemistry)"); however, it is also predicted to differ from the lighter alkaline earth metals in some properties.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1)

The main reason for the predicted differences between unbinilium and the other alkaline earth metals is the [spin–orbit (SO) interaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin%E2%80%93orbit_interaction "Spin–orbit interaction")—the mutual interaction between the electrons' motion and [spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_(physics) "Spin (physics)"). The SO interaction is especially strong for the superheavy elements because their electrons move faster—at velocities comparable to the [speed of light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light "Speed of light")—than those in lighter atoms.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Thayer-4) In unbinilium atoms, it lowers the 7p and 8s electron energy levels, stabilizing the corresponding electrons, but two of the 7p electron energy levels are more stabilized than the other four.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Faegri-112) The effect is called subshell splitting, as it splits the 7p subshell into more-stabilized and the less-stabilized parts. Computational chemists understand the split as a change of the second ([azimuthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azimuthal_quantum_number "Azimuthal quantum number")) [quantum number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_number "Quantum number")_l_ from 1 to 1/2 and 3/2 for the more-stabilized and less-stabilized parts of the 7p subshell, respectively.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Thayer-4)[[l]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-113) Thus, the outer 8s electrons of unbinilium are stabilized and become harder to remove than expected, while the 7p 3/2 electrons are correspondingly destabilized, perhaps allowing them to participate in chemical reactions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1) This stabilization of the outermost s-orbital (already significant in radium) is the key factor affecting unbinilium's chemistry, and causes all the trends for atomic and molecular properties of alkaline earth metals to reverse direction after barium.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Pershina-114)

Due to the stabilization of its outer 8s electrons, unbinilium's first [ionization energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionization_energy "Ionization energy")—the energy required to remove an electron from a neutral atom—is predicted to be 6.0 eV, comparable to that of calcium.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1) The electron of the [hydrogen-like](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen-like_atom "Hydrogen-like atom") unbinilium atom—oxidized so it has only one electron, Ubn 119+—is predicted to move so quickly that its mass is 2.05 times that of a non-moving electron, a feature coming from the [relativistic effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativistic_quantum_chemistry "Relativistic quantum chemistry"). For comparison, the figure for hydrogen-like radium is 1.30 and the figure for hydrogen-like barium is 1.095.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Thayer-4) According to simple extrapolations of relativity laws, that indirectly indicates the contraction of the [atomic radius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_radius "Atomic radius")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Thayer-4) to around 200[pm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picometer "Picometer"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1) very close to that of strontium (215 pm); the [ionic radius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_radius "Ionic radius") of the Ubn 2+ ion is also correspondingly lowered to 160 pm.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1) The trend in electron affinity is also expected to reverse direction similarly at radium and unbinilium.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Pershina-114)

Unbinilium should be a [solid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid "Solid") at room temperature, with melting point 680°C:[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-BFricke-116) this continues the downward trend down the group, being lower than the value 700°C for radium.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-117) The boiling point of unbinilium is expected to be around 1700°C, which is lower than that of all the previous elements in the group (in particular, radium boils at 1737°C), following the downward periodic trend.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Fricke1971-3) The density of unbinilium has been predicted to be 7 g/cm 3, continuing the trend of increasing density down the group: the value for radium is 5.5 g/cm 3.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Fricke1971-3)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-B&K-2)

The chemistry of unbinilium is predicted to be similar to that of the alkaline earth metals,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1) but it would probably behave more like calcium or strontium[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1) than barium or radium. Like strontium, unbinilium should react vigorously with air to form an oxide (UbnO) and with water to form the hydroxide (Ubn(OH)2), which would be a strong [base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_(chemistry) "Base (chemistry)"), and releasing [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen") gas. It should also react with the [halogens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halogen "Halogen") to form salts such as UbnCl 2.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-emsley-118) While these reactions would be expected from [periodic trends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_trends "Periodic trends"), their lowered intensity is somewhat unusual, as ignoring relativistic effects, periodic trends would predict unbinilium to be even more reactive than barium or radium. This lowered [reactivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactivity_(chemistry) "Reactivity (chemistry)") is due to the relativistic stabilization of unbinilium's valence electron, increasing unbinilium's first ionization energy and decreasing the [metallic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_radius "Metallic radius") and [ionic radii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_radius "Ionic radius");[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-EB-119) this effect is already seen for radium.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1) On the other hand, the ionic radius of the Ubn 2+ ion is predicted to be larger than that of Sr 2+, because the 7p orbitals are destabilized and are thus larger than the p-orbitals of the lower shells.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Thayer-4)

Unbinilium may also show the +4 [oxidation state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation_state "Oxidation state"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1) which is not seen in any other alkaline earth metal,[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw-120) in addition to the +2 oxidation state that is characteristic of the other alkaline earth metals and is also the main oxidation state of all the known alkaline earth metals: this is because of the destabilization and expansion of the 7p 3/2 spinor, causing its outermost electrons to have a lower ionization energy than what would otherwise be expected.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Greenwood&Earnshaw-120) The +6 state involving all the 7p 3/2 electrons has been suggested in a [hexafluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexafluoride "Hexafluoride"), UbnF 6.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Cao2-121) The +1 state may also be isolable.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Thayer-4) Many unbinilium compounds are expected to have a large [covalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covalent "Covalent") character, due to the involvement of the 7p 3/2 electrons in the bonding: this effect is also seen to a lesser extent in radium, which shows some 6s and 6p 3/2 contribution to the bonding in [radium fluoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium_fluoride "Radium fluoride") (RaF 2) and astatide (RaAt 2), resulting in these compounds having more covalent character.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Thayer-4) The [standard reduction potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_reduction_potential "Standard reduction potential") of the Ubn 2+/Ubn couple is predicted to be −2.9 V, which is almost exactly the same as that for the Sr 2+/Sr couple of strontium (−2.899 V).[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-BFricke-116)

In the gas phase, the alkaline earth metals do not usually form covalently bonded diatomic molecules like the alkali metals do, since such molecules would have the same number of electrons in the bonding and antibonding orbitals and would have very low [dissociation energies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissociation_energy "Dissociation energy").[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Be2-122) Thus, the M–M bonding in these molecules is predominantly through [van der Waals forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Waals_force "Van der Waals force").[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Pershina-114) The metal–metal [bond lengths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bond_length "Bond length") in these M 2 molecules increase down the group from Ca 2 to Ubn 2. On the other hand, their metal–metal [bond-dissociation energies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bond-dissociation_energy "Bond-dissociation energy") generally increase from Ca 2 to Ba 2 and then drop to Ubn 2, which should be the most weakly bound of all the group 2 homodiatomic molecules. **Unbinilium**, also known as **eka-radium** or **element 120**, is a hypothetical [chemical element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element"); it has symbol **Ubn** and [atomic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number "Atomic number") 120. _Unbinilium_ and _Ubn_ are the temporary [systematic IUPAC name and symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systematic_element_name "Systematic element name") respectively, which are used until the element is discovered, confirmed, and a permanent name is decided upon. In the [periodic table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_table "Periodic table") of the elements, it is expected to be an [s-block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S-block "S-block") element, an [alkaline earth metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline_earth_metal "Alkaline earth metal"), and the second element in the eighth [period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Period_(periodic_table) "Period (periodic table)"). It has attracted attention because of some predictions that it may be in the [island of stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_of_stability "Island of stability").

Unbinilium has not yet been synthesized, despite multiple attempts from German and Russian teams. Experimental evidence from these attempts shows that the period 8 elements would likely be far more difficult to synthesise than the previous known elements. New attempts by American, Russian, and Chinese teams to synthesize unbinilium are planned to begin in the mid-2020s; in particular, an attempt to synthesize the element was ongoing as of September 2025, at [Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Berkeley_National_Laboratory "Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory") in the United States.

Unbinilium's position as the seventh alkaline earth metal suggests that it would have similar properties to its lighter [congeners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congener_(chemistry) "Congener (chemistry)"); however, [relativistic effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relativistic_quantum_chemistry "Relativistic quantum chemistry") may cause some of its properties to differ from those expected from a straight application of [periodic trends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_trend "Periodic trend"). For example, unbinilium is expected to be less reactive than [barium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barium "Barium") and [radium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium "Radium"), be closer in behavior to [strontium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strontium "Strontium"), and while it should show the characteristic +2 [oxidation state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation_state "Oxidation state") of the alkaline earth metals, it is also predicted to show the +4 and +6 oxidation states, which are unknown in any other alkaline earth metal.

### Synthesis of superheavy nuclei

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Module:Excerpt&action=edit&section=T-1 "Edit section: Synthesis of superheavy nuclei")]

[![Image 2: A graphic depiction of a nuclear fusion reaction](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Deuterium-tritium_fusion.svg/250px-Deuterium-tritium_fusion.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Deuterium-tritium_fusion.svg)

A graphic depiction of a [nuclear fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion "Nuclear fusion") reaction. Two nuclei fuse into one, emitting a [neutron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron "Neutron"). Reactions that created new elements to this moment were similar, though varying numbers of neutrons – or alternatively charged particles – may be emitted instead.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_jinr2024-9)

A superheavy[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-13)[atomic nucleus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_nucleus "Atomic nucleus") is created in a nuclear reaction that combines two other nuclei of unequal size[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-16) into one; roughly, the more unequal the two nuclei in terms of [mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass "Mass"), the greater the possibility that the two react.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_Bloomberg-17) The material made of the heavier nuclei is made into a target, which is then bombarded by the [beam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_beam "Particle beam") of lighter nuclei. Two nuclei can only [fuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion "Nuclear fusion") into one if they approach each other closely enough; normally, nuclei (all positively charged) repel each other due to [electrostatic repulsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coulomb%27s_law "Coulomb's law"). The [strong interaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_interaction "Strong interaction") can overcome this repulsion but only within a very short distance from a nucleus; beam nuclei are thus greatly [accelerated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_accelerator "Particle accelerator") in order to make such repulsion insignificant compared to the velocity of the beam nucleus.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_n+1-18) The energy applied to the beam nuclei to accelerate them can cause them to reach speeds as high as one-tenth of the [speed of light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light "Speed of light"). However, if too much energy is applied, the beam nucleus can fall apart.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_n+1-18)

Coming close enough alone is not enough for two nuclei to fuse: when two nuclei approach each other, they usually remain together for about 10−20 seconds and then part ways (not necessarily in the same composition as before the reaction) rather than form a single nucleus.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_n+1-18)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-19) This happens because during the attempted formation of a single nucleus, electrostatic repulsion tears apart the nucleus that is being formed.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_n+1-18) Each pair of a target and a beam is characterized by its [cross section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_(physics) "Cross section (physics)")—the probability that fusion will occur if two nuclei approach one another expressed in terms of the transverse area that the incident particle must hit in order for the fusion to occur.[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-21) This fusion may occur as a result of the quantum effect in which nuclei can [tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_tunnelling#Nuclear_fusion "Quantum tunnelling") through electrostatic repulsion. If the two nuclei can stay close past that phase, multiple nuclear interactions result in redistribution of energy and an energy equilibrium.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_n+1-18)

The resulting merger is an [excited state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excited_state "Excited state")[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-23)—termed a [compound nucleus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reaction#Compound_nuclear_reactions "Nuclear reaction")—and thus it is very unstable.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_n+1-18) To reach a more stable state, the temporary merger may [fission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fission "Nuclear fission") without formation of a more stable nucleus.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_CzechNuclear-24) Alternatively, the compound nucleus may eject a few [neutrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron "Neutron"), which would carry away the excitation energy; if the latter is not sufficient for a neutron expulsion, the merger would produce a [gamma ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_ray "Gamma ray"). This happens in about 10−16 seconds after the initial nuclear collision and results in creation of a more stable nucleus.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_CzechNuclear-24) The definition by the [IUPAC/IUPAP Joint Working Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUPAC/IUPAP_Joint_Working_Party "IUPAC/IUPAP Joint Working Party") (JWP) states that a [chemical element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element "Chemical element") can only be recognized as discovered if a nucleus of it has not [decayed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_decay "Radioactive decay") within 10−14 seconds. This value was chosen as an estimate of how long it takes a nucleus to acquire [electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron") and thus display its chemical properties.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-25)[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-27)

### Decay and detection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Module:Excerpt&action=edit&section=T-2 "Edit section: Decay and detection")]

The beam passes through the target and reaches the next chamber, the separator; if a new nucleus is produced, it is carried with this beam.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_SHEhowvideo-28) In the separator, the newly produced nucleus is separated from other nuclides (that of the original beam and any other reaction products)[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-31) and transferred to a [surface-barrier detector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_detector "Semiconductor detector"), which stops the nucleus. The exact location of the upcoming impact on the detector is marked; also marked are its energy and the time of the arrival.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_SHEhowvideo-28) The transfer takes about 10−6 seconds; in order to be detected, the nucleus must survive this long.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZagrebaevKarpovGreiner20133-32) The nucleus is recorded again once its decay is registered, and the location, the [energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decay_energy "Decay energy"), and the time of the decay are measured.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_SHEhowvideo-28)

Stability of a nucleus is provided by the strong interaction. However, its range is very short; as nuclei become larger, its influence on the outermost [nucleons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleon "Nucleon") ([protons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton "Proton") and neutrons) weakens. At the same time, the nucleus is torn apart by electrostatic repulsion between protons, and its range is not limited.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeiser2003432-33) Total [binding energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_binding_energy "Nuclear binding energy") provided by the strong interaction increases linearly with the number of nucleons, whereas electrostatic repulsion increases with the square of the atomic number, i.e. the latter grows faster and becomes increasingly important for heavy and superheavy nuclei.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsAlpha-34)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsSF-35) Superheavy nuclei are thus theoretically predicted[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-36) and have so far been observed[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAudi_et_al.2017030001-129%E2%80%93030001-138-37) to predominantly decay via decay modes that are caused by such repulsion: [alpha decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_decay "Alpha decay") and [spontaneous fission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_fission "Spontaneous fission").[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-39) Almost all alpha emitters have over 210 nucleons,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeiser2003433-40) and the lightest nuclide primarily undergoing spontaneous fission has 238.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAudi_et_al.2017030001-125-41) In both decay modes, nuclei are inhibited from decaying by corresponding [energy barriers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectangular_potential_barrier "Rectangular potential barrier") for each mode, but they can be tunneled through.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsAlpha-34)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsSF-35)

[![Image 4: Apparatus for creation of superheavy elements](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Apparatus_for_creation_of_superheavy_elements_en.svg/500px-Apparatus_for_creation_of_superheavy_elements_en.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apparatus_for_creation_of_superheavy_elements_en.svg)

Scheme of an apparatus for creation of superheavy elements, based on the Dubna Gas-Filled Recoil Separator set up in the [Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flerov_Laboratory_of_Nuclear_Reactions "Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions") in JINR. The trajectory within the detector and the beam focusing apparatus changes because of a [dipole magnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_dipole "Magnetic dipole") in the former and [quadrupole magnets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadrupole_magnet "Quadrupole magnet") in the latter.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_Aksenov-42)

Alpha particles are commonly produced in radioactive decays because the mass of an alpha particle per nucleon is small enough to leave some energy for the alpha particle to be used as kinetic energy to leave the nucleus.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeiser2003432%E2%80%93433-43) Spontaneous fission is caused by electrostatic repulsion tearing the nucleus apart and produces various nuclei in different instances of identical nuclei fissioning.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsSF-35) As the atomic number increases, spontaneous fission rapidly becomes more important: spontaneous fission partial half-lives decrease by 23 orders of magnitude from [uranium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranium "Uranium") (element 92) to [nobelium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobelium "Nobelium") (element 102),[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_Oganessian12-44) and by 30 orders of magnitude from [thorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thorium "Thorium") (element 90) to [fermium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermium "Fermium") (element 100).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-45) The earlier [liquid drop model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_drop_model "Liquid drop model") thus suggested that spontaneous fission would occur nearly instantly due to disappearance of the [fission barrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fission_barrier "Fission barrier") for nuclei with about 280 nucleons.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsSF-35)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_Oganessian04-46) The later [nuclear shell model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_shell_model "Nuclear shell model") suggested that nuclei with about 300 nucleons would form an [island of stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_of_stability "Island of stability") in which nuclei will be more resistant to spontaneous fission and will primarily undergo alpha decay with longer half-lives.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_BrusselsSF-35)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_Oganessian04-46) Subsequent discoveries suggested that the predicted island might be further than originally anticipated; they also showed that nuclei intermediate between the long-lived actinides and the predicted island are deformed, and gain additional stability from shell effects.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-47) Experiments on lighter superheavy nuclei,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-48) as well as those closer to the expected island,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_Oganessian12-44) have shown greater than previously anticipated stability against spontaneous fission, showing the importance of shell effects on nuclei.[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-49)

Alpha decays are registered by the emitted alpha particles, and the decay products are easy to determine before the actual decay; if such a decay or a series of consecutive decays produces a known nucleus, the original product of a reaction can be easily determined.[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-53) (That all decays within a decay chain were indeed related to each other is established by the location of these decays, which must be in the same place.)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Superheavy_element_SHEhowvideo-28) The known nucleus can be recognized by the specific characteristics of decay it undergoes such as decay energy (or more specifically, the [kinetic energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinetic_energy "Kinetic energy") of the emitted particle).[[i]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-54) Spontaneous fission, however, produces various nuclei as products, so the original nuclide cannot be determined from its daughters.[[j]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-57)

The information available to physicists aiming to synthesize a superheavy element is thus the information collected at the detectors: location, energy, and time of arrival of a particle to the detector, and those of its decay. The physicists analyze this data and seek to conclude that it was indeed caused by a new element and could not have been caused by a different nuclide than the one claimed. Often, provided data is insufficient for a conclusion that a new element was definitely created and there is no other explanation for the observed effects; errors in interpreting data have been made.[[k]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-63)

Elements 114 to 118 ([flerovium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flerovium "Flerovium") through [oganesson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oganesson "Oganesson")) were discovered in "hot fusion" reactions bombarding the actinides [plutonium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium "Plutonium") through [californium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Californium "Californium") with [calcium-48](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium-48 "Calcium-48"), a quasi-stable neutron-rich isotope which could be used as a projectile to produce more neutron-rich isotopes of superheavy elements.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Folden-64) This cannot easily be continued to elements 119 and 120, because it would require a target of the next actinides [einsteinium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einsteinium "Einsteinium") and [fermium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermium "Fermium"). Tens of milligrams of these would be needed to create such targets, but only micrograms of einsteinium and picograms of fermium have so far been produced.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-usprogram-65) More practical production of further superheavy elements would require bombarding actinides with projectiles heavier than 48 Ca,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Folden-64) but this is expected to be more difficult.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-usprogram-65) Attempts to synthesize elements 119 and 120 push the limits of current technology, due to the decreasing [cross sections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_(physics) "Cross section (physics)") of the production reactions and their probably short [half-lives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-life "Half-life"),[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZagrebaevKarpovGreiner2013-66) expected to be on the order of microseconds.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Haire-1)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Hofmann-67)

Following their success in obtaining [oganesson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oganesson "Oganesson") by the reaction between [249 Cf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Californium-249 "Californium-249") and 48 Ca in 2006, the team at the [Joint Institute for Nuclear Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Institute_for_Nuclear_Research "Joint Institute for Nuclear Research") (JINR) in [Dubna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubna "Dubna") started experiments in March–April 2007 to attempt to create unbinilium with a [58 Fe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron-58 "Iron-58") beam and a [244 Pu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium-244 "Plutonium-244") target.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-68)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-69) The attempt was unsuccessful,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Oganessian120-70) and the Russian team planned to upgrade their facilities before attempting the reaction again.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Oganessian120-70)

No atoms were detected. The GSI repeated the experiment with higher sensitivity in three separate runs in April–May 2007, January–March 2008, and September–October 2008, all with negative results, reaching a cross section limit of 90 fb.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-GSI08-71)

In 2011, after upgrading their equipment to allow the use of more radioactive targets, scientists at the GSI attempted the rather asymmetrical fusion reaction:[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Duellmann-72)

It was expected that the change in reaction would quintuple the probability of synthesizing unbinilium,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-73) as the yield of such reactions is strongly dependent on their asymmetry.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZagrebaevKarpovGreiner2013-66) Although this reaction is less asymmetric than the 249 Cf+50 Ti reaction, it also creates more neutron-rich unbinilium isotopes that should receive increased stability from their proximity to the shell closure at _N_ = 184.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Hofmann2016-74) Three signals were observed in May 2011; a possible assignment to 299 Ubn and its daughters was considered,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-EXON-75) but could not be confirmed,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Hoffman-76)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-77)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Hofmann2016-74) and a different analysis suggested that what was observed was simply a random sequence of events.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-78)

In August–October 2011, a different team at the GSI using the TASCA facility tried a new, even more asymmetrical reaction:[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Duellmann-72)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Yakushev-79)

No unbinilium atoms were identified.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium#cite_note-Yakushev-79)

This reaction was investigated again in April to September 2012 at the GSI. This experiment used a 249 Bk target and a 50 Ti beam to produce [element 119](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ununennium "Ununennium"), but since 249 Bk decays to 249 Cf with a half-life of about 327 days, both elements 119 and 120 could be searched for simultaneously:
