Germany and India rejected Snowden's application outright, while Austria, Ecuador, Finland, Norway, Italy, the Netherlands, and Spain said he must be on their territory to apply.[[253]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-asylumreq-254)[[254]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-255)[[255]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NovumAsylumNL-256) In November 2014, Germany announced that Snowden had not renewed his previously denied request and was not being considered for asylum.[[256]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-TheLocal-257) Glenn Greenwald later reported that [Sigmar Gabriel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigmar_Gabriel "Sigmar Gabriel"), [Vice-Chancellor of Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice-Chancellor_of_Germany "Vice-Chancellor of Germany"), told him the U.S. government had threatened to stop sharing intelligence if Germany offered Snowden asylum or arranged for his travel there.[[257]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-258)

Putin said on July 1, 2013, that if Snowden wanted to be granted [asylum in Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Federation_Law_on_Refugees "Russian Federation Law on Refugees"), he would be required to "stop his work aimed at harming our American partners".[[258]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-259) A spokesman for Putin subsequently said that Snowden had withdrawn his asylum application upon learning of the conditions.[[259]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-260)

In a July 12 meeting at Sheremetyevo Airport with representatives of human rights organizations and lawyers, organized in part by the Russian government,[[260]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-nytimes-261) Snowden said he was accepting all offers of asylum that he had already received or would receive. He added that Venezuela's grant of asylum formalized his legal status as an asylum-seeker, removing any basis for state interference with his right to asylum.[[261]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-20130712Telegraph-262) He also said he would request asylum in Russia until he resolved his travel problems.[[262]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-usatasylum0712-263) Slovenian correspondent Polonca Frelih, the only journalist, who presented at the July 12 meeting with Snowden and photographed him,[[263]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Frelih.org-264) reported that he "looked like someone without daylight for long time but strong enough psychologically" while expressing worries about his medical condition.[[264]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-delo-265) Russian [Federal Migration Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Migration_Service_(Russia) "Federal Migration Service (Russia)") officials confirmed on July 16 that Snowden had submitted an application for temporary asylum.[[265]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-TempAsyl-266) On July 24, Kucherena said his client wanted to find work in Russia, travel and create a life for himself, and had already begun learning Russian.[[266]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-267)

Amid media reports in early July 2013 attributed to U.S. administration sources that Obama's one-on-one meeting with Putin, ahead of a [G20 meeting in St Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_G-20_Saint_Petersburg_summit "2013 G-20 Saint Petersburg summit") scheduled for September, was in doubt due to Snowden's protracted sojourn in Russia,[[267]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-VenezuelaNYT-268) top U.S. officials repeatedly made it clear to Moscow that Snowden should immediately be returned to the United States to face charges for the unauthorized leaking of classified information.[[268]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-disappointing-269)[[269]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-flap-270)[[270]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Carneybrief-271) His Russian lawyer said Snowden needed asylum because he faced persecution by the U.S. government and feared "that he could be subjected to torture and capital punishment."[[271]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-272)

On April 16, 2020, CNN reported that Edward Snowden had requested a three-year extension of his Russian residency permit.[[272]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-russian-residency-2020-273)

In October 2020, Snowden was granted permanent residency in Russia. His lawyer said that granting an unlimited residence permit became possible after changes in the migration legislation of the Russian Federation in 2019.[[273]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-274)[[274]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-275)[[275]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-276)

On September 26, 2022, Putin granted Snowden Russian citizenship, making it impossible to extradite him to any country.[[276]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-277)

### Eric Holder letter to Russian justice minister

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Eric Holder letter to Russian justice minister")]

In a letter to Russian Minister of Justice [Aleksandr Konovalov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Konovalov_(judge) "Aleksandr Konovalov (judge)") dated July 23, 2013, U.S. Attorney General [Eric Holder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Holder "Eric Holder") repudiated Snowden's claim to refugee status and offered a limited validity passport good for direct return to the U.S.[[277]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-holderletter-278) He stated that Snowden would not be subject to torture or the death penalty, and would receive a trial in a civilian court with proper legal counsel.[[278]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NoDeathPenalty-279) The same day, the Russian president's spokesman reiterated that his government would not hand over Snowden, commenting that Putin was not personally involved in the matter and that it was being handled through talks between the FBI and Russia's [FSB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Security_Service "Federal Security Service").[[279]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-280)

 DOJ Press Release

On June 14, 2013, United States federal prosecutors filed a criminal complaint[[280]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-wp-snowden-charged-281) against Snowden, charging him with three felonies: theft of government property and two counts of violating the Espionage Act of 1917 (18 U. S. C. Sect. 792 et. seq.; Publ. L. 65-24) through unauthorized communication of national defense information and willful communication of classified communications intelligence information to an unauthorized person.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-wapocharges-3)[[277]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-holderletter-278)

Specifically, the charges filed in the Criminal Complaint were:

*   18 U.S.C. 641 Theft of Government Property
*   18 U.S.C. 793(d) Unauthorized Communication of National Defense Information
*   18 U.S.C. 798(a)(3) Willful Communication of Classified Intelligence Information to an Unauthorized Person

Each of the three charges carries a maximum possible prison term of ten years. The criminal complaint was initially secret but was unsealed a week later.

### Analysis of Criminal Complaint

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Analysis of Criminal Complaint")]

Stephen P. Mulligan and Jennifer K. Elsea, Legislative attorneys for the [Congressional Research Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Research_Service "Congressional Research Service"), provide a 2017 analysis[[281]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-mulligan-elsea-crs-analysis-282) of the uses of the Espionage Act to prosecute unauthorized disclosures of classified information, based on what was disclosed, to whom, and how; the burden of proof requirements e.g. degrees of [Mens Rea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mens_Rea "Mens Rea") (guilty mind), and the relationship of such considerations to the First Amendment framework of protections of free speech are also analyzed. The analysis includes the charges against Snowden, among several other cases. The discussion also covers gaps in the legal framework used to prosecute such cases.

### Snowden response to Criminal Complaint

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Snowden response to Criminal Complaint")]

Snowden was asked in a January 2014 interview about returning to the U.S. to face the charges in court, as Obama had suggested a few days prior. Snowden explained why he rejected the request:

> What he doesn't say are that the crimes that he's charged me with are crimes that don't allow me to make my case. They don't allow me to defend myself in an open court to the public and convince a jury that what I did was to their benefit. ... So it's, I would say, illustrative that the president would choose to say someone should face the music when he knows the music is a show trial.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ARDtranscript-56)[[282]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-283)

Snowden's legal representative, [Jesselyn Radack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesselyn_Radack "Jesselyn Radack"), wrote that "the Espionage Act effectively hinders a person from defending himself before a jury in an open court." She said that the "arcane World War I law" was never meant to prosecute whistleblowers, but rather spies who betrayed their trust by selling secrets to enemies for profit.[[283]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-WSJRadackEspionage-284)

 EDVA Court Ruling

On September 17, 2019, the United States filed a lawsuit, Civil Action No. 1:19-cv-1197-LO-TCB, against Snowden for alleged violations of non-disclosure agreements with the CIA and NSA.[[284]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-civilcharges20190917-285) The two-count civil complaint alleged that Snowden had violated prepublication obligations related to the publication of his memoir _[Permanent Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent\_Record\_(autobiography) "Permanent Record (autobiography)")_. The complaint listed the publishers [Macmillan Publishing Group, LLC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macmillan_Inc. "Macmillan Inc.") d.b.a. Henry Holt and Company and [Holtzbrink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holtzbrinck_Publishing_Group "Holtzbrinck Publishing Group"), as relief-defendants.[[285]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Case1:19-cv-01197-286) The Hon. [Liam O'Grady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liam_O%27Grady "Liam O'Grady"), a judge in the Alexandria Division of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia found for the United States (Plaintiff) by summary judgment, on both counts of the action.[[286]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-civil-verdit-287) The judgment also found that Snowden had been paid speaker honorariums totaling $1.03 million for a series of 56 speeches delivered by video link. The effect of the ruling was that the US government can collect the proceeds from his book and speeches and means that Snowden has to relinquish more than $5.2 million earned to a "constructive trust", created to transfer the money to the government.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Paid_speeches-9)

On June 23, 2013, Snowden landed at Moscow's Sheremetyevo Airport aboard a commercial Aeroflot flight from Hong Kong.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Loiko-220)[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NYT:_back_in_the_game-206)[[287]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-288) After 39 days in the transit section, he left the airport on August 1 and was granted [temporary asylum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugees_and_asylum_in_Russia "Refugees and asylum in Russia") in Russia for one year by the [Federal Migration Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Migration_Service_(Russian_Federation) "Federal Migration Service (Russian Federation)").[[288]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-289)

Snowden had the choice to apply for renewal of his temporary refugee status for 12 months or requesting a permit for temporary stay for three years.[[289]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-290) A year later, his temporary refugee status having expired, Snowden received a three-year temporary residency permit allowing him to travel freely within Russia and to go abroad for up to three months. He was not granted permanent political asylum.[[290]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ResidencyNBC-291) In 2017, his temporary residency permit was extended for another three years.[[291]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-:1-292)[[292]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-293)

In December 2013, Snowden told journalist Barton Gellman that supporters in Silicon Valley had donated enough [bitcoin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin "Bitcoin") for him to live on.[[293]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Dark_Mirror-294) (A single bitcoin was then worth about $1,000.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Paid_speeches-9)) In 2017, Snowden secretly married Lindsay Mills.[[294]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-:0-295) By 2019, he no longer felt the need to be disguised in public and lived what was described by _The Guardian_ as a "more or less normal life." He was able to travel around Russia and make a living from speaking arrangements, locally and over the internet.[[294]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-:0-295)

Snowden's memoir _Permanent Record_ was released internationally on September 17, 2019, and while U.S. royalties were expected to be seized, he was able to receive an [advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advance_payment "Advance payment")[[294]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-:0-295) of $4 million.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Paid_speeches-9) The memoir reached the top position on [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon.com "Amazon.com")'s bestseller list that day.[[295]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-296) Snowden said his work for the NSA and CIA showed him that the United States Intelligence Community (IC) had "hacked the Constitution", and that he had concluded there was no option for him but to expose his revelations via the [press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_media "News media"). In the memoir he wrote, "I realized that I was crazy to have imagined that the Supreme Court, or Congress, or President Obama, seeking to distance his administration from President George W. Bush's, would ever hold the IC legally responsible – for anything".[[296]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-APBarrVehement-297) Of Russia he said, "One of the things that is lost in all the problematic politics of the Russian government is the fact this is one of the most beautiful countries in the world" with "friendly" and "warm" people.[[294]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-:0-295)

Snowden has also used the pseudonym John Dobbertin (after cryptographer [Hans Dobbertin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Dobbertin "Hans Dobbertin")). In 2016, from Russia, Snowden participated in the [creation ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ceremony_(cryptography) "The Ceremony (cryptography)") of the [zcash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zcash "Zcash") cryptocurrency as John Dobbertin, by briefly holding a part of the private [cryptographic key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptographic_key "Cryptographic key") for the zcash [genesis block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_(blockchain) "Genesis (blockchain)"), before destroying it.[[297]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-forbes202204-298)

On November 1, 2019, new amendments took effect introducing a permanent residence permit for the first time and removing the requirement to renew the pre-2019 so-called "permanent" residence permit every five years.[[298]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-299)[[299]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-300) The new permanent residence permit must be replaced three times in a lifetime like an ordinary [internal passport for Russian citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_passport_of_Russia "Internal passport of Russia").[[300]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-301) In accordance with that law, Snowden was in October 2020 granted permanent residence in Russia instead of another extension.[[291]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-:1-292)[[301]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-302)

In April 2020, an amendment to [Russian nationality law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_nationality_law "Russian nationality law") allowing foreigners to obtain Russian citizenship without renouncing a foreign citizenship came into force.[[302]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-303) In November 2020, Snowden announced that he and his wife, Lindsay, who were expecting their son in late December, were applying for dual U.S.-Russian citizenship in order not to be separated from each other "in this era of pandemics and closed borders."[[303]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Applies_for_Russian_citizenship-304) On September 26, 2022, President Vladimir Putin granted Snowden Russian citizenship.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-wp_citizenship-38)[[304]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-poder_citizenship-305) The couple by then had two young sons born in Russia.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-wp_citizenship-38) On December 1, Snowden swore an oath of allegiance to Russia and received a Russian passport, according to his lawyer.[[305]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-306)[[306]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-307)

Prior to the [2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine"), he described the warnings from the United States about an imminent invasion as a "disinformation campaign".[[307]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-308) Snowden explained in June 2022 that he avoids publicly discussing the [Russo-Ukrainian war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Ukrainian_war_(2022%E2%80%93present) "Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)") because his comments could be taken out of context, while feeling those who are very opinionated on the conflict are often manipulated by their respective [information bubbles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filter_bubble "Filter bubble").[[308]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-309)

Snowden has said that, in the [2008 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_United_States_presidential_election "2008 United States presidential election"), he voted for a [third-party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_party_(U.S._politics) "Third party (U.S. politics)") candidate; he also said that he "believed in Obama's promises". Following the election, he said that [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") was continuing policies instated by [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush").[[309]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-guardian-qa-310)

In accounts published in June 2013, interviewers noted that Snowden's laptop displayed stickers supporting Internet freedom organizations including the [Electronic Frontier Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Frontier_Foundation "Electronic Frontier Foundation") (EFF) and the [Tor Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tor_(anonymity_network) "Tor (anonymity network)").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-guardian-reveal-27) A week after publication of his leaks began, _[Ars Technica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ars\_Technica "Ars Technica")_ confirmed that Snowden had been an active participant at the site's [online forum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_forum "Online forum") and [IRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IRC "IRC") channels from 2001 through May 2012, discussing a variety of topics under the pseudonym "TheTrueHOOHA". In an IRC discussion in 2009, Snowden said: "I went to London just last year it's where all of your Muslims live I didn't want to get out of the car. I thought I had gotten off of the plane in the wrong country... It was terrifying." In a January 2009 entry, TheTrueHOOHA exhibited strong support for the U.S. security state apparatus and said leakers of classified information "should be shot in the balls".[[310]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-arstechnica.com-311) Snowden disliked Obama's CIA director appointment of [Leon Panetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_Panetta "Leon Panetta"), saying: "Obama just named a fucking politician to run the CIA."[[311]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-newrepublic-312) Snowden was also offended by a possible ban on assault weapons, writing: "Me and all my lunatic, gun-toting NRA compatriots would be on the steps of Congress before the C-Span feed finished."[[311]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-newrepublic-312) Snowden disliked Obama's economic policies, was against Social Security, and favored [Ron Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Paul "Ron Paul")'s call for a return to the [gold standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_standard "Gold standard").[[311]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-newrepublic-312)

In 2019, Snowden said that U.S. Senator and then-presidential candidate [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") is "the most fundamentally decent man in politics".[[312]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-313) In 2024, following the [United States Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court "United States Supreme Court")'s [decision of Donald Trump's presidential immunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trump_v._United_States_(2024) "Trump v. United States (2024)"), Snowden blamed the [DNC's interference in the 2016 primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Democratic_National_Committee_email_leak#Bernie_Sanders's_campaign "2016 Democratic National Committee email leak") for Donald Trump's election, stating that "[t]he DNC is the only reason you're not currently enjoying a second-term [Bernie] Sanders and a sane Supreme Court."[[313]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-314)

In response to outrage by European leaders, President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") said in early July 2013 that all nations collect intelligence, including those expressing outrage. His remarks came in response to an article in the German magazine _[Der Spiegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der\_Spiegel "Der Spiegel")_.[[314]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-315)

In 2014, Obama stated, "our nation's defense depends in part on the fidelity of those entrusted with our nation's secrets. If any individual who objects to government policy can take it into their own hands to publicly disclose classified information, then we will not be able to keep our people safe, or conduct foreign policy." He objected to the "sensational" way the leaks were reported, saying the reporting often "shed more heat than light." He said that the disclosures had revealed "methods to our adversaries that could impact our operations."[[315]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-316)

During a November 2016 interview with the German broadcaster [ARD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARD_(broadcaster) "ARD (broadcaster)") and the German paper _Der Spiegel_, then-outgoing President Obama said he "can't" pardon Edward Snowden unless he is physically submitted to US authorities on US soil.[[316]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-obama-pardon-317)

In 2013, [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") made a series of tweets in which he referred to Snowden as a "traitor", saying he gave "serious information to China and Russia" and "should be executed". Later that year he added a caveat, tweeting "if it and he could reveal Obama's [birth] records, I might become a major fan".[[317]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-WaPoTrumpTweets-318)[[318]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-319)

In August 2020, Trump said during a press conference that he would "take a look" at [pardoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pardon "Pardon") Snowden, and added that he was "not that aware of the Snowden situation".[[319]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ReutersTrumpPardon-320)[[320]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-HillTrumpPardon-321) He stated, "There are many, many people– it seems to be a split decision that many people think that he should be somehow treated differently, and other people think he did very bad things, and I'm going to take a very good look at it."[[296]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-APBarrVehement-297)

_[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")_ described Trump's willingness to consider a pardon as "leagues away" from his 2013 views. Snowden responded to the announcement saying, "the last time we heard a White House considering a pardon was 2016, when the very same Attorney General who once charged me conceded that, on balance, my work in exposing the NSA's unconstitutional system of mass surveillance had been 'a public service'."[[321]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ForbedSnowdenTrumpRe-322) Top members of the [House Armed Services Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Armed_Services_Committee "House Armed Services Committee") immediately voiced strong opposition to a pardon, saying Snowden's actions resulted in "tremendous harm" to national security, and that he needed to stand trial. [Liz Cheney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Cheney "Liz Cheney") called the idea of a pardon "unconscionable". A week prior to the announcement, Trump also said he had been thinking of letting Snowden return to the U.S. without facing any time in jail.[[320]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-HillTrumpPardon-321)

Days later, [Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_General "United States Attorney General")[William Barr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Barr "William Barr") told the Associated Press he was "vehemently opposed" to the idea of a pardon, saying Snowden "was a traitor and the information he provided our adversaries greatly hurt the safety of the American people, he was peddling it around like a commercial merchant. We can't tolerate that."[[296]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-APBarrVehement-297)[_[dead link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Link\_rot "Wikipedia:Link rot")_]

_[Pentagon Papers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagon\_Papers "Pentagon Papers")_ leaker [Daniel Ellsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Ellsberg "Daniel Ellsberg") called Snowden's release of NSA material the most significant leak in U.S. history.[[322]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-323)[[323]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ellsbergstasi-324) Shortly before the September 2016 release of his biographical thriller film _[Snowden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowden\_(film) "Snowden (film)"),_ a semi-fictionalized drama based on the life of Edward Snowden with a short appearance by Snowden himself, [Oliver Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Stone "Oliver Stone") said that Snowden should be pardoned, calling him a "patriot above all" and suggesting that he should run the NSA himself.[[324]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-wendy-mesley-325)

In a December 18, 2013, CNN editorial, former NSA whistleblower [J. Kirk Wiebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trailblazer_Project "Trailblazer Project"), known for his involvement in the NSA's Trailblazer Project, noted that a federal judge for the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia "District of Columbia"), the [Hon. Richard J. Leon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_J._Leon "Richard J. Leon"), had ruled in a contemporaneous case before him that the NSA warrantless surveillance program was likely unconstitutional; Wiebe then proposed that Snowden should be granted [amnesty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty "Amnesty") and allowed to return to the United States.[[325]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-wiebe-editorial-326)

#### Government officials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Government officials")]

Numerous high-ranking current or former [U.S. government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States") officials reacted publicly to Snowden's disclosures.

*   Director of National Intelligence [James Clapper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clapper "James Clapper") condemned the leaks as doing "huge, grave damage" to U.S. intelligence capabilities.[[326]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-327) Ex-CIA director [James Woolsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._James_Woolsey,_Jr. "R. James Woolsey, Jr.") said that if Snowden were convicted of treason, he should be hanged.[[327]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Fox_News_Channel-328)
*   FBI director [Robert Mueller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mueller "Robert Mueller") said that the U.S. government is "taking all necessary steps to hold Edward Snowden responsible for these disclosures."[[328]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-329)

*   [House Intelligence Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Intelligence_Committee "House Intelligence Committee") chairman [Mike Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Rogers_(Michigan_politician) "Mike Rogers (Michigan politician)") and ranking member [Dutch Ruppersberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Ruppersberger "Dutch Ruppersberger") said a classified Pentagon report written by military intelligence officials contended that Snowden's leaks had put U.S. troops at risk and prompted terrorists to change their tactics and that most files copied were related to current U.S. military operations.[[329]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-330)
*   Former congressman [Ron Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Paul "Ron Paul") began a petition urging the Obama administration to grant Snowden [clemency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemency "Clemency").[[330]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-APPaul-331) Paul released a video on his website saying, "Edward Snowden sacrificed his livelihood, citizenship, and freedom by exposing the disturbing scope of the NSA's worldwide spying program. Thanks to one man's courageous actions, Americans know about the truly egregious ways their government is spying on them."[[331]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-WaPoPaul-332)
*   [Mike McConnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Michael_McConnell "John Michael McConnell")—former NSA director and current vice chairman at Booz Allen Hamilton—said that Snowden was motivated by revenge when the NSA did not offer him the job he wanted. "At this point," said McConnell, "he being narcissistic and having failed at most everything he did, he decides now I'm going to turn on them."[[332]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-333)
*   Former President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") said that if he were still president today he would "certainly consider" giving Snowden a pardon were he to be found guilty and imprisoned for his leaks.[[333]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-334)
*   Former Secretary of State [Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton") said, "[W]e have all these protections for whistleblowers. If [Snowden] were concerned and wanted to be part of the American debate...it struck me as...sort of odd that he would flee to China because Hong Kong is controlled by China, and that he would then go to Russia—two countries with which we have very difficult cyberrelationships." As Clinton saw it, "turning over a lot of that material—intentionally or unintentionally—drained, gave all kinds of information, not only to big countries but to networks and terrorist groups and the like. So I have a hard time thinking that somebody who is a champion of privacy and liberty has taken refuge in Russia, under Putin's authority."[[334]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-335) Clinton later said that if Snowden wished to return to the U.S., "knowing he would be held accountable," he would have the right "to launch both a legal defense and a public defense, which can, of course, affect the legal defense."[[335]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ClintonJuly4-336)
*   Secretary of State [John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry "John Kerry") said Snowden had "damaged his country very significantly" and "hurt operational security" by telling terrorists how to evade detection. "The bottom line," Kerry added, "is this man has betrayed his country, sitting in Russia where he has taken refuge. You know, he should man up and come back to the United States."[[336]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ManUp-337)
*   Former Vice President [Al Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore "Al Gore") said Snowden "clearly violated the law so you can't say OK, what he did is all right. It's not. But what he revealed in the course of violating important laws included violations of the U.S. Constitution that were way more serious than the crimes he committed. In the course of violating important law, he also provided an important service. ... Because we did need to know how far this has gone."[[337]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-GuardianAlGore-338)
*   In 2014, [deputy defense secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Defense "United States Deputy Secretary of Defense") and later [defense secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Defense "United States Secretary of Defense")[Ashton Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashton_Carter "Ashton Carter") said, "We had a cyber Pearl Harbor. His name was Edward Snowden." Carter charged that U.S. security officials "screwed up spectacularly in the case of Snowden. And this knucklehead had access to destructive power that was much more than any individual person should have access to."[[338]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-339)

In the U.S., Snowden's actions precipitated an intense debate on privacy and warrantless domestic surveillance.[[339]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-usatoday1-340)[[340]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-341) President Obama dismissed the idea of using force to acquire Snowden, saying "I'm not going to be scrambling jets to get a 29-year-old hacker."[[341]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-342)[[342]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-343)[[343]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-344) In August 2013, Obama rejected the suggestion that Snowden was a patriot,[[344]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-CNN081313-345) and in November said that "the benefit of the debate he generated was not worth the damage done, because there was another way of doing it."[[345]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-346)

In June 2013, U.S. Senator [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") of Vermont shared a "must-read" news story on his blog by [Ron Fournier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Fournier "Ron Fournier"), stating "Love him or hate him, we all owe Snowden our thanks for forcing upon the nation an important debate. But the debate shouldn't be about him. It should be about the gnawing questions his actions raised from the shadows."[[346]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-347) In 2015, Sanders stated that "Snowden played a very important role in educating the American public" and that although Snowden should not go unpunished for breaking the law, "that education should be taken into consideration before the sentencing."[[347]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-348)

Snowden said in December 2013 that he was "inspired by the global debate" ignited by the leaks and that NSA's "culture of indiscriminate global espionage ... is collapsing."[[348]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-autogenerated8-349)

At the end of 2013, _The Washington Post_ said that the public debate and its offshoots had produced no meaningful change in policy, with the status quo continuing.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-autogenerated12-155)

In 2016, on _[The Axe Files](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Axe\_Files "The Axe Files")_[podcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_podcast "Political podcast"), former U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder said that Snowden "performed a public service by raising the debate that we engaged in and by the changes that we made." Holder nevertheless said that Snowden's actions were inappropriate and illegal.[[349]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-350)

In September 2016, the bipartisan [U.S. House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._House_Permanent_Select_Committee_on_Intelligence "U.S. House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence") completed a review of the Snowden disclosures and said that the federal government would have to spend millions of dollars responding to the fallout from Snowden's disclosures.[[350]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-HouseReport-351) The report also said that "the public narrative popularized by Snowden and his allies is rife with falsehoods, exaggerations, and crucial omissions."[[351]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-352) The report was denounced by _Washington Post_ reporter [Barton Gellman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barton_Gellman "Barton Gellman"), who, in an opinion piece for [The Century Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Century_Foundation "The Century Foundation"), called it "aggressively dishonest" and "contemptuous of fact."[[352]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-353)

In August 2013, President Obama said that he had called for a review of U.S. surveillance activities before Snowden had begun revealing details of the NSA's operations,[[344]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-CNN081313-345) and announced that he was directing DNI James Clapper "to establish a review group on intelligence and communications technologies."[[353]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-354)[[354]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-355) In December, the task force issued 46 recommendations that, if adopted, would subject the NSA to additional scrutiny by the courts, Congress, and the president, and would strip the NSA of the authority to infiltrate American computer systems using [backdoors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backdoor_(computing) "Backdoor (computing)") in hardware or software.[[355]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-reviewpanel-356) Panel member [Geoffrey R. Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_R._Stone "Geoffrey R. Stone") said there was no evidence that the bulk collection of phone data had stopped any [terror attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terror_attacks "Terror attacks").[[356]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-357)

#### Court rulings (United States)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: Court rulings (United States)")]

On June 6, 2013, in the wake of Snowden's leaks, conservative public interest lawyer and [Judicial Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_Watch "Judicial Watch") founder [Larry Klayman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Klayman "Larry Klayman") filed a lawsuit claiming that the federal government had unlawfully collected metadata for his telephone calls and was harassing him. In _[Klayman v. Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klayman\_v.\_Obama "Klayman v. Obama")_, Judge Richard J. Leon referred to the NSA's "almost-Orwellian technology" and ruled the bulk telephone metadata program to be likely unconstitutional.[[357]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-WaPoUnconstitutional-358) Leon's ruling was stayed pending an appeal by the government. Snowden later described Judge Leon's decision as vindication.[[358]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-PoliticoPulizer-359)

On June 11, the ACLU filed a lawsuit against James Clapper, Director of National Intelligence, alleging that the NSA's phone records program was unconstitutional. In December 2013, ten days after Judge Leon's ruling, Judge [William H. Pauley III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_H._Pauley_III "William H. Pauley III") came to the opposite conclusion. In _[ACLU v. Clapper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACLU\_v.\_Clapper "ACLU v. Clapper")_, although acknowledging that privacy concerns are not trivial, Pauley found that the potential benefits of surveillance outweigh these considerations and ruled that the NSA's collection of phone data is legal.[[359]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NYTBulkLegal-360)

[Gary Schmitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Schmitt "Gary Schmitt"), former staff director of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, wrote that "The two decisions have generated public confusion over the constitutionality of the NSA's data collection program—a kind of judicial 'he-said, she-said' standoff."[[360]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-361)

On May 7, 2015, in the case of _ACLU v. Clapper_, the [United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Second_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit") said that [Section 215](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_215 "Section 215") of the [Patriot Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriot_Act "Patriot Act") did not authorize the NSA to collect Americans' calling records in bulk, as exposed by Snowden in 2013. The decision voided U.S. District Judge William Pauley's December 2013 finding that the NSA program was lawful, and remanded the case to him for further review. The appeals court did not rule on the constitutionality of the bulk surveillance and declined to enjoin the program, noting the pending expiration of relevant parts of the Patriot Act. Circuit Judge [Gerard E. Lynch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_E._Lynch "Gerard E. Lynch") wrote that, given the national security interests at stake, it was prudent to give Congress an opportunity to debate and decide the matter.[[361]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-362)

On September 2, 2020, a US federal court ruled that the [US intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_intelligence "US intelligence")'s mass surveillance program, exposed by Edward Snowden, was illegal and possibly unconstitutional. They also stated that the US intelligence leaders, who publicly defended it, were not telling the truth.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-reuters.com-11)

On June 2, 2015, the U.S. Senate passed, and President Obama signed, the [USA Freedom Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA_Freedom_Act "USA Freedom Act") which restored in modified form several provisions of the Patriot Act that had expired the day before, while for the first time imposing some limits on the bulk collection of telecommunication data on U.S. citizens by American intelligence agencies. The new restrictions were widely seen as stemming from Snowden's revelations.[[362]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-CNN_passes-363)[[363]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-364)

In an official report published in October 2015, the [United Nations special rapporteur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_special_rapporteur "United Nations special rapporteur") for the promotion and protection of the right to freedom of speech, Professor [David Kaye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Kaye_(law_professor) "David Kaye (law professor)"), criticized the U.S. government's harsh treatment of, and bringing criminal charges against, whistleblowers, including Edward Snowden. The report found that Snowden's revelations were important for people everywhere and made "a deep and lasting impact on law, policy, and politics."[[364]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-365)[[365]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-366) The [European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Parliament "European Parliament") invited Snowden to make a pre-recorded video appearance to aid their NSA investigation.[[366]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-367)[[367]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-368) Snowden gave written testimony in which he said that he was seeking asylum in the EU, but that he was told by European Parliamentarians that the U.S. would not allow EU partners to make such an offer.[[368]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NPREUasyl-369) He told the Parliament that the NSA was working with the security agencies of EU states to "get access to as much data of EU citizens as possible."[[369]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-PCworldEU-370) He said that the NSA's Foreign Affairs Division lobbies the EU and other countries to change their laws, allowing for "everyone in the country" to be spied on legally.[[370]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BoingBoingEU-371)

#### Austria, Italy and Switzerland

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: Austria, Italy and Switzerland")]

Snowden applied for asylum in [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria"),[[371]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-asylum-austria-reuters-372) Italy[[372]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-asylum-italy-reuters-373) and Switzerland.[[373]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-asylum-switzerland-independent-374)[[374]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-asylum-switzerland-npr-375)[[375]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-asylum-switzerland-bbc-376) Snowden, speaking to an audience in [Geneva, Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva,_Switzerland "Geneva, Switzerland") via video link from Moscow, said he would love to return to Geneva, where he had previously worked undercover for the CIA. Swiss media said that the Swiss Attorney General had determined that Switzerland would not extradite Snowden if the US request were considered "politically motivated". Switzerland would grant Snowden asylum if he revealed the extent of espionage activities by the United States government. According to the paper _Sonntags Zeitung_, Snowden would be granted safe entry and residency in Switzerland, in return for his knowledge of American intelligence activities. Swiss paper _Le Matin_ reported that Snowden's activity could be part of criminal proceedings or part of a parliamentary inquiry.

On September 16, 2019, it was reported that Snowden had said he "would love" to get political asylum in France.[[376]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-france-asylum-377) Snowden first applied unsuccessfully for asylum in France in 2013, under then French President [François Hollande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Hollande "François Hollande"). His second request, under President [Emmanuel Macron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron "Emmanuel Macron"), was favorably received by Justice Minister [Nicole Belloubet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicole_Belloubet "Nicole Belloubet"). However, no other members of the French government were known to express support for Snowden's asylum request, possibly due to the potential adverse diplomatic consequences.

[Hans-Georg Maaßen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans-Georg_Maa%C3%9Fen "Hans-Georg Maaßen"), head of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany's domestic security agency, speculated that Snowden could have been working for the Russian government.[[377]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-378)[[378]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-379) Snowden rejected this insinuation,[[379]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-380) speculating on Twitter in German that "it cannot be proven if Maaßen is an agent of the [SVR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Intelligence_Service_(Russia) "Foreign Intelligence Service (Russia)") or FSB."[[380]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-381) On October 31, 2013, Snowden met with German Green Party lawmaker [Hans-Christian Ströbele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans-Christian_Str%C3%B6bele "Hans-Christian Ströbele") in Moscow to discuss the possibility of Snowden giving testimony in Germany.[[381]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-stroebele-382) At the meeting, Snowden gave Ströbele a letter to the German government, parliament, and federal Attorney-General, the details of which were to later be made public. Germany later blocked Snowden from testifying in person in an NSA inquiry, citing a potential _grave strain_ on US-German relations.[[382]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-germany-blocked-383)

The FBI demanded that Nordic countries arrest Snowden should he visit their countries.[[383]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-scandinavia-384) Snowden made asylum requests to Sweden, [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"), [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland") and [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark").[[244]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Guardian21CountriesAsylum-245) All requests were ultimately denied, with varying degrees of severity in the response. According to Finnish foreign ministry spokeswoman [Tytti Pylkkö](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tytti_Pylkk%C3%B6&action=edit&redlink=1 "Tytti Pylkkö (page does not exist)"), Snowden made an asylum request to Finland by sending an application to the Finnish embassy in Moscow while he was confined to the transit area of the Sheremetyevo International Airport in Moscow, but was told that Finnish law required him to be on Finnish soil.[[384]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-finland-385) According to SVT News, Snowden met with three Swedish MPs; [Matthias Sundin](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Matthias_Sundin&action=edit&redlink=1 "Matthias Sundin (page does not exist)") (L), [Jakop Dalunde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakop_Dalunde "Jakop Dalunde") (MP) and [Cecilia Magnusson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecilia_Magnusson "Cecilia Magnusson") (M), in Moscow, to discuss his views on mass surveillance.[[385]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snoden-sweden-386) The meeting was organized by the Right Livelihood Award Foundation, which awarded Snowden the _Right Livelihood Honorary Award_,[[386]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-swedish-award-387) often called Sweden's "Alternative Nobel Prize". According to the foundation, the prize was for Snowden's work on press freedom. Sweden ultimately rejected Snowden's asylum, however, so the award was accepted by his father, Lon Snowden, on his behalf.

Snowden was granted a freedom of speech award by the Oslo branch of the writer's group [PEN International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PEN_International "PEN International"). He applied for asylum in Norway but Norwegian Justice Secretary [Pål Lønseth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A5l_L%C3%B8nseth "Pål Lønseth") insisted that the application be made on Norwegian soil and further expressed doubt that Snowden met the criteria for gaining asylum– being "important for foreign political reasons". Snowden then filed a lawsuit for free passage through Norway in order to receive his freedom of speech award, through Oslo's District Court, followed by an appeals court, and finally Norway's Supreme Court. The lawsuit was ultimately rejected by the Norwegian Supreme Court.[[387]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-norway-bbc-388)[[388]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-norway-independent-389)[[389]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-norway-reuters-390) Snowden also applied for asylum in Denmark, but this was rejected by the center-right Danish Prime Minister [Lars Løkke Rasmussen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lars_L%C3%B8kke_Rasmussen "Lars Løkke Rasmussen"), who said he could see no reason to grant Snowden asylum, calling him a "criminal".[[390]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-denmark-asylum-391) Apparently, under an agreement with the Danish government, a US government jet lay in wait on standby in [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen"), to transfer Snowden back to the United States from any Scandinavian country.[[391]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-us-jet-snowden-copenhagen-392)

Germany and France spearheaded a proposal for an EU-only integrated electronic communication/system network in response to the Snowden revelations.[[392]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-chi-393)[[393]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-394) Germany and France wished to control their own networks without the United States being a [middleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermediary "Intermediary").[[394]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-395)[[395]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-396)

The proposal was first announced in 2011,[[396]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-usf-397) although in 2014, the US trade representatives voiced their opposition to Schengen Cloud.[[392]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-chi-393)[[396]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-usf-397) It was also unclear that the system would prevent surveillance, but would limit access for EU corporations to international markets. The necessary regulatory alignment across multiple EU member states, to create the scheme, was not pursued.[[397]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-398): 62

### Latin and South America

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=44 "Edit section: Latin and South America")]

Support for Snowden came from Latin and South American leaders including the Argentinian President [Cristina Fernández de Kirchner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cristina_Fern%C3%A1ndez_de_Kirchner "Cristina Fernández de Kirchner"), Brazilian President [Dilma Rousseff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilma_Rousseff "Dilma Rousseff"), Ecuadorian President Rafael Correa, Bolivian President Evo Morales, Venezuelan President [Nicolás Maduro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro "Nicolás Maduro"), and Nicaraguan President [Daniel Ortega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Ortega "Daniel Ortega").[[398]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-399)[[399]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-400)

[![Image 15](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/DigiGes_PRISM_Yes_we_scan_-_Demo_am_Checkpoint_Charlie_June_2013.jpg/250px-DigiGes_PRISM_Yes_we_scan_-_Demo_am_Checkpoint_Charlie_June_2013.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DigiGes_PRISM_Yes_we_scan_-_Demo_am_Checkpoint_Charlie_June_2013.jpg)

A demonstration at [Checkpoint Charlie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkpoint_Charlie "Checkpoint Charlie") in Berlin during Barack Obama's visit on June 18, 2013

Crediting the Snowden leaks, the [United Nations General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly") unanimously adopted Resolution 68/167 in December 2013. The non-binding resolution denounced unwarranted digital surveillance and included a symbolic declaration of the right of all individuals to online privacy.[[400]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-401)[[401]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-402)[[402]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-403)

In July 2014, [Navi Pillay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navi_Pillay "Navi Pillay"), UN [High Commissioner for Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Commissioner_for_Human_Rights "High Commissioner for Human Rights"), told a news conference in Geneva that the U.S. should abandon its efforts to prosecute Snowden, since his leaks were in the public interest.[[403]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NaviPillay-404)

### Public opinion polls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=46 "Edit section: Public opinion polls")]

[![Image 16](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/-FsA14_-_Freiheit_statt_Angst_065_%2814898354439%29_%282%29.jpg/250px--FsA14_-_Freiheit_statt_Angst_065_%2814898354439%29_%282%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:-FsA14_-_Freiheit_statt_Angst_065_(14898354439)_(2).jpg)

A rally in Germany in support of Snowden on August 30, 2014

Surveys conducted by news outlets and professional polling organizations found that American public opinion was divided on Snowden's disclosures and that those polled in Canada and Europe were more supportive of Snowden than respondents in the U.S., although more Americans have grown more supportive of Snowden's disclosure. In Germany, Italy, France, the Netherlands, and Spain, more than 80% of people familiar with Snowden view him positively.[[404]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-405)

For his global surveillance disclosures, Snowden has been honored by publications and organizations based in Europe and the United States. He was voted as _The Guardian_'s person of the year 2013, garnering four times the number of votes as any other candidate.[[405]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-406)

### Teleconference speaking engagements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=48 "Edit section: Teleconference speaking engagements")]

In March 2014, Snowden spoke at the [South by Southwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_by_Southwest "South by Southwest") (SXSW) Interactive technology conference in [Austin, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas"), in front of 3,500 attendees. He participated by teleconference carried over multiple routers running the [Google Hangouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Hangouts "Google Hangouts") platform. On-stage moderators were [Christopher Soghoian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Soghoian "Christopher Soghoian") and Snowden's legal counsel Wizner, both from the ACLU.[[406]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-407) Snowden said that the NSA was "setting fire to the future of the internet", and that the SXSW audience was "the firefighters".[[407]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-DeLuca2014-408)[[408]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-409)[[409]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-410) Attendees could use Twitter to send questions to Snowden, who answered one by saying that information gathered by corporations was much less dangerous than that gathered by a government agency, because "governments have the power to deprive you of your rights".[[407]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-DeLuca2014-408) Then-Representative [Mike Pompeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pompeo "Mike Pompeo") (R-KS) of the House Intelligence Committee, later [director of the CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_the_Central_Intelligence_Agency "Director of the Central Intelligence Agency") and [secretary of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), had tried unsuccessfully to get the SXSW management to cancel Snowden's appearance; instead, SXSW director Hugh Forrest said that the NSA was welcome to respond to Snowden at the 2015 conference.[[407]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-DeLuca2014-408)

[![Image 17](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Edward_Snowden%27s_Surprise_Appearance_at_TED.jpg/250px-Edward_Snowden%27s_Surprise_Appearance_at_TED.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_Snowden%27s_Surprise_Appearance_at_TED.jpg)

Snowden addressing a TED conference from Russia via telepresence robot

Later that month, Snowden appeared by teleconference at the [TED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TED_(conference) "TED (conference)") conference in [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver"), British Columbia. Represented on stage by a robot with a video screen, video camera, microphones, and speakers, Snowden conversed with TED curator [Chris Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Anderson_(entrepreneur) "Chris Anderson (entrepreneur)") and told the attendees that online businesses should act quickly to encrypt their websites. He described the NSA's PRISM program as the U.S. government using businesses to collect data for them, and that the NSA "intentionally misleads corporate partners" using, as an example, the [Bullrun decryption program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullrun_(decryption_program) "Bullrun (decryption program)") to create backdoor access.[[410]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Rowan2014-411) Snowden said he would gladly return to the U.S. if given [immunity from prosecution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunity_from_prosecution_(international_law) "Immunity from prosecution (international law)"), but that he was more concerned about alerting the public about abuses of government authority.[[410]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Rowan2014-411) Anderson invited Internet pioneer [Tim Berners-Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Berners-Lee "Tim Berners-Lee") on stage to converse with Snowden, who said that he would support Berners-Lee's concept of an "internet Magna Carta" to "encode our values in the structure of the internet".[[410]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Rowan2014-411)[[411]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-412)

On September 15, 2014, Snowden appeared via remote video link, along with Julian Assange, on [Kim Dotcom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Dotcom "Kim Dotcom")'s _Moment of Truth_ town hall meeting held in [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland "Auckland").[[412]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-413) He made a similar video link appearance on February 2, 2015, along with Greenwald, as the keynote speaker at the World Affairs Conference at [Upper Canada College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Canada_College "Upper Canada College") in Toronto.[[413]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-414)

In March 2015, while speaking at the [FIFDH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Film_Festival_and_Forum_on_Human_Rights "International Film Festival and Forum on Human Rights") (international human rights film festival), he made a public appeal for Switzerland to grant him asylum, saying he would like to return to live in Geneva, where he once worked undercover for the Central Intelligence Agency.[[414]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-415)

In April 2015, [John Oliver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Oliver "John Oliver"), the host of [Last Week Tonight with John Oliver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Week_Tonight_with_John_Oliver "Last Week Tonight with John Oliver"), flew to Moscow to interview Edward Snowden.[[415]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-416)

On November 10, 2015, Snowden appeared at the [Newseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newseum "Newseum"), via remote video link, for [PEN American Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PEN_American_Center "PEN American Center")'s "Secret Sources: Whistleblowers, National Security and Free Expression", event.[[416]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-417)

In 2015, Snowden earned over $200,000 from digital speaking engagements in the U.S.[[417]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-418)

[Video 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/4/49/Edward_Snowden_LibrePlanet_2016.webm/Edward_Snowden_LibrePlanet_2016.webm.480p.vp9.webm)

Edward Snowden speaking at LibrePlanet 2016

On March 19, 2016, Snowden delivered the opening keynote address of the [LibrePlanet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LibrePlanet "LibrePlanet") conference, a meeting of international [free software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_software "Free software") activists and developers presented by the [Free Software Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Software_Foundation "Free Software Foundation"). The conference was held at the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") and was the first such time Snowden spoke via teleconference using a full free software stack, end-to-end.[_[jargon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style#Technical\_language "Wikipedia:Manual of Style")_][[418]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-419)[[419]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-420)[[420]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-421)[[421]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-422)

On July 21, 2016, Snowden and hardware hacker [Bunnie Huang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Huang_(hacker) "Andrew Huang (hacker)"), in a talk at [MIT Media Lab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIT_Media_Lab "MIT Media Lab")'s Forbidden Research event, published research for a smartphone case, the so-called _Introspection Engine_, that would monitor signals received and sent by that phone to provide an alert to the user if his or her phone is [transmitting or receiving information when it should not be](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellphone_surveillance "Cellphone surveillance") (for example when it is turned off or in airplane mode), a feature described by Snowden to be useful for journalists or activists operating under hostile governments that would otherwise track their activities through their phones.[[422]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-423)[[423]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-424)[[424]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-425)[[425]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-426)

In August 2020, a court filing by the Department of Justice indicated that Snowden had collected a total of over $1.2 million in speaking fees in addition to advances on books since 2013.[[426]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-427) In September 2021, _[Yahoo! Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahoo!\_Finance "Yahoo! Finance")_ reported that for 67 speaking appearances by video link from September 2015 to May 2020, Snowden had earned more than $1.2 million. In March 2021, [Iowa State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_State_University "Iowa State University") paid him $35,000 for one such speech, his first at a public U.S. college since February 2017, when the [University of Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pittsburgh "University of Pittsburgh") paid him $15,000.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Paid_speeches-9)

In April 2021, Snowden appeared at a Canadian investment conference sponsored by Sunil Tulsiani, a former policeman who had been barred from trading for life after dishonest behavior.[[427]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ctv.tulsiani-428) Snowden took the opportunity to affirm his role as a whistleblower, inform viewers of Tulsiani's background, and encourage investors to conduct proper research before spending any money.[[427]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ctv.tulsiani-428)[[428]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-boing.tulsiani-429)

### The "Snowden effect"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=49 "Edit section: The \"Snowden effect\"")]

In July 2013, media critic [Jay Rosen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Rosen "Jay Rosen") defined the "Snowden effect" as "Direct and indirect gains in public knowledge from the cascade of events and further reporting that followed Edward Snowden's leaks of classified information about the surveillance state in the U.S."[[429]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-RosenSnowdenEffect-430) In December 2013, _The Nation_ wrote that Snowden had sparked an overdue debate about national security and individual privacy.[[430]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NationSnowdenEffect-431) In _Forbes_, the effect was seen to have nearly united the U.S. Congress in opposition to the massive [post-9/11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-9/11 "Post-9/11") domestic intelligence gathering system.[[431]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-432) In its Spring 2014 Global Attitudes Survey, the [Pew Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pew_Research_Center "Pew Research Center") found that Snowden's disclosures had tarnished the image of the United States, especially in Europe and Latin America.[[432]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-PewJuly2014-433)

On November 2, 2018, Snowden provided a court [declaration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_(law) "Declaration (law)") in _[Jewel v. National Security Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewel\_v.\_NSA "Jewel v. NSA"),_ confirming that a document relied upon in the case, discussing the mass surveillance program known as [Stellar Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_Wind "Stellar Wind"), is actually the same document that he came upon during the course of his employment as an NSA contractor.[[433]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-434)[[434]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-435)[[435]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-436)

Yuen said he spoke to U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder by phone to reinforce the request for details "absolutely necessary" for the detention of Snowden. Yuen said "As the US government had failed to provide the information by the time Snowden left Hong Kong, it was impossible for the Department of Justice to apply to a court for a temporary warrant of arrest.
