"Washington, D.C.") His maternal grandfather, [Edward J. Barrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_J._Barrett "Edward J. Barrett"),[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-21) a [rear admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rear_admiral "Rear admiral") in the Coast Guard, became a senior official with the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") and was at [the Pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pentagon "The Pentagon") in 2001 during the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NBCNews_Motive_Revealed-22) Edward Snowden said that he had expected to work for the federal government, as had the rest of his family.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23) His parents divorced in 2001,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NBCNews_Timeline-24) and his father remarried.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-25)

In the early 1990s, while still in grade school, Snowden moved with his family to the area of [Fort Meade, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Meade,_Maryland "Fort Meade, Maryland").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NBCNews_Man_Who_Spilled-26)[Mononucleosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infectious_mononucleosis "Infectious mononucleosis") caused him to miss high school for almost nine months.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23) Rather than returning to school, he claims to have passed the [GED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Educational_Development "General Educational Development") test.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-guardian-reveal-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-:4-28) He took classes at [Anne Arundel Community College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Arundel_Community_College "Anne Arundel Community College").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NBCNews_Snowden-17) Although Snowden had no undergraduate college degree,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Despiteresume-29) he worked online toward a master's degree in computer security at the [University of Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Liverpool "University of Liverpool") in 2011.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-30) He was interested in [Japanese popular culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_popular_culture "Japanese popular culture"), had studied the [Japanese language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"),[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-31) and worked for a now defunct start-up [anime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anime "Anime") company based in the U.S.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-33) He also said he had a basic understanding of [Mandarin Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Chinese "Standard Chinese") and was deeply interested in [martial arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_arts "Martial arts"). At age 20, he listed his religion as [Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism "Buddhism") after working at a [U.S. military base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_American_military_installations#Japan "List of American military installations") in Japan.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-nyt-ambition-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-36)

In September 2019, as part of interviews relating to the release of his memoir _[Permanent Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent\_Record\_(autobiography) "Permanent Record (autobiography)")_, Snowden revealed to _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ that he married [Lindsay Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindsay_Mills "Lindsay Mills") in a courthouse in Moscow.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-I_was_very_much_a_person_the_most_powerful_government_in_the_world_wanted_to_go_away-10) The couple's first son was born in December 2020,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-37) and their second son was born sometime before September 2022.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-wp_citizenship-38)

Snowden enlisted in the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") on May 7, 2004, and became a [Special Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_special_operations_forces "United States special operations forces") candidate through its [18X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Forces_(United_States_Army)#Special_Forces_MOS_descriptions "Special Forces (United States Army)") enlistment option.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-39) He did not complete the training[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BirthDate-12) due to a leg injury and was given an administrative discharge[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-40) on September 28, 2004.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-41)

Snowden was then employed for less than a year in 2005 as a security guard at the [University of Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland "University of Maryland")'s Center for Advanced Study of Language, a research center sponsored by the National Security Agency (NSA).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-42) According to the university, this is not a classified facility,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-43) though it is heavily guarded.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-44) In June 2014, Snowden told _[Wired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wired\_(magazine) "Wired (magazine)")_ that his job as a security guard required a high-level [security clearance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_clearance "Security clearance"), for which he passed a [polygraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygraph "Polygraph") exam and underwent a stringent background investigation.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23)

### Employment at the CIA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Employment at the CIA")]

After attending a 2006 job-fair focused on intelligence agencies, Snowden accepted an offer for a position at the CIA.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-JacobJijo-45) The Agency assigned him to the global communications division at [CIA headquarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIA_headquarters "CIA headquarters") in [Langley, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langley,_Virginia "Langley, Virginia").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23)

In May 2006, Snowden wrote in _[Ars Technica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ars\_Technica "Ars Technica")_ that he had no trouble getting work because he was a "computer wizard".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-nyt-ambition-34) Snowden was sent to the CIA's secret school for technology specialists, where he lived in a hotel for six months while studying and training full-time.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-:4-28)

In March 2007, the CIA stationed Snowden with [diplomatic cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_cover "Diplomatic cover") in [Geneva, Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva,_Switzerland "Geneva, Switzerland"), where he was responsible for maintaining computer-network security.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-46) Assigned to the [U.S. Permanent Mission to the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Mission_to_the_United_Nations "United States Mission to the United Nations") – a [diplomatic mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_mission "Diplomatic mission") representing U.S. interests before the [UN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") and other [international organizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_organizations "International organizations"), Snowden received a diplomatic passport and a four-bedroom apartment near [Lake Geneva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Geneva "Lake Geneva").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23)

According to Greenwald, while there Snowden said he was "considered the top technical and cybersecurity expert" in that country and "was hand-picked by the [CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency") to support the president at the 2008 [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") summit in [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania "Romania")".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-:5-48) A 2016 report from the US House of Representatives Select Committee on Intelligence said that Snowden's official position at CIA was an entry-level technical services officer.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-:4-28)

Snowden described his CIA experience in Geneva as formative, stating that the CIA deliberately got a Swiss banker drunk and encouraged him to drive home. Snowden said that when the latter was arrested for drunk driving, a CIA operative offered to help in exchange for the banker becoming an informant.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-49)[Ueli Maurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ueli_Maurer "Ueli Maurer"), [President of the Swiss Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Swiss_Confederation "President of the Swiss Confederation") for the year 2013, publicly disputed Snowden's claims in June of that year: "This would mean that the CIA successfully bribed the Geneva police and judiciary. With all due respect, I just can't imagine it."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-50) In February 2009, after his supervisor grew suspicious that Snowden was trying to access files he was not authorized to view, Snowden resigned from the CIA.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-from-loyal-51)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-:5-48)

In 2009, Snowden began work as a contractor for [Dell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dell "Dell"),[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ReutersDell-52) which manages computer systems for multiple government agencies. Assigned to an NSA facility at [Yokota Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yokota_Air_Base "Yokota Air Base") near [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo"), Snowden instructed top officials and military officers on how to defend their networks from Chinese hackers.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23) Snowden looked into [mass surveillance in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_surveillance_in_China "Mass surveillance in China") which prompted him to investigate and then expose Washington's mass surveillance program after he was asked in 2009 to brief a conference in Tokyo.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-53)

During his four years with Dell, he rose from supervising NSA computer system upgrades to working as what his résumé termed a "cyber strategist" and an "expert in cyber counterintelligence" at several U.S. locations.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-DrewShaneNYT-54) In 2010, he had a brief stint in [New Delhi, India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi,_India "New Delhi, India"), where he enrolled himself in a local IT institute to learn core [Java programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_programming "Java programming") and advanced [ethical hacking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_hat_(computer_security) "White hat (computer security)").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-55)

In 2011, he returned to [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"), where he spent a year as system administrator and pre-sales technical engineer on Dell's CIA account. In that capacity, he was consulted by the chiefs of the CIA's technical branches, including the agency's [chief information officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_information_officer "Chief information officer") and its [chief technology officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_technology_officer "Chief technology officer").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23) U.S. officials and other sources familiar with the investigation said Snowden began downloading documents describing the government's electronic spying programs while working for Dell in April 2012.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ReutersDell-52) Investigators estimated that of the 50,000 to 200,000 documents Snowden gave to Greenwald and Poitras, most were copied by Snowden while working at Dell.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-VanityFair-2)

In March 2012, Dell reassigned Snowden to Hawaii as lead technologist for the NSA's information-sharing office.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23)

On March 15, 2013—three days after what he later called his "breaking point" of "seeing the [Director of National Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_National_Intelligence "Director of National Intelligence"), [James Clapper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clapper "James Clapper"), directly lie under oath to Congress"[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ARDtranscript-56)—Snowden quit his job at Dell.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Epstein-57) Although he has said his career high annual salary was $200,000,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-qa-58) Snowden said he took a pay cut to work at consulting firm [Booz Allen Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booz_Allen_Hamilton "Booz Allen Hamilton"),[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-qa-58) where he sought employment in order to gather data and then release details of the NSA's worldwide surveillance activity.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-SCMPJune24-59)

At the time of his departure from the U.S. in May 2013, he had been employed for 15 months inside the NSA's [Hawaii regional operations center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunia_Regional_SIGINT_Operations_Center "Kunia Regional SIGINT Operations Center"), which focuses on the electronic monitoring of [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") and [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-VanityFair-2) first for Dell and then for two months with Booz Allen Hamilton.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Two-Person-60) While intelligence officials have described his position there as a [system administrator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_administrator "System administrator"), Snowden has said he was an infrastructure analyst, which meant that his job was to look for new ways to break into Internet and telephone traffic around the world.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-nytinfrastructure-61) An anonymous source told [Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters "Reuters") that, while in Hawaii, Snowden may have persuaded 20–25 co-workers to give him their login credentials by telling them he needed them to do his job.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-62) The NSA sent a memo to Congress saying that Snowden had tricked a fellow employee into sharing his personal [private key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_key_infrastructure "Public key infrastructure") to gain greater access to the NSA's computer system.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-64) Snowden disputed the memo,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-genius_among-65) saying in January 2014, "I never stole any passwords, nor did I trick an army of co-workers."[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-WaPo01242014-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-live-67) Booz Allen terminated Snowden's employment on June 10, 2013, the day after he went public with his story, and three weeks after he had left [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii") on a leave of absence.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-20130611usatoday-68)

The former colleague said Snowden was given full administrator privileges with virtually unlimited access to NSA data. Snowden was offered a position on the NSA's elite team of [hackers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacker_(computer_security) "Hacker (computer security)"), [Tailored Access Operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tailored_Access_Operations "Tailored Access Operations"), but turned it down to join Booz Allen.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-genius_among-65) An anonymous source later said that Booz Allen's hiring screeners found possible discrepancies in Snowden's résumé but still decided to hire him.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Despiteresume-29) Snowden's résumé stated that he attended computer-related classes at [Johns Hopkins University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_University "Johns Hopkins University"). A spokeswoman for Johns Hopkins said that the university did not find records to show that Snowden attended the university and suggested that he may instead have attended Advanced Career Technologies, a private for-profit organization that operated as the Computer Career Institute at Johns Hopkins University.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Despiteresume-29) The University of Maryland University College acknowledged that Snowden had attended a summer session at a UM campus in Asia. Snowden's résumé stated that he estimated he would receive a University of Liverpool computer security master's degree in 2013. The university said that Snowden registered for an online master's degree program in computer security in 2011 but was inactive as a student and had not completed the program.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Despiteresume-29)

In his May 2014 interview with [NBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_News "NBC News"), Snowden accused the U.S. government of trying to use one position here or there in his career to distract from the totality of his experience, downplaying him as a "low-level analyst". In his words, he was "trained as a spy in the traditional sense of the word in that I lived and worked undercover overseas—pretending to work in a job that I'm not—and even being assigned a name that was not mine." He said he had worked for the NSA undercover overseas, and for the [DIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_Intelligence_Agency "Defense Intelligence Agency") had developed sources and methods to keep information and people secure "in the most hostile and dangerous environments around the world. So when they say I'm a low-level systems administrator, that I don't know what I'm talking about, I'd say it's somewhat misleading."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NBCNews_Motive_Revealed-22) In a June interview with [Globo TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globo_TV "Globo TV"), Snowden reiterated that he "was actually functioning at a very senior level".[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Globo-69) In a July interview with _The Guardian_, Snowden explained that, during his NSA career, "I began to move from merely overseeing these systems to actively directing their use. Many people don't understand that I was actually an analyst and I designated individuals and groups for targeting."[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-EditedTranscript-70) Snowden subsequently told _Wired_ that while at Dell in 2011, "I would sit down with the CIO of the CIA, the CTO of the CIA, the chiefs of all the technical branches. They would tell me their hardest technology problems, and it was my job to come up with a way to fix them."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23)

During his time as an NSA analyst, directing the work of others, Snowden recalled a moment when he and his colleagues began to have severe ethical doubts. Snowden said 18 to 22 year-old analysts were suddenly

> thrust into a position of extraordinary responsibility, where they now have access to all your private records. In the course of their daily work, they stumble across something that is completely unrelated in any sort of necessary sense—for example, an intimate nude photo of someone in a sexually compromising situation. But they're extremely attractive. So what do they do? They turn around in their chair and they show a co-worker ... and sooner or later this person's whole life has been seen by all of these other people.

Snowden observed that this behavior happened routinely every two months but was never reported, being considered one of the "[fringe benefits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fringe_benefits "Fringe benefits")" of the work.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Ispy-71)

### Whistleblower status

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Whistleblower status")]

Snowden has described himself as a whistleblower,[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-wired-72) a description used by many sources, including [CNBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNBC "CNBC"),[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-cnbc-73)_[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_,[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-newyorker-74) Reuters,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-reuters-75) and _The Guardian_,[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-guardian-76) among others.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-nation-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-usatoday-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-79) The term has both informal and legal meanings.

Snowden said that he had told multiple employees and two supervisors about his concerns, but the NSA disputes his claim.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-WPSnowdenInterview20131224-80) Snowden elaborated in January 2014, saying "[I] made tremendous efforts to report these programs to co-workers, supervisors, and anyone with the proper clearance who would listen. The reactions of those I told about the scale of the constitutional violations ranged from deeply concerned to appalled, but no one was willing to risk their jobs, families, and possibly even freedom to go to [_[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic")_] through what [Thomas Andrews] [Drake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_A._Drake "Thomas A. Drake") did."[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-live-67)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-newyorker01232014-81) In March 2014, during testimony to the European Parliament, Snowden wrote that before revealing classified information he had reported "clearly problematic programs" to ten officials, who he said did nothing in response.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-WaPo10reports-82) In a May 2014 interview, Snowden told NBC News that after bringing his concerns about the legality of the NSA spying programs to officials, he was told to stay silent on the matter. He said that the NSA had copies of emails he sent to their Office of General Counsel, oversight, and compliance personnel broaching "concerns about the NSA's interpretations of its legal authorities. I had raised these complaints not just officially in writing through email, but to my supervisors, to my colleagues, in more than one office."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NBCNews_Motive_Revealed-22)

In May 2014, U.S. officials released a single email that Snowden had written in April 2013 inquiring about legal authorities but said that they had found no other evidence that Snowden had expressed his concerns to someone in an oversight position.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-83) In June 2014, the NSA said it had not been able to find any records of Snowden raising internal complaints about the agency's operations.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-84) That same month, Snowden explained that he had not produced the communiqués in question because of the ongoing nature of the dispute, disclosing for the first time that "I am working with the NSA in regard to these records and we're going back and forth, so I don't want to reveal everything that will come out."[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-85)

Self-description as a whistleblower and attribution as such in news reports does not determine whether he qualifies as a whistleblower within the meaning of the [Whistleblower Protection Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whistleblower_Protection_Act "Whistleblower Protection Act") of 1989 (5 USC 2303(b)(8)-(9); Pub. Law 101-12). However, Snowden's potential status as a whistleblower under the 1989 Act is not directly addressed in the criminal complaint against him in the [United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_District_Court_for_the_Eastern_District_of_Virginia "United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia") (see below) (Case No. 1:13 CR 265 (0MH)). These and similar and related issues are discussed in an essay by David Pozen, in a chapter of the book _Whistleblowing Nation_, published in March 2020,[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-whistleblower-nation-86) an adaptation of which[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-87) also appeared on _Lawfare Blog_ in March 2019.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-88) The unclassified portion of a September 15, 2016, report by the [United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Permanent_Select_Committee_on_Intelligence "United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence") (HPSCI), initiated by the chairman and Ranking Member in August 2014, and posted on the website of the [Federation of American Scientists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_American_Scientists "Federation of American Scientists"), concluded that Snowden was not a whistleblower in the sense required by the Whistleblower Protection Act.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-hpsci-report-89) The bulk of the report is classified.

## Surveillance disclosures

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Surveillance disclosures")]

### Size and scope of disclosures

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Size and scope of disclosures")]

The exact size of Snowden's disclosure is unknown,[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-autogenerated6-90) but Australian officials have estimated 15,000 or more [Australian intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Intelligence_Community "Australian Intelligence Community") files[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-91) and British officials estimate at least 58,000 [British intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_intelligence_agencies_of_the_United_Kingdom "List of intelligence agencies of the United Kingdom") files were included.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-92) NSA Director [Keith Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_B._Alexander "Keith B. Alexander") initially estimated that Snowden had copied anywhere from 50,000 to 200,000 NSA documents.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Hosenball-93) Later estimates provided by U.S. officials were in the order of 1.7 million,[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-mostpentagon-94) a number that originally came from [Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") talking points.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ViceNewsJune2015-95) In July 2014, _The Washington Post_ reported on a cache previously provided by Snowden from domestic NSA operations consisting of "roughly 160,000 intercepted e-mail and instant-message conversations, some of them hundreds of pages long, and 7,900 documents taken from more than 11,000 online accounts."[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-WaPoTargets-96) A DIA report declassified in June 2015 said that Snowden took 900,000 Department of Defense files, more than he downloaded from the NSA.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ViceNewsJune2015-95)

[Venafi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venafi "Venafi"), a cybersecurity company, has claimed to have figured out how Snowden was able to fabricate [SSH keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SSH_key "SSH key") and [self-signed certificates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-signed_certificate "Self-signed certificate") to access and exfiltrate the classified documents.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-darkreading/how-snowden-97)

### Potential impact on U.S. national security

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Potential impact on U.S. national security")]

In March 2014, Army General [Martin Dempsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Dempsey "Martin Dempsey"), [Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Joint_Chiefs_of_Staff "Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff"), told the [House Armed Services Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_Armed_Services "United States House Committee on Armed Services"), "The vast majority of the documents that Snowden ... exfiltrated from our highest levels of security ... had nothing to do with exposing government oversight of domestic activities. The vast majority of those were related to our military capabilities, operations, tactics, techniques, and procedures."[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-98) When asked in a May 2014 interview to quantify the number of documents Snowden stole, retired NSA director Keith Alexander said there was no accurate way of counting what he took, but Snowden may have downloaded more than a million documents.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-AlexanderTrascriptDontKnowWhatHeTook-99) The September 15, 2016 HPSCI report[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-hpsci-report-89) estimated the number of downloaded documents at 1.5 million.

In a 2013 [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") interview, [Glenn Greenwald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Greenwald "Glenn Greenwald") stated:

> In order to take documents with him that proved that what he was saying was true he had to take ones that included very sensitive, detailed blueprints of how the NSA does what they do.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Greenwald-ap-2013-100)

Thus, the Snowden documents allegedly contained sensitive NSA _blueprints_ detailing how the NSA operates, which would allow someone who read them to evade or even duplicate NSA surveillance. Further, a 2015 _[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Times "New York Times")_ article[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-nyt-july-2015-101) reported that the [Islamic State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State "Islamic State") group had studied Snowden's revelations about how the United States gathered information on militants. As a result, the group's top leaders used couriers or encrypted channels to avoid being tracked or monitored by Western analysts.

According to Snowden, he did not indiscriminately turn over documents to journalists, stating that "I carefully evaluated every single document I disclosed to ensure that each was legitimately in the public interest. There are all sorts of documents that would have made a big impact that I didn't turn over"[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-guardian-reveal-27) and that "I have to screen everything before releasing it to journalists ... If I have time to go through this information, I would like to make it available to journalists in each country."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-SCMPJune24-59) Despite these measures, the improper redaction of a document by _The New York Times_ resulted in the exposure of intelligence activity against [al-Qaeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qaeda "Al-Qaeda").[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-102)

In June 2014, the NSA's recently installed director, [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy")[Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiral_(United_States) "Admiral (United States)")[Michael S. Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_S._Rogers "Michael S. Rogers"), said that while some terrorist groups had altered their communications to avoid surveillance techniques revealed by Snowden, the damage done was not significant enough to conclude that "the sky is falling."[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-SkyNotFalling-103) Nevertheless, in February 2015, Rogers said that Snowden's disclosures had a material impact on the NSA's detection and evaluation of terrorist activities worldwide.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-104)

On June 14, 2015, the London _[Sunday Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_Times "Sunday Times")_ reported that Russian and Chinese intelligence services had decrypted more than 1 million classified files in the Snowden cache, forcing the UK's [MI6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MI6 "MI6") intelligence agency to move agents out of live operations in hostile countries. Sir [David Omand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Omand "David Omand"), a former director of the UK's [GCHQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GCHQ "GCHQ") intelligence gathering agency, described it as a huge strategic setback that was harming Britain, America, and their NATO allies. _The Sunday Times_ said it was not clear whether Russia and China stole Snowden's data or whether Snowden voluntarily handed it over to remain at liberty in Hong Kong and Moscow.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-106) In April 2015, the [Henry Jackson Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Jackson_Society "Henry Jackson Society"), a British [neoconservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoconservative "Neoconservative")[think tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Think_tank "Think tank"), published a report claiming that Snowden's intelligence leaks negatively impacted Britain's ability to fight terrorism and organized crime.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-107) Gus Hosein, executive director of [Privacy International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy_International "Privacy International"), criticized the report for, in his opinion, presuming that the public became concerned about privacy only after Snowden's disclosures.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-108)

### Release of NSA documents

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Release of NSA documents")]

Snowden's decision to leak NSA documents developed gradually following his March 2007 posting as a technician to the Geneva CIA station.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Risen-109) Snowden later made contact with Glenn Greenwald, a journalist working at _The Guardian_.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Maass-110) He contacted Greenwald anonymously as "Cincinnatus"[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-111)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-112) and said he had sensitive documents that he would like to share.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-autogenerated1-113) Greenwald found the measures that the source asked him to take to secure their communications, such as encrypting email, too annoying to employ. Snowden then contacted documentary filmmaker [Laura Poitras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Poitras "Laura Poitras") in January 2013.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-poitras-how-114) According to Poitras, Snowden chose to contact her after seeing her _New York Times_ article about NSA whistleblower [William Binney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Binney_(U.S._intelligence_official) "William Binney (U.S. intelligence official)").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-115) What originally attracted Snowden to Greenwald and Poitras was a _[Salon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon\_(website) "Salon (website)")_ article written by Greenwald detailing how Poitras's controversial films had made her a target of the government.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-autogenerated1-113)

Greenwald began working with Snowden in either February[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-politico-journalist-spat-116) or April 2013, after Poitras asked Greenwald to meet her in New York City, at which point Snowden began providing documents to them.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Maass-110)[Barton Gellman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barton_Gellman "Barton Gellman"), writing for _The Washington Post_, says his first direct contact was on May 16, 2013.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-gellman-recount-117) According to Gellman, Snowden approached Greenwald after the _Post_ declined to guarantee publication within 72 hours of all 41 PowerPoint slides that Snowden had leaked exposing the [PRISM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PRISM_(surveillance_program) "PRISM (surveillance program)") electronic data mining program, and to publish online an encrypted code allowing Snowden to later prove that he was the source.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-gellman-recount-117)

Snowden communicated using [encrypted email](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Email_encryption "Email encryption"),[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-poitras-how-114) and going by the codename "[Verax](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/verax "wikt:verax")". He asked not to be quoted at length for fear of identification by [stylometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylometry "Stylometry").[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-gellman-recount-117)

According to Gellman, before their first meeting in person, Snowden wrote, "I understand that I will be made to suffer for my actions and that the return of this information to the public marks my end."[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-gellman-recount-117) Snowden also told Gellman that until the articles were published, the journalists working with him would also be at mortal risk from the [United States Intelligence Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Intelligence_Community "United States Intelligence Community") "if they think you are the single point of failure that could stop this disclosure and make them the sole owner of this information."[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-gellman-recount-117)

In May 2013, Snowden was permitted temporary leave from his position at the NSA in Hawaii, on the pretext of receiving treatment for his [epilepsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epilepsy "Epilepsy").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-guardian-reveal-27) In mid-May, Snowden gave an electronic interview to Poitras and [Jacob Appelbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Appelbaum "Jacob Appelbaum") which was published weeks later by _[Der Spiegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der\_Spiegel "Der Spiegel")_.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Der_Spiegel-118)

After disclosing the copied documents, Snowden promised that nothing would stop subsequent disclosures. In June 2013, he said, "All I can say right now is the US government is not going to be able to cover this up by jailing or murdering me. Truth is coming, and it cannot be stopped."[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-119)

On May 20, 2013, Snowden flew to Hong Kong,[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowdenfirstguardianvideo-120) where he was staying when the initial articles based on the leaked documents were published,[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-121) beginning with _The Guardian_ on June 5.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-122) Greenwald later said Snowden disclosed 9,000 to 10,000 documents.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-123)

Within months, documents had been obtained and published by media outlets worldwide, most notably _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ (Britain), _[Der Spiegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der\_Spiegel "Der Spiegel")_ (Germany), _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_ and _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ (U.S.), _[O Globo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O\_Globo "O Globo")_ (Brazil), _[Le Monde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_Monde "Le Monde")_ (France), and similar outlets in [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), and [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia").[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-124) In 2014, [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC") broke its first story based on the leaked documents.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NBCGreenwaldSIGDEV-125) In February 2014, for reporting based on Snowden's leaks, journalists Glenn Greenwald, Laura Poitras, Barton Gellman and _The Guardian′_ s Ewen MacAskill were honored as co-recipients of the 2013 [George Polk Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Polk_Award "George Polk Award"), which they dedicated to Snowden.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-GuardianPolkDedication-126) The NSA reporting by these journalists also earned _The Guardian_ and _The Washington Post_ the 2014 [Pulitzer Prize for Public Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Public_Service "Pulitzer Prize for Public Service")[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-PoliticoSnowdensPrize-127) for exposing the "widespread surveillance" and for helping to spark a "huge public debate about the extent of the government's spying". _The Guardian_'s chief editor, [Alan Rusbridger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Rusbridger "Alan Rusbridger"), credited Snowden for having performed a public service.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-HuffPoPulitzer-128)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/NSA_Muscular_Google_Cloud.jpg/250px-NSA_Muscular_Google_Cloud.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NSA_Muscular_Google_Cloud.jpg)

Slide from an NSA presentation on "Google Cloud Exploitation" from its [MUSCULAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MUSCULAR_(surveillance_program) "MUSCULAR (surveillance program)") program;[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-autogenerated10-129) the sketch shows where the "Public Internet" meets the internal "Google Cloud" where user data resides.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-autogenerated11-130)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/US_intelligence_budget.png/250px-US_intelligence_budget.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_intelligence_budget.png)

Data visualization of U.S. intelligence [black budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_budget "Black budget") (2013)

The ongoing publication of leaked documents has revealed previously unknown details of a [global surveillance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_surveillance "Global surveillance") apparatus run by the NSA[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-guardian1-131) in close cooperation with three of its four [Five Eyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Eyes "Five Eyes") partners: Australia's [ASD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Signals_Directorate "Australian Signals Directorate"),[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-132) the UK's [GCHQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GCHQ "GCHQ"),[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-gchqpartner-133) and Canada's [CSE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_Security_Establishment_Canada "Communications Security Establishment Canada").[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-cbcspy-134)

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Prism-slide-8.jpg/250px-Prism-slide-8.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prism-slide-8.jpg)

PRISM: a [clandestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clandestine_operation "Clandestine operation")[surveillance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_surveillance "Global surveillance") program under which the NSA collects user data from companies including [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft"), [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google "Google"), [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."), [Yahoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahoo "Yahoo"), [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") and [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube")

On June 5, 2013, media reports documenting the existence and functions of classified surveillance programs and their scope began and continued throughout the entire year. The first program to be revealed was PRISM, which allows for direct access to data on the servers of Microsoft, Yahoo, Google, Facebook, PalTalk, AOL, Skype, YouTube, and Apple.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-135)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-136) Barton Gellman of _The Washington Post_ was the first journalist to report on Snowden's documents. He said the U.S. government urged him not to specify by name which companies were involved, but Gellman decided that to name them "would make it real to Americans."[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-137) Reports also revealed details of [Tempora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempora "Tempora"), a secret British surveillance program run by the NSA's British partner, GCHQ.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-138) The initial reports included details about [NSA call database](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSA_call_database "NSA call database"), [Boundless Informant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boundless_Informant "Boundless Informant"), and a secret court order requiring [Verizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verizon "Verizon") to hand the NSA millions of Americans' phone records daily,[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-139) as well as the surveillance of phone and Internet records of French citizens, with specific targets of French people either "suspected of association with terrorist activities" or in "the worlds of business, politics or French state administration."[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-140)[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-141)[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-142)[XKeyscore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XKeyscore "XKeyscore"), an analytical tool that allows for collection of "almost anything done on the internet," was described by _The Guardian_ as a program that shed light on one of Snowden's most controversial statements: "I, sitting at my desk [could] wiretap anyone, from you or your accountant, to a federal judge or even the president, if I had a personal email."[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-143)

The NSA's top-secret [black budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_budget "Black budget"), obtained from Snowden by _The Washington Post_, exposed the successes and failures of the 16 spy agencies comprising the U.S. intelligence community,[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-144) and revealed that the NSA was paying U.S. private tech companies for clandestine access to their communications networks.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-145) The agencies were allotted $52 billion for the 2013 fiscal year.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-146)

It was revealed that the NSA was harvesting millions of email and instant messaging contact lists,[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-147) searching email content,[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-148) tracking and mapping the location of cell phones,[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-149) undermining attempts at [encryption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encryption "Encryption") via [Bullrun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullrun_(code_name) "Bullrun (code name)")[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NYT9513-150)[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-register20130905-151) and that the agency was using [cookies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP_cookies "HTTP cookies") to piggyback on the same tools used by Internet advertisers "to pinpoint targets for government hacking and to bolster surveillance."[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-152) The NSA was shown to be secretly accessing Yahoo and Google data centers to collect information from hundreds of millions of account holders worldwide by tapping undersea cables using the [MUSCULAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MUSCULAR_(surveillance_program) "MUSCULAR (surveillance program)") surveillance program.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-autogenerated10-129)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-autogenerated11-130)

The NSA, the [CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIA "CIA") and GCHQ spied on users of _[Second Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second\_Life "Second Life")_, [Xbox Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_Live "Xbox Live") and _[World of Warcraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World\_of\_Warcraft "World of Warcraft")_, and attempted to recruit would-be informants from the sites, according to documents revealed in December 2013.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-153)[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-PCWorldWarCraft-154) Leaked documents showed NSA agents also spied on their own "love interests", a practice NSA employees termed [LOVEINT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LOVEINT "LOVEINT").[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-autogenerated12-155)[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-156) The NSA was shown to be tracking the online sexual activity of people they termed "radicalizers" in order to discredit them.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-157) Following the revelation of Blackpearl, a program targeting private networks, the NSA was accused of extending beyond its primary mission of national security. The agency's intelligence-gathering operations had targeted, among others, oil giant [Petrobras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrobras "Petrobras"), Brazil's largest company.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-158) The NSA and the GCHQ were also shown to be surveilling charities including [UNICEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF "UNICEF") and [Médecins du Monde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9decins_du_Monde "Médecins du Monde"), as well as allies such as [European Commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission")[Joaquín Almunia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joaqu%C3%ADn_Almunia "Joaquín Almunia") and [Israeli Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Prime_Minister "Israeli Prime Minister")[Benjamin Netanyahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu "Benjamin Netanyahu").[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-159)

In October 2013, Glenn Greenwald said "the most shocking and significant stories are the ones we are still working on, and have yet to publish."[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-160) In November, _The Guardian_'s editor-in-chief Alan Rusbridger said that only one percent of the documents had been published.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-161) In December, [Australia's Minister for Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Defence_(Australia) "Minister for Defence (Australia)")[David Johnston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Johnston_(Australian_politician) "David Johnston (Australian politician)") said his government assumed the worst was yet to come.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-162)

By October 2013, Snowden's disclosures had created tensions[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-163)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-164) between the U.S. and some of its close allies after they revealed that the U.S. had spied on [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico"),[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-165)[Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"),[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-166)[China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"),[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-167)[Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"),[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-168) and [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"),[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-169) as well as 35 world leaders,[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-170) most notably [German Chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Chancellor "German Chancellor")[Angela Merkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Merkel "Angela Merkel"), who said "spying among friends" was unacceptable[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-171)[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-172) and compared the NSA with the [Stasi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stasi "Stasi").[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-173) Leaked documents published by _Der Spiegel_ in 2014 appeared to show that the NSA had targeted 122 high-ranking leaders.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-SpiegelPoitrasWorldLeaders-174)

An NSA mission statement titled "SIGINT Strategy 2012–2016" affirmed that the NSA had plans for the continued expansion of surveillance activities. Their stated goal was to "dramatically increase mastery of the global network" and to acquire adversaries' data from "anyone, anytime, anywhere."[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-175) Leaked slides revealed in Greenwald's book _[No Place to Hide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No\_Place\_to\_Hide\_(Greenwald\_book) "No Place to Hide (Greenwald book)")_, released in May 2014, showed that the NSA's stated objective was to "Collect it All," "Process it All," "Exploit it All," "Partner it All," "Sniff it All" and "Know it All."[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-WaPoCollecItAllKnowItAll-176)

Snowden said in a January 2014 interview with German television that the NSA does not limit its data collection to national security issues, accusing the agency of conducting [industrial espionage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_espionage "Industrial espionage"). Using the example of German company [Siemens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siemens "Siemens"), he said, "If there's information at Siemens that's beneficial to US national interests—even if it doesn't have anything to do with national security—then they'll take that information nevertheless."[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ReutersIndustrialEsp-177) In the wake of Snowden's revelations and in response to an inquiry from the [Left Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Left_(Germany) "The Left (Germany)"), Germany's domestic security agency [Bundesamt für Verfassungsschutz (BfV)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Office_for_the_Protection_of_the_Constitution "Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution") investigated and found no concrete evidence that the U.S. conducted economic or industrial espionage in Germany.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-178)

In February 2014, during testimony to the European Union, Snowden said of the remaining undisclosed programs, "I will leave the public interest determinations as to which of these may be safely disclosed to responsible journalists in coordination with government stakeholders."[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-USNewsDisclosures-179)

In March 2014, documents disclosed by Glenn Greenwald writing for _The Intercept_ showed the NSA, in cooperation with the GCHQ, has plans to infect millions of computers with [malware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malware "Malware") using a program called [TURBINE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TURBINE_(US_government_project) "TURBINE (US government project)").[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-InterceptMalware-180) Revelations included information about [QUANTUMHAND](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XKeyscore#Workings "XKeyscore"), a program through which the NSA set up a fake Facebook server to intercept connections.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-InterceptMalware-180)

According to a report in _The Washington Post_ in July 2014, relying on information furnished by Snowden, 90% of those placed under surveillance in the U.S. are ordinary Americans and are not the intended targets. The newspaper said it had examined documents including emails, message texts, and online accounts that support the claim.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NSAusa-181)

In an August 2014 interview, Snowden for the first time disclosed a [cyberwarfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberwarfare "Cyberwarfare") program in the works, codenamed [MonsterMind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MonsterMind "MonsterMind"), that would automate the detection of a foreign [cyberattack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberattack "Cyberattack") as it began and automatically fire back. "These attacks can be [spoofed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spoofing_attack "Spoofing attack")," said Snowden. "You could have someone sitting in China, for example, making it appear that one of these attacks is originating in Russia. And then we end up shooting back at a Russian hospital. What happens next?"[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-BamfordWired-23)

[Video 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/a/ae/PRISM_-_Snowden_Interview_-_Laura_Poitras_HQ.webm/PRISM_-_Snowden_Interview_-_Laura_Poitras_HQ.webm.480p.vp9.webm)

Snowden speaks about the NSA leaks, in Hong Kong, filmed by Laura Poitras.

Snowden first contemplated leaking confidential documents around 2008 but held back, partly because he believed the newly elected Barack Obama might introduce reforms.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-VanityFair-2) After the disclosures, his identity was made public by _The Guardian_ at his request on June 9, 2013.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-politico-journalist-spat-116) "I do not want to live in a world where everything I do and say is recorded ... My sole motive is to inform the public as to that which is done in their name and that which is done against them."[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowdenfirstguardianvideo-120)

Snowden said he wanted to "embolden others to step forward" by demonstrating that "they can win".[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-gellman-recount-117) He also said that the system for reporting problems did not work. "You have to report wrongdoing to those most responsible for it." He cited a lack of whistleblower protection for government contractors, the use of the [Espionage Act of 1917](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Espionage_Act_of_1917 "Espionage Act of 1917") to prosecute leakers and the belief that had he used internal mechanisms to "sound the alarm", his revelations "would have been buried forever".[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Risen-109)[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-182)

In December 2013, upon learning that a U.S. federal judge had ruled the collection of U.S. phone metadata conducted by the NSA as likely unconstitutional, Snowden said, "I acted on my belief that the NSA's mass surveillance programs would not withstand a constitutional challenge, and that the American public deserved a chance to see these issues determined by open courts ... today, a secret program authorized by a secret court was, when exposed to the light of day, found to violate Americans' rights."[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-20131217Times-183)

In January 2014, Snowden said his "breaking point" was "seeing the [Director of National Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_National_Intelligence "Director of National Intelligence"), [James Clapper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clapper "James Clapper"), directly lie under oath to Congress".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ARDtranscript-56) This referred to testimony on March 12, 2013—three months after Snowden first sought to share thousands of NSA documents with Greenwald,[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Maass-110) and nine months after the NSA says Snowden made his first illegal downloads during the summer of 2012[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-VanityFair-2)—in which Clapper denied to the [U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Select_Committee_on_Intelligence "United States Senate Select Committee on Intelligence") that the NSA wittingly collects data on millions of Americans.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-184) Snowden said, "There's no saving an intelligence community that believes it can lie to the public and the legislators who need to be able to trust it and regulate its actions. Seeing that really meant for me there was no going back. Beyond that, it was the creeping realization that no one else was going to do this. The public had a right to know about these programs."[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NDRSnowdenInterview-185) In March 2014, Snowden said he had reported policy or legal issues related to spying programs to more than ten officials, but as a contractor had no legal avenue to pursue further whistleblowing.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-WaPo10reports-82)

Snowden made a number of claims about the [Government Communications Security Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Communications_Security_Bureau "Government Communications Security Bureau") (GCSB) of [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"). He accused the agency of conducting surveillance on New Zealand citizens and engaging in espionage between 2008 and 2016, when [John Key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Key "John Key") served as the [Prime Minister of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_New_Zealand "Prime Minister of New Zealand").[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-186)[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-187)

## Flight from the United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Flight from the United States")]

In May 2013, Snowden quit his job, telling his supervisors he required epilepsy treatment, but instead fled the United States for Hong Kong on May 20. He chose Hong Kong for its "spirited [commitment to free speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_Hong_Kong "Human rights in Hong Kong") and the right of political dissent" at the time.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-guardian-reveal-27)[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-188) Snowden remained in his room at the [Mira Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mira_Hong_Kong "The Mira Hong Kong") after his arrival in the city, rarely going out.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-189)

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Is_Snowden_a_Hero%3F_SnowdenHK_%E9%A6%99%E6%B8%AF%E8%81%B2%E6%8F%B4%E6%96%AF%E8%AB%BE%E7%99%BB%E9%81%8A%E8%A1%8C_Hong_Kong_Rally_to_Support_Snowden_SML.20130615.7D.42298.jpg/250px-Is_Snowden_a_Hero%3F_SnowdenHK_%E9%A6%99%E6%B8%AF%E8%81%B2%E6%8F%B4%E6%96%AF%E8%AB%BE%E7%99%BB%E9%81%8A%E8%A1%8C_Hong_Kong_Rally_to_Support_Snowden_SML.20130615.7D.42298.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Is_Snowden_a_Hero%3F_SnowdenHK_%E9%A6%99%E6%B8%AF%E8%81%B2%E6%8F%B4%E6%96%AF%E8%AB%BE%E7%99%BB%E9%81%8A%E8%A1%8C_Hong_Kong_Rally_to_Support_Snowden_SML.20130615.7D.42298.jpg)

Hong Kong rally to support Snowden, June 15, 2013

Snowden vowed to challenge any extradition attempt by the U.S. government, and engaged Hong Kong-based Canadian human rights lawyer Robert Tibbo as a legal adviser.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-VanityFair-2)[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-190)[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-191) Snowden told the _[South China Morning Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South\_China\_Morning\_Post "South China Morning Post")_ that he planned to remain in Hong Kong for as long as its government would permit.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-southchina-interview-192)[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-193) Snowden also told the _Post_ that "the United States government has committed a tremendous number of crimes against Hong Kong [and] the [PRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") as well",[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-194) going on to identify Chinese Internet Protocol addresses that the NSA monitored and stating that the NSA collected text-message data for Hong Kong residents. Glenn Greenwald said Snowden was motivated by a need to "ingratiate himself to the people of Hong Kong and China".[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-195)

After leaving the Mira Hotel, Snowden was housed for two weeks in several apartments by other refugees seeking asylum in Hong Kong, an arrangement set up by Tibbo to hide Snowden from the US authorities.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-196)[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-197)

The Russian newspaper _[Kommersant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kommersant "Kommersant")_ subsequently reported that Snowden was living at the Russian consulate shortly before his departure from Hong Kong to Moscow.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-198)

[Anatoly Kucherena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoly_Kucherena "Anatoly Kucherena"), who became Snowden's lawyer in July 2013 when Snowden asked him for help in seeking temporary asylum in Russia,[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-GuardianSnowdenMeetsKucherena-199) said in August 2013 that Snowden did not communicate with Russian diplomats while he was in Hong Kong.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-AsiaPacificCubaWontAllowSnowdenToLand-200)[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-tass47-201) In early September 2013, however, Russian president [Vladimir Putin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Putin "Vladimir Putin") said that, a few days before boarding a plane to Moscow, Snowden met in Hong Kong with Russian diplomatic representatives.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-WSJcontact-202)[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-:22-203)

[Ben Wizner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Wizner "Ben Wizner"), a lawyer with the [American Civil Liberties Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_Liberties_Union "American Civil Liberties Union") (ACLU) and legal adviser to Snowden, later disputed this, saying in January 2014, "Every news organization in the world has been trying to confirm that story. They haven't been able to, because it's false."[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Mayer/New_Yorker-204)

On June 22, 2013, 18 days after the publication of Snowden's NSA documents began, officials revoked his U.S. passport.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-205) On June 23, Snowden boarded a commercial [Aeroflot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeroflot "Aeroflot") flight, SU213, to Moscow, accompanied by [Sarah Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Harrison_(journalist) "Sarah Harrison (journalist)") of [WikiLeaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WikiLeaks "WikiLeaks"), with an intended final destination of Ecuador arranged in an Ecuadorian emergency travel document that Snowden had acquired. However, Snowden became initially stranded in Russia upon his landing in Moscow when his U.S. passport was revoked.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NYT:_back_in_the_game-206)[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-207)[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-dm300919-208) Hong Kong authorities said that Snowden had not been detained for the U.S. because the request had not fully complied with Hong Kong law[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-209)[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-210) and there was no legal basis to prevent Snowden from leaving.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-hkce-1-211)[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-hksj-1-212)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-215) On June 24, a U.S. State Department spokesman rejected the explanation of technical noncompliance, accusing the Hong Kong government of deliberately releasing a fugitive despite a valid arrest warrant and after having sufficient time to prohibit his travel.[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Daily_Press_Briefing-216) That same day, [Julian Assange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Assange "Julian Assange") said that WikiLeaks had paid for Snowden's lodging in Hong Kong and his flight out.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-217) Assange also asked Fidel Narváez, consul at the Ecuadorian embassy in London, to sign an emergency travel document for Snowden. Snowden said that having the document gave him "the confidence, the courage to get on that plane to begin the journey".[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-dm300919-208)

In October 2013, Snowden said that before flying to Moscow, he gave all the classified documents he had obtained to journalists he met in Hong Kong and kept no copies for himself.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Risen-109) In January 2014, he told a German TV interviewer that he gave all of his information to American journalists reporting on American issues.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ARDtranscript-56) During his first American TV interview, in May 2014, Snowden said he had protected himself from Russian leverage by destroying the material he had been holding before landing in Moscow.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NBCNews_Motive_Revealed-22)

In January 2019, Vanessa Rodel, one of the refugees who had housed Snowden in Hong Kong, and her 7-year-old daughter were granted asylum by Canada.[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-218) In 2021, Supun Thilina Kellapatha, Nadeeka Dilrukshi Nonis and their children found refuge in Canada, leaving only one of Snowden's Hong Kong helpers waiting for asylum.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-219)

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Edward_Joseph_Snowden_-_Arrival_at_Sheremetyevo_International_Airport_02.jpg/250px-Edward_Joseph_Snowden_-_Arrival_at_Sheremetyevo_International_Airport_02.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_Joseph_Snowden_-_Arrival_at_Sheremetyevo_International_Airport_02.jpg)

Ecuador embassy car at [Sheremetyevo Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheremetyevo_International_Airport "Sheremetyevo International Airport") in Moscow on June 23, 2013

On June 23, 2013, Snowden landed at Moscow's [Sheremetyevo Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheremetyevo_International_Airport "Sheremetyevo International Airport").[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Loiko-220) WikiLeaks said he was on a circuitous but safe route to asylum in [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador "Ecuador").[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-221) Snowden had a seat reserved to continue to [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba")[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Castro-222) but did not board that onward flight, saying in a January 2014 interview that he intended to transit through Russia but was stopped en route. He said "a planeload of reporters documented the seat I was supposed to be in" when he was ticketed for [Havana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana "Havana"), but the U.S Department of State canceled his passport.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Mayer/New_Yorker-204) He said the U.S. wanted him to stay in Moscow so "they could say, 'He's a Russian spy.'"[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Globo-69) Greenwald's account differed on the point of Snowden being already ticketed. According to Greenwald, Snowden's passport was valid when he departed Hong Kong but was revoked during the hours he was in transit to Moscow, preventing him from obtaining a ticket to leave Russia. Greenwald said Snowden was thus forced to stay in Moscow and seek asylum.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-FrontlineUnitedStatesofSecrets-223)

According to one Russian report, Snowden planned to fly from Moscow through Havana to Latin America; however, Cuba told Moscow it would not allow the Aeroflot plane carrying Snowden to land.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-AsiaPacificCubaWontAllowSnowdenToLand-200) The Russian newspaper _Kommersant_ reported that Cuba had a change of heart after receiving pressure from U.S. officials,[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-CSMCubaSaidNoDueToPressureFromUS-224) leaving him stuck in the transit zone because at the last minute Havana told officials in Moscow not to allow him on the flight.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ReutersRussianSourceCubaSaysNoGo-225)_The Washington Post_ contrasted this version with what it called "widespread speculation" that Russia never intended to let Snowden proceed.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-226)[Fidel Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro "Fidel Castro") called claims that Cuba would have blocked Snowden's entry a "lie" and a "libel".[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Castro-222) Describing Snowden's arrival in Moscow as a surprise and likening it to "an unwanted Christmas gift",[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-surprise-227) Russian president Putin said that Snowden remained in the transit area of Sheremetyevo Airport, had committed no crime in Russia, was free to leave and should do so.[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-signals-228)[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-surprise-227)
