Following Snowden's arrival in Moscow, the White House expressed disappointment at Hong Kong's decision to allow him to leave.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-nytimes.com-229)[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-CarneyBriefJun24-230)[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Daily_Press_Briefing-216) An anonymous U.S. official not authorized to discuss the matter told the Associated Press Snowden's passport had been revoked before he left Hong Kong, but that a senior official in a country or airline could order subordinates to overlook the withdrawn passport.[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-APSnowdensPassportRevokedBeforeLeavingHK-231) U.S. Secretary of State [John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry "John Kerry") said that Snowden's passport was canceled "within two hours" of the charges against Snowden being made public[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-KerryPassport-4) which was Friday, June 21.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-wapocharges-3) In a July 1 statement, Snowden said, "Although I am convicted of nothing, [the U.S. government] has unilaterally revoked my passport, leaving me a stateless person. Without any judicial order, the administration now seeks to stop me exercising a basic right. A right that belongs to everybody. The right to seek asylum."[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-232)

Four countries offered Snowden permanent asylum: Ecuador, Nicaragua, Bolivia, and Venezuela.[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-MSNBCFourOffersAsylumLatinAmerica-233) No direct flights between Moscow and Venezuela, Bolivia, or Nicaragua existed, however, and the U.S. pressured countries along his route to hand him over. Snowden said in July 2013 that he decided to bid for asylum in Russia because he felt there was no safe way to reach Latin America.[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ABCSnowdenPromises_RussiaHeWillQuitLeaking-234) Snowden said he remained in Russia because "when we were talking about possibilities for asylum in Latin America, the United States forced down the Bolivian president's plane", citing the [Morales plane incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evo_Morales_grounding_incident "Evo Morales grounding incident"). According to Snowden, "the CIA has a very powerful presence [in Latin America] and the governments and the security services there are relatively much less capable than, say, Russia.... they could have basically snatched me".[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-235) On the issue, he said "some governments in Western European and North American states have demonstrated a willingness to act outside the law, and this behavior persists today. This unlawful threat makes it impossible for me to travel to Latin America and enjoy the asylum granted there in accordance with our shared rights."[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-CNNSnowdenCitesMoralesPlaneIncident-236) Snowden said that he would travel from Russia if there was no interference from the U.S. government.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Mayer/New_Yorker-204)

Four months after Snowden received asylum in Russia, Julian Assange commented: "While Venezuela and Ecuador could protect him in the short term, over the long term there could be a change in government. In Russia, he's safe, he's well-regarded, and that is not likely to change. That was my advice to Snowden, that he would be physically safest in Russia."[[236]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-237)

In an October 2014 interview with _[The Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Nation "The Nation")_ magazine, Snowden reiterated that he had originally intended to travel to Latin America: "A lot of people are still unaware that I never intended to end up in Russia." According to Snowden, the U.S. government "waited until I departed Hong Kong to cancel my passport in order to trap me in Russia". Snowden added, "If they really wanted to capture me, they would've allowed me to travel to Latin America because the CIA can operate with impunity down there. They did not want that; they chose to keep me in Russia."[[237]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-nationinterview-238)

#### Morales plane incident

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Morales plane incident")]

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Grounding_of_Evo_Morales_presidential_plane.svg/250px-Grounding_of_Evo_Morales_presidential_plane.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grounding_of_Evo_Morales_presidential_plane.svg)

Spain, France, and Italy (red) denied Bolivian president [Evo Morales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evo_Morales "Evo Morales") permission to cross their airspace. Morales's plane landed in Austria (yellow).

On July 1, 2013, president [Evo Morales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evo_Morales "Evo Morales") of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), who had been attending a conference in Russia, suggested during an interview with [RT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RT_(TV_network) "RT (TV network)") (formerly Russia Today) that he would consider a request by Snowden for asylum.[[238]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-239) The following day, Morales's plane, en route to [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz"), was rerouted to Austria and landed there, after France, Spain, and Italy denied access to their airspace. While the plane was parked in Vienna, the Spanish ambassador to Austria arrived with two embassy personnel and asked to search the plane but they were denied permission by Morales himself.[[239]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-240) U.S. officials had raised suspicions that Snowden may have been on board.[[240]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-241) Morales blamed the U.S. for putting pressure on European countries and said that the grounding of his plane was a violation of international law.[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-242)

In April 2015, Bolivia's ambassador to Russia, María Luisa Ramos Urzagaste, accused Julian Assange of inadvertently putting Morales's life at risk by intentionally providing to the U.S. false rumors that Snowden was on Morales's plane. Assange responded that "we weren't expecting this outcome. The result was caused by the United States' intervention. We can only regret what happened."[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-243)[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-244)

#### Asylum applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Asylum applications")]

Snowden applied for political asylum to 21 countries.[[244]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Guardian21CountriesAsylum-245)[[245]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-asylum-siliconrepublic-246) A statement attributed to him contended that the U.S. administration, and specifically then–Vice President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"), had pressured the governments to refuse his asylum petitions. Biden had telephoned Ecuadorian President [Rafael Correa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Correa "Rafael Correa") days prior to Snowden's remarks, asking the Ecuadorian leader not to grant Snowden asylum.[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-247) Ecuador had initially offered Snowden a temporary travel document but later withdrew it,[[247]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-248) and Correa later called the offer a mistake.[[248]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-EcuadorBlunder-249)

On July 1, 2013, Snowden accused the U.S. government of "using citizenship as a weapon" and using what he described as "old, bad tools of political aggression". Citing Obama's promise to not allow "wheeling and dealing" over the case, Snowden commented, "This kind of deception from a world leader is not justice, and neither is the extralegal penalty of exile."[[249]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-250) Several days later, WikiLeaks announced that Snowden had applied for asylum in six additional countries, but declined to name them, alleging attempted U.S. interference.[[250]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-251)

After evaluating the law and Snowden's situation, the [French interior ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_the_Interior_(France) "Minister of the Interior (France)") rejected his request for asylum.[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-252)[_[unreliable source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable\_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")_] Poland refused to process his application because it did not conform to legal procedure.[[252]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-20130703thenews-253)[Brazil's Foreign Ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_External_Relations_(Brazil) "Ministry of External Relations (Brazil)") said the government planned no response to Snowden's asylum request. Germany and India rejected Snowden's application outright, while Austria, Ecuador, Finland, Norway, Italy, the Netherlands, and Spain said he must be on their territory to apply.[[253]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-asylumreq-254)[[254]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-255)[[255]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NovumAsylumNL-256) In November 2014, Germany announced that Snowden had not renewed his previously denied request and was not being considered for asylum.[[256]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-TheLocal-257) Glenn Greenwald later reported that [Sigmar Gabriel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigmar_Gabriel "Sigmar Gabriel"), [Vice-Chancellor of Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice-Chancellor_of_Germany "Vice-Chancellor of Germany"), told him the U.S. government had threatened to stop sharing intelligence if Germany offered Snowden asylum or arranged for his travel there.[[257]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-258)

Putin said on July 1, 2013, that if Snowden wanted to be granted [asylum in Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Federation_Law_on_Refugees "Russian Federation Law on Refugees"), he would be required to "stop his work aimed at harming our American partners".[[258]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-259) A spokesman for Putin subsequently said that Snowden had withdrawn his asylum application upon learning of the conditions.[[259]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-260)

In a July 12 meeting at Sheremetyevo Airport with representatives of human rights organizations and lawyers, organized in part by the Russian government,[[260]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-nytimes-261) Snowden said he was accepting all offers of asylum that he had already received or would receive. He added that Venezuela's grant of asylum formalized his legal status as an asylum-seeker, removing any basis for state interference with his right to asylum.[[261]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-20130712Telegraph-262) He also said he would request asylum in Russia until he resolved his travel problems.[[262]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-usatasylum0712-263) Slovenian correspondent Polonca Frelih, the only journalist, who presented at the July 12 meeting with Snowden and photographed him,[[263]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Frelih.org-264) reported that he "looked like someone without daylight for long time but strong enough psychologically" while expressing worries about his medical condition.[[264]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-delo-265) Russian [Federal Migration Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Migration_Service_(Russia) "Federal Migration Service (Russia)") officials confirmed on July 16 that Snowden had submitted an application for temporary asylum.[[265]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-TempAsyl-266) On July 24, Kucherena said his client wanted to find work in Russia, travel and create a life for himself, and had already begun learning Russian.[[266]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-267)

Amid media reports in early July 2013 attributed to U.S. administration sources that Obama's one-on-one meeting with Putin, ahead of a [G20 meeting in St Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_G-20_Saint_Petersburg_summit "2013 G-20 Saint Petersburg summit") scheduled for September, was in doubt due to Snowden's protracted sojourn in Russia,[[267]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-VenezuelaNYT-268) top U.S. officials repeatedly made it clear to Moscow that Snowden should immediately be returned to the United States to face charges for the unauthorized leaking of classified information.[[268]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-disappointing-269)[[269]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-flap-270)[[270]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-Carneybrief-271) His Russian lawyer said Snowden needed asylum because he faced persecution by the U.S. government and feared "that he could be subjected to torture and capital punishment."[[271]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-272)

On April 16, 2020, CNN reported that Edward Snowden had requested a three-year extension of his Russian residency permit.[[272]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-snowden-russian-residency-2020-273)

In October 2020, Snowden was granted permanent residency in Russia. His lawyer said that granting an unlimited residence permit became possible after changes in the migration legislation of the Russian Federation in 2019.[[273]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-274)[[274]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-275)[[275]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-276)

On September 26, 2022, Putin granted Snowden Russian citizenship, making it impossible to extradite him to any country.[[276]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-277)

### Eric Holder letter to Russian justice minister

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Eric Holder letter to Russian justice minister")]

In a letter to Russian Minister of Justice [Aleksandr Konovalov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Konovalov_(judge) "Aleksandr Konovalov (judge)") dated July 23, 2013, U.S. Attorney General [Eric Holder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Holder "Eric Holder") repudiated Snowden's claim to refugee status and offered a limited validity passport good for direct return to the U.S.[[277]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-holderletter-278) He stated that Snowden would not be subject to torture or the death penalty, and would receive a trial in a civilian court with proper legal counsel.[[278]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-NoDeathPenalty-279) The same day, the Russian president's spokesman reiterated that his government would not hand over Snowden, commenting that Putin was not personally involved in the matter and that it was being handled through talks between the FBI and Russia's [FSB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Security_Service "Federal Security Service").[[279]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-280)

 DOJ Press Release

On June 14, 2013, United States federal prosecutors filed a criminal complaint[[280]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-wp-snowden-charged-281) against Snowden, charging him with three felonies: theft of government property and two counts of violating the Espionage Act of 1917 (18 U. S. C. Sect. 792 et. seq.; Publ. L. 65-24) through unauthorized communication of national defense information and willful communication of classified communications intelligence information to an unauthorized person.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-wapocharges-3)[[277]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-holderletter-278)

Specifically, the charges filed in the Criminal Complaint were:

*   18 U.S.C. 641 Theft of Government Property
*   18 U.S.C. 793(d) Unauthorized Communication of National Defense Information
*   18 U.S.C. 798(a)(3) Willful Communication of Classified Intelligence Information to an Unauthorized Person

Each of the three charges carries a maximum possible prison term of ten years. The criminal complaint was initially secret but was unsealed a week later.

### Analysis of Criminal Complaint

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Analysis of Criminal Complaint")]

Stephen P. Mulligan and Jennifer K. Elsea, Legislative attorneys for the [Congressional Research Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Research_Service "Congressional Research Service"), provide a 2017 analysis[[281]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-mulligan-elsea-crs-analysis-282) of the uses of the Espionage Act to prosecute unauthorized disclosures of classified information, based on what was disclosed, to whom, and how; the burden of proof requirements e.g. degrees of [Mens Rea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mens_Rea "Mens Rea") (guilty mind), and the relationship of such considerations to the First Amendment framework of protections of free speech are also analyzed. The analysis includes the charges against Snowden, among several other cases. The discussion also covers gaps in the legal framework used to prosecute such cases.

### Snowden response to Criminal Complaint

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Snowden&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Snowden response to Criminal Complaint")]

Snowden was asked in a January 2014 interview about returning to the U.S. to face the charges in court, as Obama had suggested a few days prior. Snowden explained why he rejected the request:

> What he doesn't say are that the crimes that he's charged me with are crimes that don't allow me to make my case. They don't allow me to defend myself in an open court to the public and convince a jury that what I did was to their benefit. ... So it's, I would say, illustrative that the president would choose to say someone should face the music when he knows the music is a show trial.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-ARDtranscript-56)[[282]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-283)

Snowden's legal representative, [Jesselyn Radack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesselyn_Radack "Jesselyn Radack"), wrote that "the Espionage Act effectively hinders a person from defending himself before a jury in an open court." She said that the "arcane World War I law" was never meant to prosecute whistleblowers, but rather spies who betrayed their trust by selling secrets to enemies for profit.[[283]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden#cite_note-WSJRadackEspionage-284)
